Richardson and colleagues make the CARLA driving simulator reproduce real stop-and-go traffic waves, the phantom jams that ripple through highways without any obvious cause. Instead of calibrating car-following models until waves emerge, they treat recorded traffic from the I-24 MOTION testbed as boundary conditions around one ego vehicle sampled from the data. It sits on an auto-generated one-mile stretch of the I-24 freeway in Tennessee.

A cosimulation module injects the empirical traffic into CARLA around the ego vehicle, simulating visible nearby traffic directly and steering the rest with ghost cells upstream and downstream. The full time-space pattern of the real waves is the target to match. In both low- and high-congestion scenarios the emergent behavior closely mirrored the recorded traffic, giving researchers a perceptually realistic testbed for wave-mitigation controllers and perception-driven autonomy that abstract ring-road simulations cannot provide.
arxiv-2511-23336:
Gernandt and Roschkowski develop two local energy methods for distributed port-Hamiltonian systems. These systems are the energy-based models of physical systems spread along a one-dimensional domain, like strings, beams, and pipelines. They exchange energy with their surroundings through boundary ports. Their goal is a practical test for engineers for exponential stability, whether disturbances die out at a guaranteed exponential rate. The classical criteria require resolvent computations that are often impossible to carry out.

The methods characterize exponential stability directly through the energy that passes across the boundary over a chosen time horizon, generalizing a well-known sufficient condition from the literature. The new characterization succeeds in full on a network of vibrating strings where the older condition cannot be applied at all. The second method dissects the short-time behavior of systems with boundary damping, a regime recently studied under the name hypocoercivity.
arxiv-2512-00236:
Many systems mix a slow, noisy process with a fast, jumpy environment. Hongjiang Qian proves moderate deviation principles for such stochastic differential equations in 2025. The slow process carries small noise, while the fast process is a rapidly changing pure jump process on finitely many states.

Moderate deviation principles describe the probability of rare fluctuations that are larger than typical noise but smaller than extreme events. They refine both central limit behavior and large deviation theory. Results of this kind support risk estimates in physics, finance, and engineering wherever two time scales collide. Two time scales appear in climate, biology, and markets, so the principles travel widely.
arxiv-2512-00536:
Dataset distillation compresses a big training set into a tiny synthetic one that teaches almost as well. Aaryan Gupta, Rishi Saket, and Aravindan Raghuveer provide algorithmic guarantees for distilling datasets in 2025, covering supervised learning and offline reinforcement learning. Models trained on the synthetic set should match those trained on the original.

Guarantees matter because distilled sets are now shared and sold, yet their fidelity is usually judged only by experiments. Provable bounds tell users when a small synthetic dataset can be trusted to stand in for the real thing. That trust underlies cheaper training, dataset sharing under privacy limits, and reproducible benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-00736:
Jacob Thompson, Emiliano Garcia-Lopez, and Yonatan Bisk test how well AI models reason about space in a 2025 paper. People build mental maps that stay stable as they move around. Those maps let us track objects and how they relate, even from a new viewpoint.

The authors argue that large multimodal models, despite heavy video training, lack this basic skill. That gap matters for embodied uses, like robots that act in the world. Their REM evaluation uses multi-frame trajectories, sequences of views along a path, to probe the weakness. A clear test is the first step toward closing the gap.
arxiv-2512-00836:
Emily Howerton and Justin Lessler wrote a 2025 paper on a common planning habit: asking what would happen if. Counterfactual scenarios help leaders plan for outbreaks, policies, and other futures. Yet the projections these exercises produce are rarely checked later against what really happened.

When a projection misses, the error can come from two places. The real world may drift from the assumed scenario, or the model itself may be miscalibrated. Howerton and Lessler work on telling those two apart, which they call assessing model error in counterfactual worlds. The split matters, because each kind of error calls for a different fix.
arxiv-2512-01036:
Breandan Considine describes an exact sampler for small programs in a 2025 paper. The setting is a simply-typed, first-order functional programming language, where every function has a declared type. Sampling a random well-typed function sounds simple, but most random programs fail the type check.

Given a finite automaton that describes allowed shapes, the sampler draws a function uniformly, without replacement, from all well-typed functions the automaton accepts. Uniform sampling matters for testing compilers and program analyzers, since biased samples hide bugs. An exact sampler gives fair coverage of the program space, letting tools be tested against rare cases too.
arxiv-2512-01936:
Driving a physical system slowly and gently wastes the least energy when the path follows the geometry of its control settings. Omer Basri and Oren Raz study in 2025 what happens to that geometric picture near a phase transition, where a substance changes state, such as water turning to steam.

Away from transitions, a Riemannian metric on the control space measures wasted energy, and the best driving paths are its geodesics, the straightest routes. Near a second-order transition the metric blows up and those routes may stop existing. The authors work through this breakdown, which matters for designing efficient processes in systems that must cross a transition.
arxiv-2512-02136:
When a star wanders too close to a black hole, tides shred it in a flare called a tidal disruption event. Kristen Dage and a large team describe AT2022zod in 2025, an unusual such flare in an elliptical galaxy at moderate redshift, valuable because these events reveal otherwise hidden black holes.

Tidal disruptions act as beacons for black holes that emit nothing while idle, letting astronomers census them out to high redshift. AT2022zod's unusual character makes it a stress test for the standard picture of how shredded stars fall back and glow. Each well-observed event sharpens estimates of black hole demographics and behavior across cosmic time.
arxiv-2512-02236:
The Fagnano problem is a classic puzzle: find the inscribed triangle of smallest perimeter inside a given triangle, equivalently a billiard path that closes after three reflections. Maxim Arnold and Jaewoo Park study in 2025 a modified version where the mirror is imperfect and the sides carry different weights.

With weights, the problem becomes a Snell billiard, named for the law governing how light bends at a boundary. The goal is the inscribed triangle of minimal weighted perimeter, or the matching periodic trajectory. The note connects a beloved geometry puzzle to the physics of refraction, showing how a classical answer deforms when reflection turns into bending.
arxiv-2512-02336:
Boston's transit authority, the MBTA, runs trains, subways, and buses whose delays and swinging ridership frustrate riders and planners alike. Sai Siddharth Nalamalpu and three co-authors benchmark in 2025 statistical and machine learning models for forecasting the system's dynamics.

The study compares model families head to head on performance, giving the authority an evidence base for choosing forecasting tools. Ridership swings and delays interact, so a model must capture the system's behavior, not just one series. Dependable forecasts support scheduling, staffing, and the everyday reliability that riders judge transit by.
arxiv-2512-02436:
Prediction markets let folks trade on real-world events. But the field is split by thousands of like contracts. Some say the same thing twice. Some clash in secret. Agostino Capponi, Alfio Gliozzo, and Brian Zhu built an AI pipeline in 2025 to sort them.

The pipeline reads the text and tags of each contract. It groups like markets into clear themes. Then it flags pairs in a group whose outcomes must match or must clash. A cleaner market map makes prices mean more. It also makes clashes free for machines to spot and trade on.
arxiv-2512-02636:
Xinyue Ai and six co-authors make likelihood scores cheaper for diffusion and flow based generators. A likelihood says how probable a sample is under the model, enabling model comparison and some fine tuning. Paradoxically, today's best generators need hundreds or thousands of network runs for one likelihood.

Their joint distillation approach trains a faster stand in for both likelihood evaluation and sampling. Cutting that cost opens downstream uses that were too slow to run before. Cheaper likelihoods could help detect odd samples, rank models fairly, and tune generators with clearer feedback. Fast scores also let teams test new forms of a model on the same day they dream them up.
arxiv-2512-02736:
Sajid Ali, Rajkumar Santra, and Gautam Gangopahyay extract a nuclear property of gallium-72 from capture data. The gamma ray strength function describes how a nucleus emits or absorbs gamma rays. For medium mass, neutron rich nuclei like gallium-72, that function is hard to measure directly.

The team applies Hauser-Feshbach statistical analysis to neutron capture on gallium-71. From the fit they also reevaluate averaged cross sections used at stellar temperatures. Better nuclear data sharpens models of how stars forge elements, and how reactors and detectors behave. Star codes eat such cross checks for lunch, and each new one trims the range of what stars can do.
arxiv-2512-03236:
A supersonic jet can sing a loud, steady tone. Melissa Yeung and Yiyang Sun work on controlling that tone in this 2025 work. Their jet has two streams, a fast core and a slower bypass, which mix into a shear layer.

Shed vortices in that layer cause the high-frequency tone. The authors apply adaptive control in real time to tame the flow. Feedback that adjusts on the fly suits flows that change fast. Quieter, steadier jets matter for aircraft engines and for test rigs on the ground. Real-time feedback suits jets whose tone changes with thrust and flight conditions.
arxiv-2512-03736:
Kenneth Stewart and colleagues report a milestone for space robotics in a 2025 preprint: a learning-based controller flew a free-floating robot in orbit. The robot was NASA's Astrobee, aboard the International Space Station. Controllers trained in simulation often fail on real hardware, and the authors set out to cross that simulation-to-reality gap deliberately.

Their pipeline trained a deep neural network inside a graphics-accelerated physics simulator, using curriculum learning that gradually hardens the task. The trained network replaced Astrobee's standard attitude and translation control, letting the robot navigate in microgravity. Repeated randomised training runs in the simulator checked robustness before upload. The successful flight, the authors argue, shows policies trained on Earth can transfer to space. That matters for future servicing, assembly, and manufacturing work in orbit, where conditions change and controllers must adapt quickly.
arxiv-2512-04236:
Some points on the unit interval are stubbornly hard to approximate, and a game invented by McMullen decides which sets of them are large. David Lambert, David Simmons, and Jiajie Zheng extend that game in a 2025 dynamical systems preprint. They twist the target: at each step, the point's image must avoid not a fixed value but one set by a function that changes with the step.

Their systems are beta-transformations and the Gauss map of continued fractions. For a constant sequence of target functions, the avoiding sets were already known to be winning in McMullen's game, hence of full Hausdorff dimension. The authors prove the same conclusion for every equicontinuous sequence of functions. The twist can therefore vary from step to step, within equicontinuity, without shrinking the exceptional set.
arxiv-2512-04336:
Zhen Liu, Kun-Feng Lyu, and Tong Arthur Wu show that the Large Hadron Collider can test a deep rule of physics called positivity. Positivity bounds say certain particle interaction strengths must stay above zero for any sound theory. Photon pairs offer a clean test bed at colliders. Their 2025 arXiv paper works out how far present and future machines can push the test.

Thanks to spin rules, the lowest-order terms tied to two photons either vanish or face tight limits from other data. The team shows the LHC can, for the first time, probe the next order of terms that involve colored particles. They fit the full pattern of photon-pair angles and energies. The reach runs to a few trillion electron volts at the upgraded LHC. A planned hundred-TeV machine would push past five, giving a sharp check on new physics.
arxiv-2512-04436:
Chen Chen and a team of co-authors present ReFuzz, a testing framework that carries hard-won bug hunts from old chips over to new ones. Chip designs grow by tweaking prior designs, so flaws often echo across generations. Fuzzing, which feeds random inputs to hunt for faults, works well on processors. Yet each new design is usually fuzzed from scratch, ignoring what old tests revealed. Their 2025 arXiv paper closes that wasteful gap.

ReFuzz treats strong tests from prior processors as a reusable stock. A contextual bandit method learns which old tests deserve a try on the chip under test, based on context. It then fine-tunes the hunt toward known flaw families and their new variants. The adaptive loop spends effort where history says bugs hide. That focus can cut the time to find serious flaws in complex new designs, where full testing grows harder each generation.
arxiv-2512-04736:
Rahul Samanta, Santanu Maiti, and Shreekantha Sil study the tiny electric current that circles forever in a quantum ring threaded by magnetic flux. Such persistent currents are a hallmark of mesoscopic physics. The team models electrons that repel each other through Hubbard interactions, both on single sites and between neighbors. Disorder, which scatters electrons, enters as well. Their 2025 arXiv paper mixes exact diagonalization with a Hartree-Fock mean-field treatment inside a tight-binding frame.

A linear table formalism builds the full many-body Hamiltonian, a bookkeeping trick rarely used here. In clean rings, stronger on-site repulsion steadily chokes the current. Extended repulsion acts by filling: at low filling it suppresses the current, while near half filling it boosts the current up to a turning point, then cuts it. Mapping these swings helps design ring devices where interaction is a knob, not a nuisance.
arxiv-2512-05536:
Johannes Ellemose and Niklas Elmqvist ask whether the complexity of a chart can be measured — and find it lives in the beholder. Designers need expressive yet legible charts, but how graphical features drive perceived complexity is poorly understood. The authors crowdsourced human ratings of perceived complexity across diverse charts. They used the ratings as ground truth against which to test automatic estimators.

Three estimators compete: image-analysis metrics, regression on hand-coded chart features, and a large language model asked to rate and extract features with no examples. The image metrics show no correlation with human perception at all. Hand-coding works fairly well but costs heavy effort. The zero-shot language model, by contrast, rates complexity strongly and extracts what matters. The finding suggests perceived complexity, while genuinely subjective, can be matched at scale. The dataset and code are released for a design question that once ran on intuition.
arxiv-2512-05736:
David Ellerman surveys the mathematics behind valuing income producing real estate, and puts its scattered formulas on one footing. Appraisers price such property from the rent it can earn, using capitalization methods with names tied to their inventors: Ellwood, Akerson, and Hoskold among them. The results live in obscure journals and books, and proofs are rarely available to working researchers. His paper gathers, generalizes, and proves them in a unified way.

The material grew out of teaching mathematically trained appraisers in the former Soviet Union and other transition economies. Those countries were building a valuation profession from near scratch. They needed the classical toolkit, including the six functions of a single rate and amortization tables, presented cleanly. Proving the recipes from shared principles shows they are one theory, not competing tricks. It remains a reference on the logic under appraisal.
arxiv-2512-05836:
Clarissa Ong and five co-authors test whether a language model can draft the personalized network maps that some therapists use to plan treatment. Such maps link a client's processes and relationships into one picture guiding treatment choices. Building them demands intensive repeated measurements. The team's pipeline works instead from what already exists: transcripts of therapy sessions.

About eight thousand utterances from seventy seven transcripts were annotated. The model first flags clinically relevant processes and their dimensions, then clusters them into meaningful groups with labels, and finally draws connections between the clusters. Judges' agreement on the quality scores varied widely, from poor to substantial. Still, the generated networks lined up with the original study data and read as coherent and interpretable. The authors stress this is a proof of concept. Whether model drawn maps improve outcomes remains untested. The path to scalable personalization is now visible.
arxiv-2512-05936:
Anne Sielemann and five co-authors build a fully synthetic training set for reading German traffic signs, so that self driving systems can learn rare signs without waiting to photograph them. Real signs weather, and new designs enter the law before they are common on roads. Their pipeline marries two kinds of modeling. A generative network paints realistic textures, complete with wear. An analytical builder places each sign under physically correct lighting, with every parameter recorded.

The dataset holds over one hundred thousand images across two hundred eleven German sign classes, including rare 2020 designs. Each image ships with a mask, a segmentation image, and rich metadata describing the sampled environment and imaging effects. Because every knob is known, the data doubles as a robustness laboratory. Realism was checked against the standard German benchmark and a synthetic rival. Such data makes the long tail of rare signs cheap to test.
arxiv-2512-06036:
Ignacy Nieweglowski, Aviv Yaish, Fahad Saleh, and Fan Zhang study the strangest new asset class in crypto: tokens launched by political figures. PoliFi tokens are memecoins with a ballot attached. The giants are the tokens bearing the names of the forty seventh president and the first lady, TRUMP and MELANIA. The authors track both over time, looking for what moves them.

A pattern they name the Trump Effect emerges: these tokens' behavior correlates positively with presidential approval ratings, a coupling not found for other cryptoassets or other administrations. Politics, priced in real time. Capital also flowed to the Solana blockchain, which saw record volumes. PoliFi tokens fuse political sentiment, speculation, and market infrastructure in one instrument, raising fresh questions for regulators and political scientists alike. Measuring the coupling is the first step to taking it seriously.
arxiv-2512-06136:
Yongzhang Li and M. Kanat Camlibel remove the model from model based control. A network of identical linear systems synchronizes when feedback makes them move as one. The classical route needs the system's equations. When the model is unknown, that route is closed. Data from a single member, plus the known topology, is all they use.

Necessary and sufficient synchronizability conditions come straight from data. A design method then produces the feedback gain from the same data. A simulation illustrates it. The result skips system identification entirely. One system's experiment speaks for the whole network. For fleets of identical units, that is a practical theorem.
arxiv-2512-06436: Roman Stasenko works on Christophersen's problem in the theory of local algebras. He studies a class of finite dimensional Gorenstein algebras and the group formed by their self maps, taking the connected piece of that group around the identity map. Stasenko defines a new subclass of these algebras and proves that, for any algebra in it, that connected group is solvable, a structured kind of group built from simple pieces. The result bears directly on the open problem named in the title.
arxiv-2512-07136:
Siyang Jiang and co-authors release CUHK-X, a large data set for teaching machines to read human activity from many sensors at once. Action recognition from cameras alone misses what depth sensors, body-worn motion units, and radar can add. Worse, the field has labels for actions but few of the rich captions that understanding and reasoning demand, and captions naively spun from labels lack logical and timing consistency.

The collection holds tens of thousands of samples across forty actions, performed by thirty people in two indoor settings. To fix the caption problem, the authors script coherent activity sequences with a language model's help, then have humans validate them. Three benchmark suites cover recognition, understanding, and reasoning across six tasks, with baseline scores reported for each. The hope is that a shared, caption-rich resource will let data-hungry methods mature for multimodal activity analysis.
arxiv-2512-07436:
Hang He and fourteen co-authors wrote this 2025 paper introducing a benchmark for search agents. Modern reasoning models can search across many sources in several steps. Most tests of that skill use general questions, not the messy needs of daily local services.

Their benchmark, LocalSearchBench, covers shops and services people use every day. Its database holds a huge pool of merchant entries across six service types and nine major cities. Its questions come from real user queries and need multi-step reasoning across merchants and products. The team also built LocalPlayground, a shared space where models can use search tools. Even the strongest model tested scored low on correctness. Most models also missed parts of answers or added claims the sources did not support. Local services, the authors argue, need their own benchmarks and training.
arxiv-2512-07636:
Suyin Zheng and Tao Zhou wrote this 2025 physics paper on a new kind of superconductor. The material is a trilayer nickelate, with three nickel-oxide planes stacked together. Its inner and outer planes host different electron behavior, which makes the physics rich.

The authors ask where the pairing that drives superconductivity mainly lives. Pairs might form within one plane or reach across between planes. To tell the two apart, they plant single impurities and watch the response. Their model uses two orbitals with a T-matrix treatment of the impurity. Self-consistent calculations track the local density of states layer by layer. Interlayer pairing leaves parts of the Fermi surface partly gapless. It also produces sharp impurity resonances when the impurity sits in the inner layer. Intralayer pairing instead raises in-gap states with no sharp resonances anywhere. Single-impurity spectroscopy, they conclude, can referee the contest between mechanisms.
arxiv-2512-07736:
Grigori Karagulyan wrote this 2025 mathematics paper in harmonic analysis. Bounded oscillation operators, a class he introduced recently, cover many classic operators at once. Calderón-Zygmund operators, martingale transforms, and maximal operators all belong to the family.

The present paper studies how those operators behave on BMO spaces. BMO measures functions by their average wiggle over balls, not their size. Working on abstract measure spaces, the author first proves new local bounds. Those bounds control what an operator does through oscillations over balls. From them, two mapping results fall out as corollaries. General bounded oscillation operators send bounded functions into BMO. Under a mild logarithmic localization condition, they also map BMO into itself.  Classic operators get BMO bounds from the theory. Wavelet-type systems in Hardy spaces gain unconditional basis properties as well.
arxiv-2512-07836:
Eun Park wrote this 2025 survey paper on Lie algebras over fields of prime characteristic. Theorems that hold over the complex numbers can fail outright in that setting. Galois theory offers the classic warning: change the field, change the facts.

Modular Lie theory is the branch built for the prime-characteristic world. Its signature tool is the p-mapping, an extra operation on the algebra. A Lie algebra equipped with that map is called a restricted Lie algebra. Park walks through how classic theorems bend or break under the new rules. Definitions, properties, and representation behavior are compared across the two worlds. Far from being a poorer cousin, the modular setting reveals new structure. The paper lays out the general framework that organizes those discoveries. It reads as a guided tour for readers raised on characteristic zero. Students of algebra gain a map of where intuition must be relearned.
arxiv-2512-08336:
Aobo Yang, Zhen Wei, Rhea Liem, and Pascal Fua, engineers and computer scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their method, Dflow SUR, improves generative inverse design for aerodynamics, where a model proposes wing or airfoil shapes that must also satisfy physics. Energy based methods guide the generation with a physical loss, but the guidance and the generation process interfere, a mismatch the authors call asynchronous.

Dflow SUR separates the two: the physical loss is optimized apart from the flow matching generation step, by differentiating throughout that process. Against the strongest baseline, it cut the physical loss by orders of magnitude and shortened design time sharply on an airfoil case, and raised lift to drag in wing design. The authors also report better guidance control, lower surrogate uncertainty, and less tuning sensitivity, offering a scalable path for generative engineering design.
arxiv-2512-09036:
Clecio Bom and coauthors investigate the host galaxy of a long gamma ray burst linked to a kilonova candidate,. The transient appeared at a large projected distance from its host, which is unusual. Two explanations are considered: a merger inside a remote globular cluster, or a pair born in the disk whose orbit was changed strongly by natal kicks at birth.

Using space telescope and spectrograph data, the team compares the site with known globular clusters and finds a cluster origin unlikely. They derive the host morphology, stellar mass, gas contribution, and rotation curve, then build a mass model. Travel times for a kicked pair to reach the observed offset are computed and compared with population synthesis simulations. Only a tiny fraction of simulated systems match the galaxy model. A disk origin remains possible, but it requires finely tuned conditions.
arxiv-2512-09136:
Sandro Franceschi, Irina Kourkova, and Maxence Petit study a random diffusion moving through a flat world split into two layers. The upper and lower half-planes have different spread patterns, and both drifts push the process away from the boundary line. They first treat the case where flow is continuous across the seam, then a wider family behaving like an oblique cousin of skew Brownian motion.

The paper gives a detailed theory of this transient process. The authors derive exact Laplace transforms of its Green's functions, work out how those functions decay along every possible path. They also find all positive harmonic functions, identifying both the full and the minimal Martin boundary. Those two boundaries differ, which is unusual for diffusions with regular coefficients. Their method extends the classical kernel technique to three variables, with separate auxiliary variables for the two half-planes.
arxiv-2512-09236:
Sridhar Tayur studies a small change to the rules of quantum mechanics. The change rewrites the link between a system's energy operator and the generator of its phase evolution, adding a term that grows with energy's logarithm. Because the generator is built from the same operator, it keeps the same energy states and does not destroy purity or the probability rule.

Tayur shows the effect is a warping of the energy spectrum, and much of it can hide in a simple rescaling. A single transition frequency cannot reveal the change, and neither can the blurring of an ensemble. The real signal sits in differences between several spectral lines. He describes a spectroscopy protocol for multilevel systems, estimates the precision of a fit, and shows an example. Two warnings apply: the result depends on where energy zero is set, and it holds for one system at a time.
arxiv-2512-09536:
François Rincon argues, in a letter, that the solar dynamo reaches an asymptotic regime when magnetic effects are strong enough. For over forty years, understanding how magnetic fields grow from turbulent flows in rotating bodies like the Sun has been a central problem in astrophysics. Simulations have struggled to say whether their answers reflect physics or their settings.

Scanning parameters in simplified three-dimensional simulations of helical turbulent dynamos, Rincon finds evidence for an ultimate regime at large magnetic Reynolds number. The regime involves fluxes of magnetic helicity between the two hemispheres. Solutions in this regime appear on both sides of a key parameter divide, and only in stripped-down setups. The analysis suggests that all realistic global models to date sit in non-asymptotic regimes that are sensitive to parameter changes. Rincon closes with ideas for reaching the ultimate regime in full spherical models at reasonable cost.
arxiv-2512-09836:
Bernhard Stöckl and Maximilian E. Schüle test whether modern database engines can speed up machine learning on joined tables. Factorized learning avoids repeated work by finding shared partial results, called cofactors, inside a join and computing them once. Earlier studies ran on traditional disk based systems, and their code was never published, so the results could not be checked on in-memory engines. The authors implement factorized learning inside the database and release their code openly.

They benchmark learning a linear regression model on factorized joins in two systems: PostgreSQL, which works from disk, and HyPer, an in-memory engine. Factorized learning on the in-memory system ran about seventy percent faster than ordinary learning there. Against the disk based setup, the gain reached a factor of about one hundred. Databases can thus precompute aggregates before data ever leaves them.
arxiv-2512-10036:
Nimesha Gunasekara and Ebrahim Bedeer study two hardware flaws that can corrupt a promising new radio waveform. The waveform, affine frequency division multiplexing, is a candidate for future networks. Real receivers suffer in-phase and quadrature imbalance, a mismatch between the two signal parts, and leftover carrier frequency offset. The authors analyze how each flaw distorts the effective channel matrix that receivers rely on. The imbalance can destroy the matrix's useful sparsity, through the conjugate step inside the waveform's transform. The frequency error instead leaks energy across the matrix in the affine domain.

To fight back, they extend a standard linear detector so it handles the distorted noise the imbalance creates well. The widened detector treats the noise as improper Gaussian, matching its actual statistics. In tests, the new detector cancels both flaws. The paper gives the new waveform a firmer footing toward real use.
arxiv-2512-10136:
Max Engelstein, Inwon Kim, and Sebastian Munoz prove that the chaotic freezing of supercooled water still has a rigorous structure. The Stefan problem models the boundary between water and ice. In the supercooled case, physics suggests the front can freeze fractally, race at infinite speed, and nucleate ice from nowhere, behavior that defeats classical regularity theory. The authors decompose the free boundary into three parts. One part is regular, advancing at finite speed. A singular part holds points of infinite speed or nucleation, but its space time dimension is controlled. A jump part can be large within one instant, yet lives on a smooth graph and occurs only at isolated times.

The boundary is the graph of a smooth freezing time function, and singularities always occur with infinite speed.
arxiv-2512-10336:
Jules Lahmi and Alexis Roger ask how to give a vision language model a second language. These models, which jointly understand images and text, are trained overwhelmingly in English, leaving most of the world's speakers with weaker tools. The authors take an English trained model and adapt it to French, comparing three strategies honestly on performance and computational cost. They compare dataset translation, low rank adapter tuning, and two stage fine tuning.

Evaluation mixes standard multimodal benchmarks translated into French with manual judgments by native speaking experts. The headline finding is a bottleneck diagnosis: dataset translation quality, not model capacity or tuning strategy, limits multilingual performance, and it degrades both training and evaluation. A benchmark translated badly cannot tell a good model from a bad one. The authors conclude that future progress depends on collecting native language datasets and improving translation strategies, rather than on cleverer adaptation recipes alone.
arxiv-2512-10436:
Anastasiia Chyzhykova, Jeroen van den Brink, and Flavio Nogueira describe a strange effect predicted by axion electrodynamics, the rules governing how a topological insulator answers electric and magnetic fields. Place a small charged probe near a spherical insulator, they show. And the sphere begins to rotate around the line joining its centre to the charge.

The spin appears when the charge's distance from the centre changes, driven by the static fields the charge induces. The authors work out the rotation rate in terms of the sphere's moment of inertia, the fine-structure constant. And the geometry, stated here in words rather than symbols. They also compute the angular momentum of the Hall currents the charge stirs on the surface, and from it an exact expression for how fast surface electrons move.
arxiv-2512-10736:
Bartosz Dziewit, Marek Zrałek, and Joris Vergeest fit lepton masses and mixing with a patterned Higgs sector. Their model has three Higgs doublets that transform as a triplet under the A4 flavour group, a symmetry famous from neutrino model building. The question is whether that single pattern can reproduce the measured neutrino mixing angles and the ordering of lepton masses at once.

Under A4, the lepton mass matrices match the experimental mixing angles to arbitrary precision while keeping the correct ordering, with the neutral leptons as Dirac neutrinos in the normal spectrum. Curiously, the vacuum values that fit the masses differ from those that fit the mixing matrix. The authors also searched every group of order up to six hundred for a better contraction pattern. They found none. That makes the A4 solution unique within the set studied. It is a tidy endorsement of the flavour-symmetric route.
arxiv-2512-10836:
Olga Lezhnina, Manuel Prinz, and Markus Stocker build a tool that writes up data analysis in a form machines can read from the start. Science aims to be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, yet findings are usually published as prose and mined back into data afterward. The authors flip the order: capture the analysis in machine-readable form while it is being done, before publication.

Their package, dtreg, ships for both Python and R. It works with registered, persistently identified data type schemata covering the most common statistical tests and machine learning methods. A user downloads the relevant schema as an editable object, fills it with the metadata of their analysis, and converts it into a lightweight linked data format. A worked example, a t-test on the classic Iris dataset, shows the flow, and the authors pitch dtreg as a practical way to honour the FAIR principles.
arxiv-2512-10936:
Kristina Korotkova and Aleksandr Katrutsa build adversarial examples with optimiser mathematics instead of folklore. Fooling a neural network with a crafted input change is the standard way to measure its robustness, and making those attacks is an optimisation problem. The usual recipes lean on projections or geometric intuition; the authors ask whether projection-free Frank-Wolfe methods, in their modern modified forms, do the job better.

They evaluate the idea in theory and in practice, as a white-box attack where the attacker knows the model. Experiments span the MNIST and CIFAR-10 image benchmarks and three model families. Multinomial logistic regression, convolutional networks, and a vision transformer. The authors compare against standard projection-based and geometry-based attacks. The comparison shows where the Frank-Wolfe approach stands on efficiency and success. It is evidence for anyone who benchmarks robustness. Such readers need attacks that are both fast and honest.
arxiv-2512-11236:
Kinfe Teweldebirhan, Rituparna Curt, and Nicholas Featherstone simulate how uneven heating at the base of a star's convection zone reshapes its spin. The study is motivated by the Sun's near surface shear layer, where flows shift from buoyancy driven near the top to spin dominated at depth. They imposed a heat flux that varies with latitude in the opposite sense to what the system would develop naturally.

Three in extent spherical model runs covered both fast and slow spin regimes. Without forcing, a strong thermal wind balance held in both. Stronger imposed variation strengthened that balance at high latitudes, weakened it at low latitudes, and eventually reversed the latitude pattern of differential spin. Above a certain spin threshold, convection mixed heat sideways efficiently enough that the imposed pattern never reached the surface. The results help explain the Sun's muted surface spin contrast and even brightness across latitudes.
arxiv-2512-11436:
Zbigniew Ficek studies two coupled bosonic modes, such as light fields in cavities, that exchange energy in two ways at once. A linear hopping interaction and a nonlinear squeezing interaction act simultaneously, while the environment drains the system. Although the underlying dynamics is conventional, the equations for the field's components behave as if the system were non Hermitian, with lopsided coupling.

That asymmetry produces striking effects. A special exceptional point governs how heat like states convert into squeezed states of a single mode, with noise suppressed in one direction. When the reservoirs themselves are squeezed, their photon pair correlations drive one way flows of population and correlation between the modes, controllable by rotating the squeezing direction. The population flow creates coherence while blocking entanglement growth. Ficek suggests applications in making squeezed light and steering transfer along bosonic chains.
arxiv-2512-11636:
Anton V Khvalyuk and Mikhail V Feigel'man explain a loss that plagues devices made from messy superconductors. Such films power qubits, sensors, and photon detectors. At low heat they waste microwave energy in ways the standard Mattis-Bardeen theory cannot explain, since their energy spectrum holds a hard gap.

The pair build a micro level theory for how losses vary with heat and frequency. They find a new kind of bulk mode, born from patchy order in the film, that soaks up energy. It makes quality factors drop fast as frequency rises. The theory fits films like indium oxide and titanium nitride, and it points to ways to cut losses in quantum gear.
arxiv-2512-12236:
Aujasvit Datta, Jiayun Wang, Asad Aali, and Anima Anandkumar present a neural operator for CT scans in a 2025 paper. Sparse view CT uses few X-ray shots to cut radiation and scan time, but rebuilding the image is then hard. Older networks fit one scan setup and fail when sampling rates or image sizes change.

Their model, CTO, learns in a continuous space, so one model works across sampling rates with no retraining. It works in both signal and image domains and uses rotation aware filters. CTO beat standard networks by over 3.4 dB PSNR in mixed settings. It also ran 500 times faster than top diffusion methods, with about 3 dB gain.
arxiv-2512-12336:
R Yu Korolkov and three co-authors study tiny egg shaped particles made of metal and dielectric in a 2025 paper. Such nanoeggs absorb and scatter light in ways set by their size and shape. Surface plasmon resonance, a collective electron wobble, gives them strong responses at certain colors of light.

The authors compute how polarizability, absorption, and scattering cross-sections vary with frequency. They derive formulas for how resonance frequencies shift with size, and explain blue and red shifts in peaks. They also track changes in peak number and height. The paper ends with advice on which materials give the best radiation efficiency in each spectral range.
arxiv-2512-12436:
Bartlomiej Starosta and six co-authors improve explanations for spectral graph clustering in a 2025 paper. Spectral clustering groups items, such as text documents, by embedding them in a spectral space. That space has no clear link to document content, so users struggle to see why a cluster formed. Unclear documents and random elements in the algorithms make explanations worse.

Their method draws on rough set theory, which handles vague boundaries between groups. It builds on the team's earlier explanation approach and is designed to beat both problems: the odd embedding space and the noise from unclear items. The goal is clustering that users can inspect and trust, with reasons stated in content terms.
arxiv-2512-12636:
Enso O Torres Alegre derives the Born rule from causal consistency in a 2025 paper. The Born rule gives the chance of a quantum outcome from the overlap of states. Alegre works in generalized probabilistic theories, a broad framework that includes quantum theory as one case. It separates a geometric transition chance from the predicted chance assigned to outcomes.

He asks which link between the two can respect causality in relativity. In theories that admit steering, only the identity link avoids faster than light signaling; any curved deviation enables it. A worked qubit example shows how curved rules create signaling channels. Combined with known rebuilding results, the Born rule emerges as the unique causally sound rule.
arxiv-2512-12836:
Harri Hakula, Oona Rainio, and Matti Vuorinen study conformal capacity, a number that helps describe shapes in the plane. They look at a bounded region that holds a compact connected set. Exact capacity values are known in only a few special cases, so good estimates matter.

The authors focus on maze-like shapes and compute capacity with a high-order finite element method. They compare the results with estimates based on length and perimeter ideas. Across their tests, the estimates behaved as hoped as maze walls moved closer to the inner set. They also proved far faster to use once the case work was done.
arxiv-2512-13336:
Karim Bounja, Lahcen Laayouni, and Abdeljalil Sakat present KD-PINN, a method that compresses physics-informed neural networks for very fast real-time use. Physics-informed networks solve partial differential equations by training a network to obey the equation itself. They are accurate but often too slow for live control or edge devices.

Knowledge distillation trains a small student network to mimic a larger trained teacher. Applied here, the student keeps the physics behavior while running at ultra-low latency. The goal is a solver that can answer in real time inside loops such as control, monitoring, or digital twins. The work targets settings where full physics-informed models cannot meet timing demands.
arxiv-2512-13436:
Friederike Butt, Lars Esser, and Markus Muller improve the decoding of three-dimensional color codes, a family of quantum error-correcting codes prized for their built-in non-Clifford gates. Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs efficient decoders, and 3D color codes had lagged there despite their gate advantages.

They extend a restriction decoder from two dimensions to three, including code boundaries. The method confines the decoding problem to part of the qubit lattice before solving it. It achieved a noise threshold of about 1.55 percent for bit and phase flip noise, nearly double earlier values for this family, with optimal error scaling. A companion Python tool visualizes codes and decoding paths.
arxiv-2512-14236:
Nando Metzger, Prune Truong, Goutam Bhat, Konrad Schindler, and Federico Tombari present Elastic3D in a 2025 paper on stereo video conversion. Demand for immersive 3D content is growing, and turning a normal single view video into a two view stereo video by hand is slow.

Elastic3D does the conversion end to end with a latent diffusion model, avoiding depth estimation and warping, which often cause artifacts. A guided VAE decoder keeps the output sharp and consistent between the two eyes. Users can also set the strength of the stereo effect with a simple scalar knob at run time. On three real world stereo datasets, the method beat both classic warping and newer warping free baselines.
arxiv-2512-14836:
Felix Forner and Felix Tellander tackle a bookkeeping problem in quantum field theory called kinetic mixing. When two fields share the same quantum numbers, their motion terms can mix, which muddles the math. Such mixing matters for models with a dark photon, a heavy cousin of the photon that barely interacts.

The authors study two U(1) gauge bosons in an extension of QED, at one loop order. A field rotation removes the mixing, yet the leftover divergences cannot be canceled by a standard counterterm, and still the theory stays renormalizable. They show that gauge dependent parts which seem to block the cleanup cancel out. Two schemes, one with mixing and one without, turn out to be the same scheme in disguise.
arxiv-2512-14936:
Qiaohong Wang and nine coauthors marry a quantum sampling method to a classical chemistry framework. The framework, LASSCF, splits a molecule into fragments and solves each fragment's electrons exactly, which is accurate but grows costly fast. Strongly correlated systems, where electrons interact intensely, are exactly where such tools are needed most.

Their hybrid, LASSQD, lets a quantum computer sample electron arrangements for each fragment, while a classical machine cleans errors and solves the fragment problem in that sampled space. On two iron based compounds, the method handled fragment sizes beyond the classical version's reach. Its energies landed within 1 kilocalorie per mole of the classical results. A follow up correction step can then recover effects from outside the active space, making the pair a practical route to hard chemistry.
arxiv-2512-15136:
Hiroshi Kobayashi and three coauthors model what happens when two Mars sized worlds collide. Planet building ends in giant impacts that can merge the pair, let one flee in a hit and run, or shatter both. The team ran smooth particle hydrodynamics simulations, varying impact speed, angle, and mass ratio to map those outcomes.

From the runs they build an analytic model based on characteristic energies, above all the energy dumped into the overlapping region of the two bodies. The model predicts the masses of the largest and second largest remnants and captures the borders between merging, hit and run, and disruption better than earlier models. Formulas averaged over likely impact angles make it ready for planet formation codes. It even matches dust aggregate collision results, so it may span from pebbles to planets.
arxiv-2512-15536:
Andres Castillo Castellanos and co authors study how Faraday surface waves mix two fluids in a 2025 paper. Two miscible fluids with a small density gap mix slowly on their own. Shaking the container up and down can excite standing Faraday waves at the interface, and the team asks how those waves speed mixing.

In experiments and simulations, the waves move the interface and can trigger secondary instabilities. Pushed harder, large crests collapse into cavities that inject bubbles and light fluid deep into the heavy layer. Mixing first speeds up, then slows as less energy enters the weakened surface. A one dimensional model with depth dependent turbulent diffusivity captures the qualitative evolution.
arxiv-2512-15636:
Gergely Hajdu and co authors report RR Lyrae stars whose average brightness varies in survey data in a 2025 paper. RR Lyrae are pulsating stars used as distance markers, and their mean magnitudes were long assumed steady. Odd changes in the OGLE survey were usually blamed on photometry problems rather than the stars.

Using long, overlapping light curves from several microlensing surveys plus infrared data, the team confirms 72 stars where the variation is most likely real. Brightness changes in the V and I bands fit variable dust extinction in most cases, though no infrared excess appears. After selection corrections, about 0.9 percent of bulge RR Lyrae show the effect.
arxiv-2512-15736:
S. K. Rithvik presents Anubuddhi, a multi agent AI system that designs and models quantum optics tests from plain language prompts, in a 2025 paper, dated December 6. Building such experiments normally demands expert coding skill. Anubuddhi aims to open computer based experiment design to students and researchers without that background.

The system arranges components from a three tier toolbox by semantic retrieval, then checks designs through physics modeling with repeated refinement. It was tested on 13 tests, from Hong Ou Mandel interference and Bell states to boson sampling and quantum teleportation. Design and model match scores reached 8 to 9 out of 10. A key lesson separates structural soundness from numeric accuracy, which still needs expert review.
arxiv-2512-16136:
Zhisheng Hu and five co-authors present a database system in their 2025 arXiv paper. Disaggregated memory splits computing from storage, so each can scale on its own. Transactions across that split rely on fast one-sided network operations, and the authors found a bottleneck: the memory nodes' network cards drown in tiny lock operations.

Their system, Lotus, moves locks onto the compute nodes instead, sharded in a way that follows the workload's locality while staying balanced. A lock-first protocol grabs all locks at the start, so clashes abort early. Locks are treated as disposable, so a failed node needs no lock rebuilding. In experiments, Lotus raised transaction throughput by up to 2.1 times and cut latency by up to 49.4 percent versus leading systems.
arxiv-2512-16236:
Tejul Pandit and three co-authors survey search technology in work posted to arXiv in 2025, accepted to a 2025 language technology conference. Reranking is the stage of a search system that reorders an initial list of candidate documents to put the best matches on top. It matters even more inside retrieval-augmented generation, where an AI's answer depends on the documents it is fed.

The authors trace rerankers from early rule-based heuristics to neural cross-encoders, sequence models like T5, and graph neural networks that use document structure. They cover knowledge distillation, a way to shrink big models into fast ones without losing much quality. The final section maps how large language models are entering reranking, through prompting tricks and fine-tuning, and weighs accuracy, cost, and speed trade-offs across all the families.
arxiv-2512-16636:
Giorgos Petsangourakis and coauthors present REGLUE, a way to teach image diffusion models richer meaning. Latent diffusion models learn to clean noisy images, but meaning seeps in slowly from that task alone, which drags training and caps quality.

REGLUE trains one backbone on three streams at once: image latents, patch-level meaning from vision foundation models, and a global image token. A small convolutional packer squeezes multi-layer meaning into a compact form, and an alignment loss pulls inner states toward frozen teacher targets. On ImageNet at 256 by 256, REGLUE beat SiT baselines and prior alignment tools on FID scores and trained faster, with spatial meaning and nonlinear packing doing the heavy lifting.
arxiv-2512-16836:
Debarghya Chakraborty and Dario Rosa build quantum many-body scar states in split systems where the two halves have perfectly linked Hamiltonians. Scar states are rare orderly states inside a mostly chaotic spectrum, and they cause a system to revive instead of settling down.

A Krylov build gives an interaction term that holds a tower of evenly spaced energy states. Any start state that purifies a balance state then revives after a fixed time, with motion set by broad traits, not fine details. The two-sided chord states of double-scaled SYK theory give a near copy of the setup. Analysis and numerics agree that wavepackets ride rigidly along one SYK spectrum.
arxiv-2512-16936:
Sanjay Shukla, Marc E. Brachet, and Rahul Pandit review the Gross-Pitaevskii-Poisson framework for self-gravitating superfluids, systems where a quantum fluid pulls on itself by its own gravity. The frame covers boson and axion stars and dark matter haloes built from such matter.

The overview shows how the same equations give minimal models of neutron stars and pulsars, including their glitches. Vortices in the neutron superfluid are tracked alongside flux tubes in the proton superconductor part. Maxwell equations for the field and a Poisson equation for self-gravity complete the coupled model, making the review a compact entry point to a wide field.
arxiv-2512-17036:
Yuan-Hung Kuan and Jr-Shin Li develop EBIF, an Exact Bilinearization Iterative Form that turns a nonlinear control-affine system into an exact finite bilinear model. Most past routes give infinite-dimensional copies, which are hard to use for control design.

EBIF builds, step by step, a finite set of smooth coordinate functions that embed the system exactly in bilinear form. Using algebra and differential geometry, the pair proves when a system can and cannot be exactly bilinearized, with matching necessary and sufficient terms. Bilinear copies ease reachability analysis and control synthesis. Theory and simulations show the frame working, a route to simpler control of nonlinear systems.
arxiv-2512-17236:
Hibiki Nakada and three co-authors study what happens when a fast proton or deuteron strikes an atomic nucleus and knocks one proton out. Experiments show the deuteron knocks out about 1.5 times as many protons as a lone proton does. That edge is real, but it is smaller than simple reasoning would suggest, and no one had pinned down why.

The team models both reactions with a method called DWIA and adds a new step for the deuteron: it can break apart mid-flight. With breakup included, the computed ratio matches the measured 1.5 well. Without it, the model falls short. The gap, they find, comes from breakup plus how much each projectile gets absorbed on the way in.
arxiv-2512-17436:
Jiaze Li and a Xiaomi team release MiMo-VL-Miloco-7B, an open vision-language model tuned for the smart home. Built on Xiaomi's MiMo-VL-7B base, it watches rooms and clips, names what people are doing, and reads hand gestures. The team also ships a smaller quantized copy and a public test kit for home scenes.

Training ran in two stages: guided fine-tuning, then reinforcement learning that rewards better answers. Extra supervision taught the model to reason step by step while watching its token budget. On home-scene tests it posted leading scores for gestures and daily activity reading. It also gained on broad video and language benchmarks, trading a little skill only on document-heavy tasks.
arxiv-2512-18036:
Connor Weyers and N. V. Vinodchandran revisit a guessing game for fractions. A hidden fraction sits between 0 and 1, its bottom number no larger than a known cap. Each question asks only whether a test value is at or below the hidden one, and the aim is to name it fast.

Their method walks a classic tree of fractions, the Stern-Brocot tree, in a compressed way that past work had missed. The same walk solves two fresh twists: the cap is unknown, or the target is any real number and the goal is its best fraction match. Clean tools for such searches matter wherever exact ratios hide behind yes or no tests.
arxiv-2512-18136:
Srishti Singh and Hema Srinivasan study Sally type semigroups, sets of whole numbers closed under addition whose smallest generator is e and whose generators all lie between e and 2e minus 1. Each such semigroup has a ring, and the paper maps the ideals that define those rings.

When the embedding dimension is e minus 2, they show the defining ideal is generically a sum of two determinantal ideals. More general members arise by deleting k integers from the generating interval. They prove that the semigroup built by deleting a block of k consecutive integers starting at j is Gorenstein exactly when j equals k, for k below half of e. For that Gorenstein case they build an explicit minimal free resolution and compute its Betti numbers, and they characterize symmetry across the family.
arxiv-2512-18436:
Chenyuan Yang and four co-authors test whether large language models can prove that system software is correct. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, focuses on programs written in Rust and checked with the Verus verifier. They built VeruSAGE-Bench, a benchmark of 849 proof tasks drawn from eight open-source verified Rust systems.

The team paired different models, including GPT-5 and Sonnet 4.5, with agent setups tuned to each model's strengths. The best pairing finished over 80 percent of the benchmark tasks. It also solved over 90 percent of a separate set of proof tasks that human experts had not yet finished. The study suggests AI agents could take on much of the proof work in verified software.
arxiv-2512-18636:
Yuri Fukaya, Keiji Yada, and Yukio Tanaka study a hybrid material in this 2025 superconductivity paper. They combine a p-wave unconventional magnet, whose spins form a noncollinear pattern, with an ordinary s-wave superconductor. Using an effective model from earlier work, they compute the surface density of states. The spin pattern gives the energy gap a spin-triplet p-wave shape, and zero-energy flat bands appear at one crystal edge.

At that edge, odd-frequency spin-triplet pairing is induced alongside the usual even-frequency singlet pairing. The team also computes the Josephson current through junctions of the hybrid, finding a phi-junction behavior at high transparency. The results map the transport signatures such hybrids could show in experiments.
arxiv-2512-19336:
Siyuan Mei, Yan Xia, Fuxin Fan, and Andreas Maier synthesize CT scans from MRI and cone-beam CT images with one unified network. Treatment planning for adaptive radiotherapy needs CT-quality anatomy, yet the scan at hand is often another kind. GANeXt, a generative adversarial network built fully from ConvNeXt blocks, does both conversions.

The generator is a three-dimensional U-shaped stack of small-kernel blocks, and a patch discriminator judges local realism. Training mixes plain, perceptual, masked, and adversarial losses, plus a segmentation head with its own losses. The design aims to serve many body regions and both source types with a single model, a practical gain for clinics.
arxiv-2512-19436:
H. A. Harutyunian and E. H. Nikogosyan argue that galaxy clusters must slowly expand, because baryonic matter gains energy through its interaction with dark energy. In their view the claim holds at every level of cosmic structure. They propose a simple statistical method to spot radial motions of galaxies inside a cluster.

The Virgo cluster serves as the test case. Its substructure resolves into galaxy groups of varied size, whose members run brighter than the cluster average and each hold an active galaxy. Inside the groups, brighter average magnitude pairs with higher average velocity. The authors read that correlation as evidence of expansion, and the groups as ejections from a central galaxy.
arxiv-2512-19736:
Gongli Xi leads an eight-author team on a practical data problem. Real network shapes are scarce. So researchers make synthetic graphs with set traits, for tests or for release. Past diffusion-based tools had flaws. Some baked the traits in and needed retraining for each new trait. Others steered after training, with no grip on scale or real-world limits.

Their tool, CoPHo, steers the diffusion while it runs. It feeds gradients from a trained graph classifier into the reverse steps. A tool from topology, persistent homology, reads the shape of each draft graph. Those readings act as guide signals at each step. On four data sets, CoPHo matched target traits better than past methods. It also moved well to the QM9 molecule data set. The work was accepted at KDD 2026.
arxiv-2512-19836:
Elisabeth Werner and Diliya Yalikun define new ways to measure the surface of a ball-convex body, a convex shape cut out by balls rather than half-spaces. Their L_p relative surface areas are shown to be valuations unchanged by rigid motions, placing them in a classical family of geometric functionals with well-understood algebraic manners. Inequalities for the new quantities follow.

A monotonicity property of these measures leads the authors to a fresh notion of entropy for ball-convex bodies. They also introduce a weighted ball floating body, a shrunken inner companion shape, and prove that differentiating volume along that shrinking recovers the L_p relative surface areas geometrically. The construction mirrors how ordinary surface area arises from floating bodies in classical convexity.
arxiv-2512-20436:
Muhammad Usman and co-authors segment stroke lesions in diffusion MRI scans with a dual-encoder Transformer. Diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient maps show complementary views of acute and subacute damage. Separating them by hand is slow, and lesion appearance varies enough to defeat simple rules.

Working on the ISLES 2022 dataset, the team first benchmarks U-Net variants, Swin-UNet, and TransUNet under one training approach. Transformers beat the convolutional benchmarks. Their proposed design gives each modality its own encoder inside a TransUNet and feeds three adjacent slices for spatial context. The dual-encoder model tops the comparison, reaching a strong Dice score on the test set. Automated delineation of this quality can speed clinical assessment.
arxiv-2512-20536:
Alex Chen Yi Zhang, Pablo Mateu Hoyos, David Brückner, and Gašper Tkačik ask how embryos could read position more precisely by sharing information. Cells infer where they are from morphogen concentrations, but noise limits that readout. Communication between cells offers nonlocal information that might sharpen the estimate.

In a Bayes-optimal approach, the answer hinges on the spatial correlations of the morphogen field and on the structural prior describing the cellular lattice. The authors bound how much positional information nonlocal readout can add. They then exhibit signal-processing methods that nearly achieve the optimum, plus simple chemical reaction schemes that implement them. The theory says correlational information, often ignored, can significantly raise developmental precision.
arxiv-2512-20636:
Dhananjay Saikumar and Blesson Varghese delete whole attention layers from language models using nothing but the weights. Their premise, the attention suppression hypothesis, says some deep attention layers learn during pretraining to mute themselves, leaving the residual stream and feed-forward layers to carry the representation. Those layers should be safe to remove.

Their criterion, Gate-Norm, ranks attention sublayers by query-key coupling and cuts the least coupled, with no calibration data, no forward passes, and no fine-tuning. On a forty-layer, thirteen-billion-parameter LLaMA model the scoring takes under a second. Removing eight to sixteen layers raises throughput by up to about thirty percent while zero-shot accuracy barely moves. The method matches data-driven pruners at a thousandth of the scoring cost.
arxiv-2512-20736:
Hamid Afshar and Mehdi Ahmadi-Jahmani work on Carrollian gravity, a version of gravity suited to settings where light cones collapse and motion behaves very differently from everyday physics. They add matter and a scaling symmetry, then recast the whole setup as a gauge theory, a framework that builds theories from symmetry rules.

Their construction loosens one conformal symmetry and enlarges the set of gravity fields. After fixing the scaling freedom, a few fields govern the theory, including a vector field tied to size changes. Suitable gauge choices then recover several known descriptions, among them Carrollian and Aristotelian pictures. The result unifies views that looked separate before.
arxiv-2512-20836:
Lachlan McGinness asks what a good concept test for quantum computing should contain. Concept inventories, standardized question sets that expose student misconceptions, have improved teaching in other fields. Quantum computing needs one as its workforce grows, but the subject's heavy mathematics raises doubts about what can be tested without it.

McGinness interviewed eight experts across quantum computing, communication, and sensing. They agreed substantial non-mathematical content exists and sketched a first list of key concepts. Building the inventory remains hard: questions must avoid jargon, stay valid, and suit students who have not yet studied quantum mechanics. The paper frames both the promise and the international teamwork the task demands.
arxiv-2512-21336:
Masked diffusion models generate text by unmasking tokens in any order, and Ziyu Chen, Xinbei Jiang, Peng Sun, and Tao Lin show the order matters enormously. They trace output quality to the predictive uncertainty accumulated along a generation path. Their measure, denoising entropy, turns that uncertainty into a number the model itself can supply.

Two algorithms put the measure to work: one picks the best finished path after the fact, the other steers generation live. Both lift accuracy on reasoning, planning, and code benchmarks. The result recasts a weakness of flexible decoding as a control signal. For builders of diffusion language models, path choice becomes an optimizable design decision rather than a coin flip.
arxiv-2512-21436:
Chinmay Giridhar, Philipp Vojta, Zohar Nussinov, Gerardo Ortiz, and Andriy H. Nevidomskyy develop the fusion rules of topological defects in a quantum lattice model. The symmetries are generalized and non-invertible, beyond ordinary group ones. Such symmetries produce exotic phases of matter outside the classic Landau picture.

The test case is a two-dimensional quantum Ising plaquette model with extra subsystem symmetries that act only on lower-dimensional slices. Combining bond-algebraic automorphisms with half-gauging, the authors expose the model's duality symmetry operators as an explicit quantum circuit. The rigid subsystem symmetries restrict how the resulting defects can move. The team then establishes the fusion algebra of these defects, the rules for combining them. They also verify the duality transformation acts as a partial isometry, matching a recent generalization of Wigner's theorem for non-invertible symmetries.
arxiv-2512-21536:
Yuan Li, Qiaoyuan Cheng, and Engui Fan prove that solutions of the Fokas-Lenells equation exist for all time, for a wide class of starting data. The Fokas-Lenells equation is a nonlinear wave equation used to model ultrashort light pulses in optical fibers. Their result covers any initial data in certain weighted Sobolev spaces, which control both smoothness and decay at infinity.

Earlier work by the same team needed extra spectral restrictions on the initial data. The new proof removes those restrictions entirely. It relies on the inverse scattering transform, recast as new Riemann-Hilbert problems, together with Zhou's bijectivity theory for such problems in square-integrable Sobolev spaces. Global existence results of this kind matter because they certify that the model's predictions never blow up in finite time.
arxiv-2512-21736:
Xindi Zhang, Bang Zhang, and their co-authors present SyncAnyone, a system for lip-syncing video to audio in uncontrolled footage. Dubbing demands accurate lip motion, sharp image quality, and preservation of identity and background. The standard training trick, masking the mouth and asking the model to repaint it, breaks the surrounding context and causes flicker and drift.

SyncAnyone works in two stages. First, a diffusion-based video transformer learns masked mouth inpainting, using its space-time modeling to generate audio-driven lip movements. Some artifacts remain around the face and background because the input was corrupted. In the second stage, the team builds synthetic training pairs by lip-syncing source videos to sampled audio, then fine-tunes the model without a mask. This self-correction pass teaches precise lip editing with consistent backgrounds. Experiments show state-of-the-art quality, temporal coherence, and identity preservation.
arxiv-2512-22136:
Mahadev Sunil Kumar and five co-authors present SlimEdge, a way to spread deep neural networks across weak edge devices without breaking them. Edge hardware has little memory and computing power, and devices can fail mid-task. Their method prunes the network in a structured way while optimizing several goals at once, respecting each device's limits and its chance of failing.

They demonstrate the system on Multi-View Convolutional Neural Networks, used for 3D object recognition from multiple camera views. By measuring how much each view contributes to accuracy, they assign pruning budgets view by view. The resulting models meet user-set accuracy and memory bounds even when several devices fail at once. Inference runs up to 4.7 times faster across simulated device setups.
arxiv-2512-22236:
Adrien Pavão ran a simple experiment with an uncomfortable result: people cannot reliably tell AI-generated images from real photographs. Participants in an interactive web test classified twenty images each, drawn from a set of 120 difficult cases. Real photos came from the CC12M dataset, and the fakes were carefully produced counterparts made with MidJourney.

Across 165 users and 233 sessions, average accuracy was 54 percent, barely above coin-flip guessing, and practice brought only limited improvement. People answered in about seven seconds on average, and some images fooled nearly everyone always. Pavão concludes that human judgment alone is becoming insufficient as synthetic media improves, and calls for greater awareness and ethical guidelines around AI-generated imagery.
arxiv-2512-22336:
Mengkang Hu and eleven co-authors present Agent2World, a system that teaches language models to write symbolic world models, the rule sets that planners reason over. Good world models, in PDDL or as executable simulators, are scarce training material, and static validation misses errors that only appear during interactive execution. Agent2World instead grounds generation in feedback from a team of specialized agents.

A Deep Researcher agent searches the web to fill specification gaps, a Model Developer writes the executable model, and a Testing Team runs adaptive unit tests and simulations. The system led its benchmarks at inference time. Its feedback loops also generate multi-turn training trajectories, and fine-tuning on them improved world-model generation by roughly thirty-one percent on average.
arxiv-2512-22536:
Qinglin Zeng, Kaitong Cai, Ruiqi Chen, Qinhan Lv, and Keze Wang present CoAgent, a system for generating longer videos that hold together as stories. Text-to-video models usually render each shot independently, so characters drift in appearance, scenes clash, and the timeline wobbles. CoAgent treats generation as a closed loop of planning, synthesis, and verification, driven by a user prompt, a style reference, and pacing constraints.

A Storyboard Planner breaks the prompt into shot-level plans naming entities, spatial relations, and temporal cues. A Global Context Manager keeps entity memory so appearances persist, while each shot is synthesized under a Visual Consistency Controller. A Verifier Agent checks intermediate results with vision-language reasoning and orders selective regeneration when something clashes. A pacing-aware editor finishes the rhythm and transitions.
arxiv-2512-22936:
Arthur Yaghjian replies to a comment disputing his claim about the classical motion of a point electric charge. The background dispute concerns radiation reaction, the force a charge feels from its own emitted radiation, and whether a consistent causal equation exists after the charge's mass is renormalized. Critics Zin and Pylak objected to how the derivation handles abrupt changes in the applied force.

His answer retraces the derivation, which starts from the motion of an extended charged sphere and takes the sphere's radius to zero. Along the way, the modified equation produces a causal version of the Lorentz-Abraham-Dirac equation. He then addresses the objection directly. Velocity jumps across short intervals near points where the force is nonanalytic do not create delta-function spikes in the radiated fields, contrary to the critics' claim. The reply is short and defensive, aiming to leave the original conclusion standing.
arxiv-2512-23136:
Junyeong Park and co-authors study why Korean students switch into Korean while practicing English conversation with an AI partner. Code-switching is studied in multilingual communities but rarely in learners talking to language models, where its teaching value is unclear. The team built LAKE, a dataset of learner-AI dialogues capturing South Korean learners' Korean-English switching during practice, with hundreds of dialogues and dozens of hours of speech.

A taxonomy of switching functions shows learners reach for Korean to flag unknown words, negotiate meaning, and express culturally marked content. Learners reuse and adapt English expressions the AI partner offered right after their switches, hinting at chances for well-timed vocabulary support. The authors release hours of human-verified code-switched speech and benchmark speech recognition on it, exposing how poorly recognizers handle learner switching. The message for designers: treat switching as a resource, not an error.
arxiv-2512-23236:
Gang Liao and a large Meta team describe KernelEvolve, an agentic system that writes and optimizes the low-level kernels behind recommendation models. Making deep learning recommendation training and inference fast is hard for three stacked reasons. Model architectures vary, kernel primitives vary, and hardware generations differ across NVIDIA and AMD graphics cards plus Meta's own accelerators. KernelEvolve takes a kernel specification and automates generation and tuning across that matrix.

The search is framed as graph exploration with a selection policy, a universal operator, and a fitness function, adapting to runtime through retrieval-augmented prompts. It works at several abstraction levels, from Triton down to hardware-agnostic low-level languages. On the KernelBench suite it passed all two hundred fifty problems, and it achieved full correctness on one hundred sixty PyTorch operators across three hardware platforms. In production, development time reportedly fell from weeks to hours, with speedups.
arxiv-2512-23336:
Marta Pita-Vidal and co-authors review a qubit platform that marries semiconductors to superconductors. Hybrid qubits have emerged as an alternative to established designs because their Josephson coupling is tunable by electric gates. That promises superconducting-style architectures with electric-field control, and a route toward scalable processors with low crosstalk. Quantum information can be stored, for instance, in the spin of a quasiparticle sitting in an Andreev bound state, combining long coherence with fast control.

The review surveys recent advances, from Andreev states in coupled quantum dot arrays to minimal Kitaev chains hosting Majorana zero modes. Hamiltonian-protected designs, which exploit superconducting phase dynamics and discrete charge or flux variables to resist local noise, get equal attention. The authors organize the field by physical mechanism, device implementation, and emerging architecture, emphasizing potential for protected quantum information processing while noting many designs remain at proof-of-concept stage.
arxiv-2512-23636:
Alberto Bemporad releases NashOpt, an open-source Python library for computing generalized Nash equilibria in games where players share constraints. In such games each player's feasible choices depend on the others, so ordinary equilibrium solvers do not apply. The library works from the joint optimality conditions of all players at once.

General nonlinear games are solved as nonlinear least-squares problems, with the JAX library supplying automatic differentiation. Linear-quadratic games are reformulated as mixed-integer linear programs, which also makes it possible to enumerate several equilibria. NashOpt further supports inverse games, where the game is inferred from observed play, and Stackelberg design problems. Examples include game-theoretic control problems built on linear quadratic regulation and model predictive control. The code is public on GitHub.
arxiv-2512-23836:
Dingmin Wang, Ji Ma, and Shankar Kumar study retrieval-augmented question answering, where a language model answers using documents fetched for it. Bigger context windows invite stuffing in more retrieved text, but irrelevant passages actively degrade answers. The authors ask how the retrieved material should be fed to the model, and what models do when the material simply does not contain the answer.

Their adaptive strategy splits the retrieved information into smaller chunks and prompts the model chunk by chunk, with chunk size tuning the trade-off between coverage and noise. Across three open-domain question answering data sets, the strategy matched standard prompting while spending fewer tokens. The sobering finding came from failure analysis: faced with insufficient information, models usually fabricated an answer instead of declining, and that behavior was a major source of error.
arxiv-2512-24036:
Fazlay Ahmed, Qiang Wu, Sushant Ghosh, and Tao Zhu ask whether gravitational waves could reveal small quantum corrections to a black hole's shape.
