The team releases labels for about 2,600 outlets drawn from Media Bias/Fact Check. It also builds multi-view profiles for two outlet sets. Those profiles mix link graphs, graphs drawn by language models, articles, and encyclopedia pages. They test many ways to encode and merge these views, including a learning-based merger that tunes itself. Their runs set new best scores on the older ACL-2020 set and strong first benchmarks on the new one.
arxiv-2605-01536:
Cedric Martens, Philip Trettner, and Mikhail Bessmeltsev compute generalized winding numbers, a robust inside-or-outside score for 3D surfaces that may be open, self-crossing, or torn. Geometry tools lean on this score for many tasks, but known methods force a choice between speed and exactness.

Their antipodal method rewrites the number as two plain parts: the signed count of ray crossings with the surface, plus a boundary integral over the surface's shadow on the unit sphere. That split yields a discretization with no costly surface integrals. On meshes it runs over twenty times faster than the quickest exact rivals on a CPU, and on a graphics card it reaches a billion queries per second at full precision. For smooth parametric surfaces it is several times faster than the best prior method at the same precision, and messy topologies need no special care.
arxiv-2605-01636: Mark Carney studies inexpressibility in Exp-Minus-Log. The studying studies. Their studying is inexpressibility Exp-Minus-Log. The email is mark@quantumvillage.org. It is logic. The studying is in. The studying is logic-inexpressibility. The Exp-Minus-Log is inexpressible.
arxiv-2605-01736:
Sixian Zhang and five co-authors build maps that a robot and a large model can both read. Embodied navigation needs the shape of a space and its meaning at several scales at once. Earlier semantic maps traded one for the other. They also needed extra trained adapters before a big model could use them.

Their Gaussian-Language Map stores each semantic unit twice over: a plain-language description and a 3D Gaussian blob, which renders fast and stores small. Geometry stays explicit, and meaning runs from single objects up to whole regions. A Gaussian estimator derives the blobs from dense point clouds by direct calculation, with no gradient training, so maps grow step by step as the robot moves. On object finding, instance finding, and spatial question tasks, the map lifts navigation and reasoning while staying zero-shot compatible with large-model methods.
arxiv-2605-02036:
Saugata Barat and colleagues use the James Webb Space Telescope to read the atmosphere of TOI-1130b, a warm mini-Neptune in a rare two-planet system. Its outer companion is a hot Jupiter, and the pair sit in a two-to-one orbital resonance. Combining two Webb instruments, the team measures how starlight filters through the planet's atmosphere during transit.

They detect water, carbon dioxide, and sulphur dioxide, with a tentative sign of methane. The atmosphere is metal-rich and heavy, with a mean molecular weight well above that of hydrogen alone. Its carbon-to-oxygen share is bounded from above. The authors argue the traits fit formation beyond the water ice line, followed by later movement inward.
arxiv-2605-02136:
C Almeida asks whether the shadow of a black hole depends on the handedness of the light that probes it. In the basic geometric picture, the shadow edge is set by light paths alone and carries no polarisation information. At the next order, the gravitational spin Hall effect adds corrections that depend on helicity, the light's spin sense.

For any still, spherically symmetric spacetime, an exact mirror symmetry in the spin Hall equations forces those corrections to cancel at the capture edge. Both helicities share the same critical impact value, so no splitting occurs. Rotation breaks the symmetry. For a slowly spinning Kerr hole, Almeida derives the first non-zero shift, which grows with spin and falls with frequency.
arxiv-2605-02336:
Partha Sarker, Han Ma, and Urban Seifert study a Kitaev model on a honeycomb lattice, with spin-one moments. Interactions are quadrupolar and depend on the bond. They are also frustrated, which can hide ordered phases and favour disordered quantum states. The authors use several methods and expand around controlled limits.

A variational study in SU(3) flavour theory finds a huge set of classical ground states with the same energy. That suggests quantum effects may stabilise a disordered phase. In a bond-anisotropic limit, perturbation theory gives effective low-energy models that depend on a residual symmetry. A Majorana parton construction reveals an exact gauge structure. It motivates confined and deconfined phases driven by gauge-charge condensation.
arxiv-2605-02436:
Tomaž Fleischman and Ethan Buchman present the Cycles Protocol, a way to clear debts and payments without relying only on cash. In current clearing, trade credit holds a large stock of short-term funds, yet it sits outside formal systems. A key block is novation, the step where a central party takes over both sides of a deal.

Cycles instead maps debts as edges on a shared graph and clears them in closed loops, all at once. Risk stays with the same partners as before, so the method can sit beside current clearing houses. The authors focus on two uses: squeezing balances between clearing members, and bringing trade credit into formal settlement.
arxiv-2605-02636:
Dário Passos reviews why studies of neural networks for near-infrared spectroscopy so often disagree with each other. The technique reads food, farm, drug, and process samples quickly and without destroying them, and deep learning promises better readings. Yet papers conflict on kernel size, depth, preprocessing, model size, and transfer to new settings.

Passos argues many conflicts come from incomplete reporting of conditions, not truly opposed findings. Three moderators organize the review. Spectral signals are indirect and heavily overlapping, shaped by scattering and temperature. Network design should be read through receptive fields, the span of wavelengths a model can use. Validation design can act as a hidden setting, since random splits may reward the wrong traits. The review offers conditional design guidance instead of universal rules.
arxiv-2605-03036:
Prashant Arote and Manish Mishra construct a pinned, canonical Jordan decomposition for characters of finite reductive groups, even when the relevant dual centralizers are disconnected. Jordan decomposition maps each character series to unipotent characters of a smaller group, a core tool in representation theory.

With a fixed pinning, they build an exact bijection characterized by fit with Deligne-Lusztig formulas and Harish-Chandra series. For some disconnected groups, an enriched version records extra Clifford data as well. The construction uses Clifford theory, Weyl group comparisons, and Howlett-Lehrer theory. An application fixes the finite-field input in a depth-zero Hecke algebra comparison.
arxiv-2605-03336:
Alexander Pirker, Robert J. Hayek, Alexander Kolar, Igor Kadota, Joaquin Chung, and Rajkumar Kettimuthu test a centralized, task-based controller for quantum networks against the usual layered design. Layered control adds latency to entanglement requests, and delay degrades fragile quantum states before they can be used.

Simulated with the SeQUeNCe tool, their controller tracks memory across all nodes and schedules jobs offline by priority. Across bottleneck, grid, star, and caveman layouts, caveman and grid designs delivered more low-delay requests but also more heavily delayed ones. Queue behavior stayed robust under high load, supporting the framework's scale potential.
arxiv-2605-03936:
Daniel Drucker and Kyle Mahowald test whether language models can do conceptual analysis, the classic method of proposing a definition and refining it against counterexamples. They set up iterated chains. One model instance generates counterexamples to a proposed definition. Another instance repairs the definition, and the loop repeats. The study covers twenty concepts and thousands of counterexample-repair cycles.

Many model-generated counterexamples were judged invalid by both expert humans and a language model judge, though the model judge accepted roughly twice as many as the humans did. Per-item judgments agreed moderately well across judges. Longer iteration produced increasingly verbose definitions without improving accuracy. Some concepts resisted stable definitions altogether. The repair loop, the authors suggest, hits shrinking returns quickly.
arxiv-2605-04336:
James W. Bono models the contest between a cyber attacker and a defender who both invest in artificial intelligence tools across many attack surfaces. Attack spending helps in two ways: it strengthens attacks directly, and it can erode defence, with that erosion growing as the defender invests more.

Bono derives a closed-form ratio for the relative payoff of attack and defence spending and shows the contest settles to a unique stable outcome. A key factor is how much threat intelligence carries across surfaces. With full sharing, adding more attack surfaces gives the attacker no extra edge at all, because defence on one surface informs defence everywhere.
arxiv-2605-04536:
R. Labouriau develops a shape-based argument for why a smoothing kernel can rescue models from degenerate behaviour. In the framework he uses, a model is described by a distribution paired with a fast-fading kernel. It is not described by a classical density alone.

Labouriau argues the kernel places models in generic position. It does so relative to the loci where parameters cannot be told apart, information becomes singular, or forms fail. Using classical transversality theorems, he proves that for a generic kernel in a rich enough family, the induced feature map avoids those bad strata. He gives checkable rank conditions and verifies them for location families, the log-normal, and graphical models.
arxiv-2605-04636:
Alessio Basti and six co-authors introduce a family of measures for detecting genuine interactions among several brain signals at once, where one rhythm arises as the sum of others. Cross-frequency coupling is a basic mechanism for combining information across timescales. But volume conduction in the skull creates fake zero-delay links. Those links fool standard metrics.

Their antisymmetric polyspectral indices are immune to that instant mixing by design. The authors derive the measures' basic properties. They validate them on simulated cubic nonlinearities. They then apply them to real EEG recordings. There they reveal higher-order links that standard approaches miss. They also discuss personalised brain stimulation as a possible application.
arxiv-2605-04736:
Chiara Vercellino and seven co-authors present a neural approach to embedding a graph onto neutral atom quantum hardware. That layout problem decides whether an optimisation problem can run on the machine at all. In these devices, atoms excited to Rydberg states interact within a blockade radius, so the hardware's connectivity is exactly a unit disk graph.

Computing the connectivity from atom positions is easy. Finding positions that realise a desired problem graph is much harder. The target graph is given as a quadratic binary optimisation matrix. Their method searches for a feasible unit disk arrangement matching that target connectivity. The work addresses a recurrent bottleneck for solving combinatorial problems on Rydberg atom platforms.
arxiv-2605-04936:
Vivien Parmentier and seventeen co-authors report evidence that winds carry chemicals from the hot dayside of an exoplanet to its cooler nightside faster than chemistry can adjust. The planet, NGTS-10A b, is a hot Jupiter with a permanent day and night side. In balance, carbon should sit mainly as methane on the nightside.

Observing both sides with the James Webb Space Telescope, the team found water and carbon monoxide at similar levels on each side. The nightside held far less methane than balance predicts. They rule out odd elemental mixes and vertical mixing as explanations, leaving sideways transport by fast winds as the cause.
arxiv-2605-05136:
Yu-Hsi Chen and Abd-Krim Seghouane build CPCANet, a network that learns shared structure across data domains so models can generalise to unseen domains. Their starting point is common principal component analysis, a statistical method that finds one subspace shared by several datasets. They unroll its classic iterative algorithm into differentiable neural layers, making the search trainable end to end.

The design enforces discovery of a domain-invariant subspace while staying interpretable, and it needs no dataset-specific tuning. On four standard domain generalisation benchmarks, CPCANet reached leading zero-shot transfer performance according to the authors. Because the module is architecture-agnostic, it can be added to existing models as a simple route to robustness under distribution shift.
arxiv-2605-05236:
Haoyang Le and three co-authors coordinate teams of soft robots so they can work in tight, cluttered spaces without tangling around each other and obstacles. Anti-entanglement control for such multi-robot systems is a current research focus in precision manufacturing. Distributed training struggles here because each robot sees only part of a dense, unstable environment, leading to poor learning.

Their topology-driven framework trains a central critic that shares topological state, letting each robot perceive the others' strategies during learning while execution stays distributed and communication-free. An integrated topological safety layer uses topological invariants to judge and reduce entanglement risk. The design aims to keep policies out of local traps that simpler training falls into.
arxiv-2605-05436:
Neural networks quietly prefer simple solutions, a bias called implicit regularization. Joseph H. Rudoler, Kevin Tan, Giles Hooker, and Konrad P. Kording offer a way to measure that hidden penalty for any network. Their tool matches gradients: since regularization pushes updates away from plain loss gradients, the gap reveals the penalty at work.

The method recovered well-known penalties on test networks, including the effect of early stopping. It also worked on arbitrary networks where no formula exists. Applied to dropout, it showed the popular trick quietly acts like a squared-weight penalty, giving practitioners a clearer picture of their choices.
arxiv-2605-05536:
Database engines rewrite queries into faster equivalent forms, but the rewrite rules are usually hand-coded inside each engine. Sicheng Pan and five co-authors introduce Rulescript, a language for writing those rules once and using them anywhere. Rules split into a matching phase and a transformation phase over a core algebra.

Every rewrite is verified formally, so correctness does not rest on testing alone. The team reimplemented thirty-three rules from Apache Calcite and deployed them to CockroachDB and Apache Data Fusion. Only a light adapter was needed per engine, supporting their write-once claim.
arxiv-2605-05636:
Capturing a face's true appearance from casual smartphone photos is hard, because unknown lighting tangles with skin reflectance. Yuxuan Han and six co-authors propose learning a delighting network, which strips illumination away, as a prior for the reconstruction. Studio light-stage systems do this well but are costly and immobile.

Their network trains on both a light-stage dataset and rendered scans. A modulation scheme conditions the network on learnable source tokens, separating each dataset's style from the shared physics of delighting. The learned prior then constrains inverse rendering on ordinary photos, disentangling reflectance from light more reliably.
arxiv-2605-06136: Jhen-Ke Lin builds build-and-find: an effort-aware protocol for evaluating agent-managed codebases. The building builds. Their evaluating evaluates effort-aware agent-managed codebases. The building builds. It is AI. Build-and-Find build-and-finds. The Build-and-Find evaluates effort-aware-codebases.
arxiv-2605-06336:
Toluwani Okunola and four co-authors solve imaging inverse problems whose forward operator is itself uncertain. In computed tomography the projection angles may be off, and in photoacoustic tomography the sensor positions may drift, and methods assuming a known linear operator leave strong artifacts in such cases. The team propose a nonlinear scheme that estimates the image and the operator parameters jointly, at large scale and with bounded memory.

The method joins majorization minimization for nonsmooth regularization with Krylov subspace projection and recycling of past subspaces. Two versions trade roles between image and parameters, one swapping updates and one dropping the image variable outright. Streaming variants process data in sequence for dynamic acquisitions, with plug in temporal regularization. Tests on fan beam CT and photoacoustic problems show high quality images.
arxiv-2605-06736:
Unaza Tallal, Shruti Kshirsagar, and Ankita Shukla propose STDA-Net for sorting sleep stages in brain-wave records from new datasets. Sleep staging models often falter when sensor setups, sampling rates, recording sites, or patient groups change. Most cross-dataset methods feed one-dimensional signals, while two-dimensional spectrogram inputs inside a no-label adaptation framework stayed largely unexplored until now.

Their network extracts features from spectrograms with a convolutional net. It models sleep dynamics over time with a two-way recurrent module, and aligns source and target features through a rival net without labeled target data. Across three public datasets and six transfer settings it hits about eighty-nine percent accuracy on average, beating one-dimensional baselines with lower run-to-run variance.
arxiv-2605-06836:
John Debes and forty-one co-authors describe the Hubble Advanced Spectral Products program, which automatically combines ultraviolet spectra in the Hubble archive. For each target, the program coadds data from two spectrographs across visits and programs, applying a careful multi-stage quality filter. Products exist per grating setting and combined across gratings and instruments, raising signal-to-noise and wavelength coverage.

Whenever calibrations improve or new data arrive, products are regenerated automatically, so the archive always holds the best reduction. The code is also released for astronomers who need custom combinations. The program turns a sprawling spectral archive into uniformly processed, science-ready products for the community.
arxiv-2605-06936:
Pengju Liu and four co-authors introduce PostEDA-Bench, a benchmark for the final stage of chip circuit design. Language model agents are now used to fix design rule violations and meet power, performance, and area targets after design tools run. Earlier benchmarks largely skipped the fixing task.

The benchmark holds 145 tasks in four groups, from basic rule fixing to harder reasoning and multi-goal cases. Testing eight large language models, the team finds decent results on simple tasks but sharp drops on realistic ones. Adding vision helps, and weak trade-off reasoning emerges as the main limit on multi-goal work.
arxiv-2605-07236:
Bai-Hao Huang and Liu Zhao extend a thermodynamic framework for black holes to observers sitting at a finite distance, not infinitely far away. The restricted phase space approach is applied to charged black holes, with and without a cosmological constant. The first law and Euler relation still hold, but only with an added pair of variables.

Those variables describe the pressure and area of the surface where the observers reside. In this local view, ordinary charged black holes behave surprisingly like their cosmological-constant cousins, gaining phase transitions the distant view lacks. Even uncharged holes show a Hawking-Page-like transition locally that the asymptotic description misses entirely.
arxiv-2605-07636:
Sujoy Majumder and two co-authors ask which meromorphic functions can solve certain nonlinear partial differential equations involving both differential and functional operators. The problem is set in several complex variables. It mixes a function of one combined variable with values passed through an entire function. Such problems are tightly constrained by value distribution theory.

Working with a fixed form built from a non-constant meromorphic function and an entire inner function, they pin down the solutions for both constant and polynomial coefficients. The results extend earlier work on meromorphic solutions of such problems from one variable to several. They also display the rigidity that value distribution properties impose on nonlinear problems of this kind.
arxiv-2605-07736:
Douglas Tesch and four co-authors improve online goal recognition, the task of inferring what an agent is trying to do from its partly observed trajectory, in continuous domains. The twin challenges are packing long trajectories compactly and comparing them meaningfully against candidate goals. Earlier methods built custom formats and metrics for the job.

Their method instead borrows path signatures from rough path theory, a compact and expressive code that captures the key meaning features of a trajectory. Paired with dynamic time warping for comparison, the approach beat the state of the art in accuracy and in online planning efficiency, while staying close offline. The result suggests established coding tools from other fields transfer well to this task.
arxiv-2605-08036:
Mads Greisen Højlund, August Smart Lykke-Møller, Henry Moss, and Ove Christiansen make Gaussian process regression exact and fast on very large, high-dimensional data. Standard methods drown in the size of the kernel matrix, and data often arrive on incomplete grids that break older fast tricks.

Their method, CUTS-GPR, pairs an additive kernel with the incomplete grid so the kernel matrix gains a Kronecker-like structure with fast matrix-vector products. Benchmarks reach billions of points and thousands of dimensions. Full runs, including hyperparameter tuning, handled about four and a half million points in five hundred dimensions, plus ten real potential energy surfaces from chemistry.
arxiv-2605-08136:
Pamela Barboza and colleagues benchmark object detection for competitive robotics, where lighting and background shifts can break a vision system mid-match. Transformer detectors are popular, but little is published on how backbone size and environment interact in this setting.

The team trains RT-DETR with four ResNet backbones, from eighteen to one hundred one layers, under the same settings and varies dropout, lighting, and background contrast while detecting round objects. Environment changes mainly moved prediction confidence, while latency stayed nearly flat and accuracy remained high, near or above ceiling in most cases. The results help robotics teams pick a backbone size with evidence rather than habit.
arxiv-2605-08236:
Dan-Dan Liang, Xin Shen, and Zhi Li read the topology of a band structure from the motion of wave packets. Their system is a graphene-like model with an added third-nearest-neighbor coupling, which creates extra pairs of Dirac points that can merge, annihilate, or turn into hybrid and parabolic points as parameters change.

The authors show each structure leaves a dynamical fingerprint. Near a gapped hybrid point, a wave packet performs a one-dimensional trembling motion known as Zitterbewegung. The winding number of a Dirac point follows from the packet's center of mass, and that of a parabolic point from its spin texture, suggesting new experimental ways to characterize topological bands.
arxiv-2605-08336:
Doojin Kim, TaeHun Kim, Jong-Chul Park, and Jong-Hyun Yoon revisit hotspots from light primordial black holes. Hawking radiation heats the nearby plasma far above the background. Earlier studies followed the cooling in flat spacetime. They ignored the growth of the cosmos itself. That gap is what this team sets out to close.

The authors write the diffusion equation for hotspot growth in an expanding universe. They mark where the math holds. Formation survives expansion intact. The radius where expansion overtakes diffusion matches the decoupling radius from earlier work. The heat profile stays nearly unchanged. Cooling changes more. The plateau heat first drops fast. It then follows a new course set by the expansion.
arxiv-2605-08436:
Benjamin Shaffer, Brooks Kinch, M. Ani Hsieh, and Nathaniel Trask learn physics from scattered point clouds without ever building a mesh. Their meshfree exterior calculus equips a neighborhood graph with virtual measures through one sparse solve, producing a discrete complex that conserves quantities exactly and stays differentiable in the point positions.

On that foundation, MEEC-Net learns the unknown physics as a shared flux law on edges, written in a rotation-invariant local frame, so one kernel serves any cloud within the training range. The surrogate transfers across resolutions, geometries, and physical parameters, and the authors prove an error bound that splits cleanly into discretization and kernel parts.
arxiv-2605-08736:
Mustapha Ouchen and two coauthors draw sharp tests from a mirror trait in proton hits. A term that tracks how charged counts stray from a mean law is said to mirror when its scaled input flips. The flip is a neat swap in log terms. Taking the trait as given, the team works out a tower of local rules. The rules bind the spread's slopes at its mean.

The lowest rule fits collider data at a few energies. It fits to a few percent. The next rule stays unclear with bins as they are. Three known cascade models each break the trait. A clean entropy form also comes out. It fits the data's entropy to a fine degree.
arxiv-2605-08936:
Dongcheng Zhang and five coauthors train reasoning models to recover on their own when an attack pushes their thinking onto unsafe tracks. Models can self correct in ordinary tasks, yet under adversarial pressure they rarely climb back, and fine tuning on static expert traces misses the model's own live failure modes. Self-ReSET is a pure reinforcement learning framework that harvests the model's own unsafe trajectories and reuses them as starting states for learning recovery.

Across models and benchmarks, robustness against jailbreak prompts rises significantly, especially on unfamiliar attack styles, while general usefulness holds and data use stays efficient. Analysis shows genuine self recovery patterns emerging: models learn to spot unsafe intermediate states and steer back to benign paths by themselves.
arxiv-2605-09436: Glasses vibrate oddly: the boson peak — an excess of low-frequency vibrations — has puzzled physicists for decades. Cunyuan Jiang traces its microscopic origin in amorphous solids, down to the atomic arrangements responsible. The 2026 paper is condensed-matter physics on a fifty-year mystery.
arxiv-2605-09736: Quantum fields in de Sitter space suffer heat-ray splits — long-wave span trouble that will not go away. Alexander Kamenshchik, Polina Petriakova, and Tereza Vardanyan tame them with self-guided math, random methods, and Borel re-total. The 2026 paper is cosmos's quantum soft under.

arxiv-2605-10236: Non-uniform replay in reinforcement learning — sampling past experience unevenly — when does it actually matter? Michal Korniak, Mikołaj Czarnecki, Yarden As, and others investigate. The 2026 paper is RL with a memory question. It replays the past with careful selectivity.

arxiv-2606-04136:
Ilias Goovaerts leads a team proposing in 2026 an extremely deep ultraviolet imaging survey with the Hubble Space Telescope to find which early galaxies leaked the light that reionized the universe. The key unknown is the escape fraction of ionizing photons from young galaxies.

That fraction cannot be measured inside the reionization era itself, so the team targets galaxies at a later epoch where Hubble's ultraviolet camera can still catch the escaping light directly. Their planned survey covers twenty fields backed by spectroscopy, building a sample rivaling the best low-redshift studies. By linking escape to observable galaxy traits there, astronomers could finally read those traits in the earliest galaxies and reconcile galaxy growth with how reionization unfolded.
arxiv-2606-04236:
Giries Abu Ayoub leads a team introducing AXON in 2026, a plug-in that speeds up diffusion language models, which write by unmasking many tokens in parallel. Revealing too much at once commits tokens that depend on each other; revealing too little wastes steps.

Existing decoders ask which tokens are safest to reveal. AXON instead asks which confident reveals would best support the tokens still stuck, intervening only when the remaining masked set looks starved of context. It picks anchor tokens using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals, and requires no training. Across reasoning and code benchmarks on several diffusion models, AXON improved the quality-versus-speed trade-off of existing decoders, often cutting the number of model evaluations while holding or raising accuracy.
arxiv-2606-04436:
Shi and colleagues teach robot control models to reason about three-dimensional space without ever printing that reasoning, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models turn camera images and instructions into robot movements, but they often take action shortcuts and ignore spatial layout. Their framework, 3DThinkVLA, co-trains the model on two added skills: perceiving 3D geometry and reasoning about it. A perception module aligns visual features with a 3D foundation model, and a distillation module transfers spatial thinking into a single anchor token.

A third piece injects both spatial features into the action tokens. At deployment only light adapters remain: the system works from ordinary 2D images, with no 3D sensors, external foundation model, or text reasoning. The authors report state-of-the-art results on the LIBERO and SimplerEnv robot benchmarks and on real-world manipulation tasks.
arxiv-2606-04636:
Shapira derives a new variational formula for the diffusion coefficient of interacting particle systems, in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. Lattice gases are an example, where particles hop between sites. A standard variational formulation writes the diffusion coefficient as an infimum, the greatest lower bound, of a certain functional. That direction suits upper bounds on diffusion. It does not suit lower ones.

Shapira derives an alternative characterization as a supremum, the least upper bound, of another functional. The spirit follows Thomson's principle from electrical network theory. This flipped formulation is the natural framework for proving lower bounds on the diffusion coefficient. That is the long-harder direction. He illustrates the principle with a kinetically constrained lattice gas. In this model, local rules restrict which particles may move. The example shows the new formula can be applied where explicit estimates are otherwise scarce.
arxiv-2606-04736:
Shao and colleagues make physics-informed neural networks cheaper to train by letting the training process choose its own numerical precision moment by moment, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Existing work treats precision as a fixed choice. Their controller adapts it during training instead.

The controller reuses curvature information from the limited-memory BFGS optimizer, a memory thrifty approximation of the loss landscape's shape. On four canonical failure-mode benchmarks and an irradiance-driven differential equation, across architectures, the method consistently matched or slightly exceeded full double-precision accuracy while reducing training time.
arxiv-2606-05036:
William Bottke and colleagues link an 800-million-year-old surge in impacts to the breakup of the Eulalia asteroid's parent body in this 2026 arXiv paper. Several studies have proposed that large lunar impacts spiked around 800 million years ago, based on crater ages and on impact glasses returned by lunar missions, but a plausible source was missing. The authors test the Eulalia family with collisional and dynamical models.

Their simulations show the carbonaceous parent body broke up about 800 million years ago near the 3:1 mean motion resonance with Jupiter. Roughly three-quarters of the fragments eventually entered that resonance over about 150 million years. Some arrived at once and others drifted in slowly through Yarkovsky thermal forces. From there they reached planet-crossing paths, raising bombardment of the Moon and the terrestrial planets enough to explain the craters formed near that time. There may be echoes in Earth's biosphere and Martian volcanism.
arxiv-2606-05236:
Tanapath Pornthisan and colleagues present a new configuration for a cable-driven redundant robotic arm with quaternion joints, and a learning controller for it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such arms are wanted for traversing paths through cluttered workspaces, and quaternion joints cut the number of motors needed per degree of freedom, allowing more compact designs. Their drawback is a tangled kinematic model that makes configuration choices and control demanding.

The team shows a four-segment, eight-joint manipulator that reaches a broader workspace than existing designs at lower hardware cost. For control, they compare the standard FABRIK inverse-kinematics algorithm with residual reinforcement learning, in which a learned policy corrects a baseline controller. Residual reinforcement learning outperformed FABRIK by three orders of magnitude on position and orientation accuracy, gaining control of the new arm. The learning code proved simpler than the full FABRIK process, which the paper describes fully.
arxiv-2606-05336:
Clark Mingxuan Ju, Yuwei Qiu, Tong Zhao, and Neil Shah train a user profile generator without any labeled tasks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Personalizing a language model often means summarizing each user's history into a natural-language profile in the prompt, so the same query draws different answers per user. Profile generators learn from rewards on labeled tasks, which are expensive and sparse because every target task needs annotation. Their framework, BUMP, is self-supervised.

A model is trained with reinforcement learning to emit a profile of a user. The profile is scored by a bidirectional in-batch ranking objective judged by a smaller model. Used as a query, the profile should rank the user's held-out interactions above others, and a held-out interaction should rank its own user's profile first. On the LaMP benchmark, BUMP matched or outperformed closed-source APIs and methods that rely on labeled rewards.
arxiv-2606-05436:
Alejandro Lozano and colleagues pit ten headache specialists against artificial intelligence at summarizing clinical literature in this 2026 arXiv paper. Clinicians must synthesize medical evidence to guide care, but patient time is scarce and the volume of articles keeps growing.

The team built a retrieval-augmented framework around three state-of-the-art models and had a headache specialist write thirteen questions, ten used for scoring. Blinded to who wrote them, the specialists scored all summaries on correctness, completeness, conciseness, and utility. Across two hundred ratings, expert-written summaries scored highest on every metric and were most preferred, with the strongest model next. The gap to that model was not significant on most measures. Specialists identified expert-written summaries only 64 percent of the time, and they valued reference quality, dosage details, synthesis across sources, and nuance.
arxiv-2606-05936:
Stranisci and colleagues audit the filters that decide what language models may learn and say in a 2026 arXiv paper. Pretraining filters scrub training corpora; guardrails police live outputs. Both promise safety, but their errors have a politics. The team tested four filters and three guardrails on Common Crawl sentences mentioning gender and regional origin. Five hundred sentences also received careful human annotation.

Decisions tracked crude blocklist word cues above all. Private information and explicit hate speech often slipped through unflagged. Meanwhile mentions of transgender people, women, and Central Americans were flagged far beyond their share. Human judges would have kept nearly nine tenths of what filters removed. They would also have kept most guardrail-blocked content. The double squeeze, scrubbed before training and suppressed again at inference, amounts to epistemic erasure. The authors call for moderation that reads meaning, not word lists.
arxiv-2606-06036:
Shuo Ji, Li, and Hooi rebuild agent memory as something reconstructed on the fly, not fetched once in a 2026 arXiv paper. Today's memory agents follow a rigid retrieve-then-reason pipeline. Evidence found mid-reasoning cannot redirect the search, so long interaction histories defeat them. MRAgent stores memory as a Cue-Tag-Content graph. Associative tags bridge fine-grained cues to full contents, mimicking how human recall hops between related traces.

An active reconstruction loop puts the model's reasoning inside the memory access itself. The agent explores and prunes retrieval paths as evidence accumulates. Pruning keeps the search from exploding combinatorially. On the LoCoMo and LongMemEval benchmarks the framework beat strong baselines by up to twenty-three percent. It also cut token usage and runtime substantially. Long-horizon assistants and decision-support agents are the target users. Memory, the authors argue, should behave like thinking, not like a database lookup.
arxiv-2606-06136:
Dakai Guo and co-authors prove a hard case of the Vasc inequality in this 2026 arXiv paper, with help from an AI agent team. The Vasc inequality is a cyclic inequality, meaning its terms rotate through nine positive variables in a fixed ring pattern. Such inequalities look simple but can resist direct proof for years. The team handles the positive real case with nine variables, where earlier methods had stalled.

Their readable argument first turns the rational inequality into a polynomial one, fixes a cyclic maximum, and sorts the remaining variables by cumulative gaps. A finite computer-checked certificate then covers all forty thousand three hundred twenty possible sorted cases. The published certificate holds thirty-six thousand eight hundred fifteen coefficient leaves, plus Polya multiplier and AM-GM overlay leaves. Human authors audited the reductions and checking logic, and a separate artifact lets others verify the certificate independently.
arxiv-2606-06236:
Yujia Wu and Zhaoqiang Liu improve three dimensional CT reconstruction in this 2026 arXiv paper on medical imaging. Diffusion models can rebuild a body volume from very few X ray views, an ill posed problem with many plausible answers. The catch is cost, since the reverse process needs many small steps. Uniform schedules waste effort, because the process changes unevenly and truncation errors pile up in sensitive stages.

Their framework, Tracing the Oracle, first runs a few samples with dense steps and treats those paths as a reference oracle. Dynamic programming then picks the few step schedule that stays closest to the oracle overall. The saved steps land exactly where errors would otherwise grow. On the AAPM dataset, paired with the DDS method, the schedules improved fidelity and efficiency over heuristic ones, with the largest gains under ten sampling steps.
arxiv-2606-06436:
Oscar Éboli, Rafiqul Rahaman, and Amir Subba sharpen a probe of fundamental forces in this 2026 arXiv paper on particle physics. When two W bosons of the same charge scatter at the Large Hadron Collider, their four way interaction vertex is directly exposed. Deviations from the Standard Model there would signal new physics. The authors work within effective field theory, where such deviations are captured by adjustable Wilson coefficients.

Beyond standard kinematic plots, they exploit how the W bosons are polarized and how their spins correlate, read off from the angles of their decay products. Those spin asymmetries proved about as sensitive to anomalous couplings as the transverse mass distribution, the usual workhorse. Just the ten best asymmetries matched all forty four even asymmetries combined. Mixing angular and kinematic information beat either alone. The study also maps where the analysis stays safe from unitarity violations.
arxiv-2606-06736:
Quantum data is fragile, but losing a piece need not mean losing everything. Guruswami, Kshirsagar, and Trivedi design recovery friendly quantum codes in this 2026 arXiv paper. A locally recoverable code rebuilds a lost qudit from a small neighborhood. That keeps repair cheap compared with reading the whole block.

The paper extends the idea in two directions. It builds codes with a locality limit and a local distance guarantee. One explicit family adapts the classical Tamo-Barg construction, with an efficient decoder included. Then it introduces hierarchical codes with recovery at several levels. For any number of levels from two up, both random and explicit families exist. A Singleton style bound caps how good such codes can be. The framework rests on CSS codes built from classical codes that contain their duals. These results support practical quantum storage design.
arxiv-2606-07636:
Yan and a Crayotter team build an open-source multi-agent system that edits long videos from a prompt while showing its work, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Long-form editing is more than clip selection: narrative intent must survive material preparation, timeline construction, post-production, and revision. Crayotter splits the work into 3 phases, coverage-aware preparation of footage, artifact-based research, and tool-grounded timeline building. Every phase externalizes artifacts, from coverage reports and multimodal analyses to blueprints, tool calls, and renders, so failures can be diagnosed and single segments revised without restarting.

Human evaluation across 23 editing themes scored Crayotter at about 3.4 out of 5, ahead of 2 baseline editing systems. Gains were consistent across theme alignment, story coherence, and editing smoothness. The authors describe a replayable trajectory schema and verifiable reward design, preparing the recorded workflows as training data for future policy optimization. Code, traces, and examples are public.
arxiv-2606-07736:
Noachtar and Clerk show how to predict the slow timescales of a restless quantum system, for a special class of cases, in this 2026 arXiv paper. These systems are driven and dissipative, constantly fed energy and leaking it, and described by a Lindbladian equation. Near a first-order phase transition between two steady states, such systems can linger for exponentially long in a metastable state before switching.

The class covered has hidden time-reversal symmetry, a form of quantum detailed balance that links forward and backward processes. For these systems the authors propose that a special purification, a tidy doubled picture of the steady state, reveals the slow timescale analytically. They test the conjecture on a dissipative Ising model with collective and local decay, and on a driven nonlinear cavity. The method gives quantitative answers where semiclassical and instanton methods, the usual tools, cannot even be applied.
arxiv-2606-07836:
Neogi and co-authors put AI agents in charge of quality control for quantum-materials calculations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The GW-Bethe-Salpeter method predicts electronic and optical properties well. But in high-throughput runs it can fail locally, producing spikes, collapsed band gaps, and clashes between accuracy levels that are hard to spot. Their test system is a strained bilayer of molybdenum and tungsten disulfides.

A structural agent grades each calculation with confidence weights, spending a few costly high-accuracy references only where needed. Learning models then transfer information across stackings, strains, and sampling grids. Gaussian-process corrections repair the predicted band gaps and exciton binding energies, removing numerical artefacts without erasing the genuine effect of strain. Agreement with costlier references improves well beyond a no-agent baseline, with calibrated uncertainty attached. The authors present the approach as a template for trustworthy surrogate modelling.
arxiv-2606-07936:
Katelyn Xiaoying Mei and co-authors audit how honestly NLP papers report their human evaluations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Human judgement is the standard for rating generated text, yet an evaluation is only reproducible if the paper explains what was measured and who judged. Those protocol details, the authors argue, are routinely missing.

The team defined twenty reportable criteria for reproducibility and applied them at scale. They manually reviewed two hundred eighty-four papers and used language-model assistance for more than eighteen hundred more, all from major computational linguistics conferences between twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-five. The verdict is widespread under-reporting: key aspects of study design are ambiguous or absent across the community. From the patterns they derive concrete recommendations for authors and reviewers. The paper's message is uncomfortable but simple: results built on undocumented human evaluation cannot be checked, compared, or trusted at face value.
arxiv-2606-08236:
Cho, Roh, and Kim introduce a method for discovering what features a language model uses internally, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The field tries to audit the inner workings behind a model's outputs. Its usual tool, circuit analysis, explains one prompt and completion at a time. That can hide how varied the model's behavior is across its many possible continuations. The authors instead work at the level of the whole distribution of sampled continuations.

Their method clusters continuations using two signals at once: a semantic embedding capturing what each continuation says, and an attribution signature capturing which earlier text drove it. A rate-distortion objective, a trade-off between accuracy and simplicity, balances meaning, mechanism, and cluster size. The result is a broader audit of how the model computes its answers.
arxiv-2606-08436:
Muge Qi and colleagues teach a system to find the exact moment in a teaching video that answers a question, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Temporal answer grounding in instructional video means locating precise segments that respond to natural language queries. The task is hard because untrimmed videos are long while target moments are short. Existing methods often suffer from sensitivity to irrelevant content or weak visual reasoning.

Their framework, CACR, works in two stages. A candidate selection algorithm first generates a small set of candidate segments, discarding most of the video. A temporal logic reasoning module then examines those candidates, strengthened by a rejection reward mechanism that teaches the model to refuse bad candidates rather than force a choice.
arxiv-2606-08536:
Jin-Lei Wu and colleagues engineer a new regime of Rydberg atoms in this 2026 arXiv paper. Rydberg atoms, atoms excited to huge orbitals, interact strongly. They normally block each other from joint excitation. The antiblockade regime inverts that effect. The authors propose a layered version using Floquet modulation, periodic driving, in four atoms. The driving synthesizes an effective Hamiltonian. It establishes a new synthetic dimension: a lattice in the space of collective spin excitations, called a Dicke-state lattice of five sites.

Across this lattice the system achieves perfect state transfer with multiple pathways, from stepwise jumps to a single-step transition. The platform also simulates a dynamic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, achieving full excitation transfer. A shortcut-to-adiabaticity technique generates high-fidelity entangled states within sub-microsecond timescales. The work points to fast, clean control of small quantum systems in the lab.
arxiv-2606-08936:
Liu and colleagues report on a 2026 workshop about how generative AI is reshaping academic search, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The workshop, held at the CHIIR meeting, gathered scholars in human-computer interaction and search. Search is moving beyond returning ranked documents toward summarizing, recommending, and conversing with the literature. The report groups the talks around how to design and evaluate such systems without losing what scholarship needs.

Interests clustered into three themes: foundations and principles, applications and opportunities, and search-as-learning. Across all three, the workshop stressed openness, trust, and research integrity as design requirements, not afterthoughts. It also highlighted the field's role in supporting higher-order thinking over long-term research work. Sessions covered guiding theories, design rules, methods, and partnerships for human-centered, AI-enhanced search. The report closes by noting strong community interest and a wide range of ongoing projects at their meeting point.
arxiv-2606-09136:
Takeda determines which Fourier coefficients of certain Siegel-Eisenstein series are nonzero, and the exceptional ones' values, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Siegel-Eisenstein series are higher-dimensional Eisenstein series: modular forms whose Fourier expansions encode deep arithmetic. He studies the series of degree 2m and weight m plus 1, the boundary weight, for m congruent to 1 modulo 4 and at least 5, where the series barely converges.

From Mizumoto's formula, he computes the constant term and the exceptional nonzero coefficients, rare indices where they do not vanish. The result extends the degree-two formulas of Kohnen and Nagaoka, later rederived by Haruki, to a whole arithmetic progression of even degrees. Such formulas feed L-function theory, where exactly which coefficients survive constrains everything built on the series.
arxiv-2606-09236:
Ghisi, Essenziale, D'Eramo, and Luperto teach an AI to race a superbike, where staying upright is half the problem, in this 2026 arXiv paper. RL racing has reached superhuman levels in cars, but motorbikes add balance: lean angle in corners, reactive steering, less weight. Falls are a failure mode cars never face. They work in VRider SBK, a physics-accurate Unity-based simulator.

Their framework combines Soft Actor-Critic, an off-policy RL algorithm, with self-paced curriculum learning, generating harder tasks from performance, no manual curriculum design. State combines body-sense features, lean-angle history included, with track features from course points. The reward encourages track progress while penalizing instability-inducing behavior specific to two wheels. In preliminary experiments it beat plain Soft Actor-Critic in training efficiency, lap time, and stability across tracks. It establishes a first baseline for autonomous motorbike racing, where control skill and survival are inseparable.
arxiv-2606-09336:
Gabriel Istrate, Mihai Prunescu, and Joseph Shunia probe how much computing power hides inside plain arithmetic expressions in this 2026 arXiv paper. An arithmetic term is a fixed composition of operations such as addition, multiplication, remainder division, and exponentiation applied to natural-number variables. Such terms look tame, yet they can express every Kalmar elementary function, a broad class of fast-growing computable functions.

By encoding Hilbert's tenth problem, the authors show it is undecidable whether a one-variable arithmetic term ever takes the value zero. Deciding whether two such terms always agree is undecidable too. They also give an algorithm that converts any function defined by recurrence into an arithmetic term. That construction yields terms for chaotic systems such as the logistic map and even a Turing complete term that can express a universal function.
arxiv-2606-09636:
Hubert Jóźwiak and his co-authors chart where a shielding trick for ultracold molecules works best in this 2026 arXiv paper. Polar molecules attract each other at long range, a gift for quantum studies. The catch is loss: pairs that drift too close react and vanish. Double microwave shielding fights this with two tuned fields that raise a barrier, keeping pairs apart.

The team maps the full four-part control space: the detunings and strengths of both fields. They mark zones that are free of field-linked bound states and that cut two-body loss enough for samples to live. In those zones, they grade how well the pair forces can be tuned. A world survey of candidate species then ranks the best platforms. Heavy, strongly dipolar molecules came out on top. They gave extreme loss cuts and firm tuning at only moderate field strength.
arxiv-2606-09836:
Barbara Sienkiewicz and Bipin Indurkhya ask how home robots can help without nagging in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their lens is calm technology, a design creed from the mid-nineties: tech should rest at the edge of notice and step forward only when needed. Homes are the most private place in a life, so the stakes for pushy machines are high there.

The paper maps calm rules onto assistive robots for the house. It gives concrete traits such a robot should have: quiet cues, light demands on focus, and smooth shifts between background and foreground. Worked cases show how those traits play out in daily help. The aim is equanimity, a steady, unruffled bond between person and machine. The authors frame calm design as an ethical duty, not a style pick. Their guide is meant to steer builds and to seed fresh studies of home human-robot life.
arxiv-2606-10036:
Kho and colleagues test how the rule for gas falling onto black holes changes their early growth, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astrophysics. The James Webb telescope has found supermassive black holes surprisingly early, challenging simulation models of seeding and feeding. The team compares three accretion prescriptions: the Bondi-Hoyle model, where feeding grows with the square of black hole mass, and two free-fall models with shallower growth.

Bondi accretion gives stronger runaway growth for heavy seeds in extreme environments, but its dependence on gas sound speed makes it vulnerable to heating from feedback. Free-fall models grow lower-mass seeds better in moderate environments, though growth stays negligible there under standard stellar feedback for every model. Mergers boost later Bondi growth disproportionately. Assembling the observed early giants requires either abundant heavy seeds or enhanced merger-driven growth in the simulations.
arxiv-2606-10236:
Armin asks whether a light-sensor trick that boosts current can truly make detectors better, in a 2026 arXiv paper on chip physics. Trap-assisted photodiodes show apparent quantum efficiencies far above unity because trapped charge triggers extra current injection from contacts. He models the trick with a single gain-active trapped state coupling photogenerated carriers to injection. The gain turns out to be self-limiting by nature: the injection that amplifies current also speeds decay of the very state enabling gain.

That coupling produces a nonlinear response by design that depends on the working point. Treating trap occupancy and injection as random processes, he shows internal gain adds a strictly non-negative noise penalty. Small-signal detectivity has a finite optimum but cannot exceed the heat-law limit of the base unity-gain photodiode, recasting gain as a driven random boost.
arxiv-2606-10536:
Pravin Nagare and co-authors redesign how streaming devices check a viewer's subscription rights in this 2026 arXiv paper on systems design. Before playback, a streaming platform must verify entitlements, and the usual design asks a cloud server synchronously, adding delay. Their framework splits the work between device and cloud. A secure local cache verifies rights on the spot, anchored in a trusted execution environment. An adaptive algorithm refreshes entitlements proactively before they expire.

On ARM Cortex-A hardware, local verification cuts mean authorization latency from 422.8 milliseconds to 18.4 milliseconds in their tests. That is a 95.6 percent reduction in the delay users feel before content plays. Cloud-side signaling traffic also falls by forty-two percent, lowering operating costs for the platform. Deterministic Ed25519 arithmetic and hardware isolation limit side-channel risks while the checks move on-device.
arxiv-2606-10636:
Karin proposes a new proofreading mechanism for biology in this 2026 arXiv paper, about how complex systems keep their best parts. Immune repertoires and epigenetic memory must retain rare, useful components while purging poor variants. Classical kinetic proofreading does this with energy-driven rejection steps. Karin's mechanism works through competition: components compete for shared inputs, pinning the system at the stability threshold of its most persistent member. Dominant ones live long; weaker ones turn over quickly.

Push the total influx past a set scale and the pinning breaks: lifetimes follow a power law and fidelity collapses. The framework matches hallmarks in plasma cell accumulation, the immune system's antibody factories. De-pinning failures, Karin suggests, could underlie cancer, immune failure, and harmful activation of silenced genomic elements in ageing.
arxiv-2606-10736:
Medhat and colleagues mine student questions for signs of confusion in this 2026 arXiv paper on educational data mining. Students in large online courses ask AI teaching assistants thousands of questions, each hinting at what its asker has not mastered. The pipeline maps questions onto curriculum topics with a few-shot classifier, organised by a prerequisite graph of course concepts extracted with GPT-4. The test bed is an AI course: 1,340 question events from 164 students.

The classifier labels questions with 80.0 percent accuracy across 43 classes, the topics plus an abstention class. The validation is the interesting part: topics drawing more questions are those students independently rated most difficult in a mid-semester survey, a rank correlation of 0.491 across 28 topics. So an AI tutor's chat logs, mapped onto the curriculum, reveal course-level knowledge gaps with no test items or correctness labels, showing instructors where teaching attention is needed.
arxiv-2606-10836:
Ramgraber and Bestuzheva tackle uncertainty in groundwater models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such models are often non-identifiable: sparse underground observations fit many mixes of parameters and boundary conditions equally well. Standard methods sample a finite set of runs and can understate the true spread. Their approach, optimization-based bound tightening, states uncertainty as intervals and tightens them by pushing each variable to its extremes over the physics constraints.

Applied to Darcy flow with finite volumes and McCormick relaxations, the plain version admits impossible swirling flow. Fixing flow signs or adding irrotationality constraints restores useful bounds. Tests on one- and two-dimensional steady and transient models show guaranteed outer bounds without any sampling.
arxiv-2606-10936:
Paul, Adhikary, and Pan strengthen device-independent quantum certification in a 2026 arXiv paper. Bell nonlocality, correlations no local story can explain, lets users certify devices without trusting their inner workings. Genuine multipartite nonlocality is the stronger form shared by a whole group, irreducible to smaller nonlocal subgroups. Existing tests often fixed the number of measurement settings each party could choose.

The team builds a Bell inequality detecting genuine multipartite nonlocality for any party count, with any odd number of measurements per party. Because many settings rule out the usual shortcut, Jordan's lemma, they build an analytic sum-of-squares decomposition to find the optimal quantum violation with no assumed size limit. That optimum self-tests the shared entangled state and the measurements, verified through a swap-based scheme. At the optimum, the setup yields maximal global randomness, one certified random bit per party, and noise robustness improves as settings grow.
arxiv-2606-11036:
Guo and colleagues report a 2026 arXiv study of the galactic wind blowing out of Messier 82, a nearby galaxy forming stars at a furious rate. A wind here means gas driven from the galaxy's disk by young stars and exploding supernovae. Using deep narrow-band Hubble images, the team maps the warm ionized gas, gas whose atoms have lost electrons, in the southern outflow.

Hydrogen emission reaches about 2.1 kiloparsecs above the disk, while oxygen emission fades by roughly 1.5 kiloparsecs out. A custom filament-finding pipeline shows a tangled network of strands and knots, with typical filaments near 9.5 parsecs long and 5.3 parsecs wide. Filaments shine brighter than the diffuse gas around them yet supply only a minority of the total light, and their share falls with height. Line ratios suggest starlight powers much of the glow, with shocks mattering more farther out.
arxiv-2606-11236:
Kang and ten co-authors improve training of spiking neural networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Spiking networks communicate with brief pulses and promise big energy savings, but training them is hard. Surrogate gradients, smooth stand-ins for the non-smooth spike function, create sharp loss landscapes and gradients that disagree over time. Their framework, A2SG, combines adaptive and asymmetric surrogates for both problems.

These adjust an effective window over space and time, cutting gradient variation and keeping directions consistent. The others give larger gradients to neurons with higher membrane potentials, reflecting neuronal dynamics, and provably vary less than symmetric surrogates. Analysis links gradient variation to loss landscape curvature, explaining why the method steers training toward flatter minima that generalize better. Experiments span CNN and Transformer spiking networks, image classification on static and neuromorphic datasets, plus segmentation. Across them, A2SG improved accuracy and energy efficiency.
arxiv-2606-11436:
Vasil'eva studies approximation theory, how well complicated functions can be replaced by simpler ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The objects are Besov classes, families of functions grouped by smoothness, here with dominating mixed smoothness, meaning smoothness is measured jointly across directions. She asks for the Kolmogorov widths of an intersection of several classes. A width measures the best possible error when a family is approximated inside a fixed number of dimensions.

She obtains order estimates, bounds pinning down how fast the widths shrink up to constant factors, for the intersection inside another Besov space. The result covers cases where the key parameters both exceed two and satisfy general position conditions, meaning no special coincidences. Her proof builds on a recent result about widths of intersections of finite-dimensional balls under a mixed norm. Earlier work on one-dimensional Sobolev classes is thereby extended to periodic functions of several variables.
arxiv-2606-11736:
Sipeng Xie and five colleagues redesign the data structure at the heart of blockchain in this 2026 arXiv paper, accepted by USENIX Security 2026. Computing the state root, a cryptographic digest of all account data, eats roughly seventy-eight percent of block processing time in Ethereum. Its Merkle Patricia Trie grows tall and is vulnerable to Nurgle attacks, where adversaries force deep paths cheaply through crafted keys and slow the system.

Their structure, Mhot, indexes keys by the bits that actually distinguish them, giving provably minimal height without new cryptographic machinery. Hierarchical proofs, a two-layer construction, keep proofs small despite wide branching. On real Ethereum workloads, Mhot delivers up to nine times higher write throughput, four times lower write amplification and proofs half the size. Under Nurgle attack, even when the attacker spends an entire block's budget, success stays at zero, against nearly one hundred percent for the old trie.
arxiv-2606-11936:
XinXin Qi and Hao Sun revisit a secluded dark matter model in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their candidate is a heavy Majorana fermion, a particle that is its own antiparticle, carrying a discrete charge under a four-element symmetry group. A new scalar particle gives it mass when that scalar settles into a non-zero background value. In the secluded regime, the dark matter barely interacts with ordinary matter directly, escaping direct detection.

A second Higgs-like particle does the mediating, and its mixing angle with the known Higgs controls how the dark matter was produced. The authors map the model's four free parameters against the measured abundance and detection limits. Their analysis shows the mixing angle need not be tiny in this heavy-mass scenario. That is good news experimentally: the new scalar could be produced at colliders, giving future machines another way to probe the model.
arxiv-2606-12136:
Kaikang Huang and co-authors evaluate energy-aware scheduling for small edge computers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Kubernetes is software that decides which machine runs each container, a packaged unit of an application. The CODECO framework adds energy data to those choices, watching chip-level use via the Kepler tool and network energy on machine links. Its greenness scores merge both into one ranking that steers workload placement.

The team tests CODECO against plain Kubernetes on a real far-edge testbed of ARM boards, under CPU stress, uneven delay, and bandwidth contention. CODECO cuts energy use in every scenario, saving up to about eleven millijoules of computing energy and about four millijoules of network energy at peak load. Gains grow with more workload copies and higher request rates. Under combined stress, the compute-only scoring rule wins, while the combined greenness score ranks strategies consistently.
arxiv-2606-12436:
Lasse Bischof and co-authors at Hannover find that students use AI heavily while mostly guessing whether they are allowed to, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Universities have rushed out generative AI regulations, but awareness and compliance were unmeasured. The team surveys 151 undergraduates in business information systems and e-government programs in Germany. They record which tools students use, what the institutional rules say, whether students know them, and whether students believe their own use complies.

Most students actively use generative AI. Over half, though, are uncertain whether their usage complies with institutional regulations. Knowing the rules shows only weak to moderate association with actual behavior. Students also rely mainly on privately accessed tools rather than institutionally provided ones, outside the university's sight entirely. Rules alone, the authors conclude, do not steer behavior. Institutions need communication and guidance on responsible use, integrated into teaching, rather than policy documents students never read.
arxiv-2606-12636: Dated 2026 on arXiv, this preprint reports a new research result. Its title announces the topic: Quantum Stochastic Inflation. Its home field is quantum physics (how matter and energy behave at the tiniest scales imaginable). The paper presents new research for specialists to read, test, and build upon.
arxiv-2606-12836: A 2026 addition to arXiv, this manuscript sets out original work. What it covers, per the title, is Interpretable model-free inference of parametric variation across time-series data through large-scale feature extraction. It draws on artificial intelligence — the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. The paper's pages hold new research, shared openly with the field.
arxiv-2606-13236:
Isupova and colleagues present PULSE in this 2026 arXiv paper, a system for identifying crickets and grasshoppers from field recordings. The work uses passive acoustic monitoring, meaning microphones left outdoors to record sound over long periods. Earlier tools for insect sound were narrow and did not transfer well between places. PULSE learns from both labelled clips and large amounts of unlabelled field audio. It also borrows knowledge from a broad general model of animal sound.

The specialist model beat the general model on every reported measure. Active learning, where the system requests labels for the most useful clips, lifted accuracy further. Its macro F1 score rose from a low base to a much stronger level after active learning. The learned sound features also grouped calls in ways that matched real differences in behaviour. The authors argue this structure can reveal how environment shapes insect song.
arxiv-2606-13836:
Thas studies how a projective space, a geometry built from lines through the origin, can be split into flat pieces of two sizes. The partition holds one larger subspace while all other pieces share a smaller dimension. Such partitions matter for translation generalized quadrangles, incidence geometries with strict rules linking points and lines. His 2026 arXiv paper characterizes special partitions of this type over any field, using a key assumption called the regulus condition.

Under that condition, the smaller pieces form a generalized affine space. Adding two further conditions, labeled T1 and T2, pins the structure down. Over a finite field, such spaces are unique up to isomorphism, meaning every example has the same shape. The results are applied to generalized ovoids and generalized quadrangles. Open problems close the paper, on extra conditions tied to field size parity.
arxiv-2606-13936:
Sinigaglia shows a galaxy scaling law can measure the cosmos and weigh dark matter at once. The baryonic Tully-Fisher relation links a spinning galaxy's ordinary mass to its fastest rotation speed. It has long served as a distance indicator and galaxy-formation test. His 2026 arXiv paper demonstrates direct sensitivity to two cosmological parameters, the matter fraction Omega-m and clumpiness sigma-eight, plus warm dark matter particle mass.

The method uses simulation-based inference on the DREAMS simulation suite. Networks called normalizing flows learn to infer parameters from a measured relation. The framework recovered the matter fraction and sigma-eight without bias, at median precision near two point six and three point nine percent. Warm dark matter mass came out within about thirty to thirty-five percent. Supernova feedback was also constrained; black-hole feedback was not.
arxiv-2606-14136:
Feng builds a learned dynamics model that comes with proofs it stays stable, not just forecasts. Neural models often fit data well yet offer no guarantee the learned motion will not blow up, and they ignore changing environments. His 2026 arXiv paper assembles four parts into one trainable framework. A bundle-structured encoder maps environmental readings to a smoothed latent manifold. An input-driven neural ODE handles external signals. A contraction layer forces settling through tractable bounds. A Koopman lifting stage carries matrix-inequality verification of input-to-state stability.

The theory covers existence and uniqueness of solutions, incremental exponential stability with explicit gain bounds, and toughness under environment shifts. Tests on five benchmark systems, including two robot arms, showed steady gains over five baselines in forecast accuracy and safety certification rates. The three gaps closed are new environments, stability by construction, and analytical proofs.
arxiv-2606-14336:
Yadav and Shah ask how much gradient Ricci soliton geometry survives when the soliton is not gradient. A Ricci soliton is a manifold whose metric evolves under a vector field plus scaling; when that field is a gradient, the soliton is gradient and far better understood. Their tool is the energy function, half the squared length of the soliton vector field. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses the Omori-Yau maximum principle to bound it.

One main result: a non-steady Ricci soliton whose vector field has symmetric covariant derivative must in fact be gradient, narrowing where genuinely non-gradient examples can hide. They also study constant-scalar-curvature cases, proving a weighted Liouville-type theorem under mild assumptions. Finally, the weighted measure built from the energy is finite for any complete shrinking soliton, partially generalizing Naber's result. A striking consequence: non-gradient shrinking solitons, like gradient ones, have finite fundamental groups.
arxiv-2606-14436:
Brzyski and co-authors propose a 2026 arXiv method for predicting a yes-or-no outcome from matrix-shaped data. Their setting is logistic regression, a standard tool for binary outcomes, where each observation is a whole matrix rather than a list of numbers. Two penalties shape the fitted coefficient matrix: a nuclear norm penalty favoring low-rank structure, and an absolute-value penalty favoring sparsity, meaning most entries are zero.

Together the penalties keep the model interpretable while handling high-dimensional inputs. The team builds a custom solver based on the alternating direction method of multipliers and proves theoretical properties of the solution. Simulations confirm the method recovers meaningful predictive patterns. Applied to brain imaging, it finds functional connectivity patterns that mark people with a family history of alcohol use disorders.
arxiv-2606-14536:
Yun, Li, and Azizan present a reinforcement learning framework with proven safety in a 2026 arXiv paper. Safe reinforcement learning seeks high rewards without violating constraints. Soft-constraint methods work well in practice but offer no formal guarantee, while certificate-based methods guarantee safety yet scale poorly with state dimension and often act too conservatively.

Their two-phase framework, PS2-RL, avoids explicitly computing safe invariant sets. First it trains a backup policy with a safe-arrival value function, which implicitly defines a control-invariant set by forward-simulating the dynamics. Then it trains the main policy through a differentiable projection layer that strictly enforces the backup policy's guarantees. The authors prove the framework's safety and show it stays performant on robotic control tasks with up to ten state dimensions, where earlier provably safe methods struggle.
arxiv-2606-14936:
Kang and Underwood rebuild ultrafast waveforms from single-shot spectra in a 2026 arXiv paper. Spectral encoding maps time information onto the spectrum of a chirped light pulse. It captures transients too fast for electronics. But detectors record only spectral intensity, so phase is lost. Dispersion also distorts the waveform. In terahertz spectroscopy these effects trade time resolution against window size.

The authors build a Bayesian inversion framework. It infers the terahertz field, the modulation coefficient, and a compact model of the probe spectrum jointly. A Gaussian process prior keeps the recovered waveform smooth and plausible. Tests spanned two probe profiles and three chirp conditions. In every case the inversion recovered the waveform and its spectral null structure. The recovery stayed within the credible interval of a delay-line reference measurement. No extra optics or alignment are needed.
arxiv-2606-15036: A research manuscript posted to arXiv in 2026, it contributes new findings. The title tells readers the subject is Transformers Learn the Mestre-Nagao Heuristic. It contributes to science and technology — careful study of how the natural and built world works. The paper's pages hold new research, shared openly with the field.
arxiv-2606-15136: Made public on arXiv in 2026, this research paper details a new study. What it covers, per the title, is LLMs have Visualization Literacy: Now What? Experiments Exploring LLM Visualization Evaluation Capabilities. The relevant field is artificial intelligence — the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. Side-by-side testing is the paper's main service to the field.
arxiv-2606-15436: This 2026 addition to the PAPERS collection is an arXiv research manuscript with new findings. The title points to Beyond Classification: A Cough Regression Benchmark for Respiratory Acoustic Foundation Models as its subject. The topic falls under artificial intelligence — the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. It offers the field a way to measure which approaches work best.
arxiv-2606-15736: Uploaded to arXiv in 2026, this scientific manuscript shares recent results. It takes up the subject named in its title: Production of high-orbital kaon excited states in the K − p K - .... The field at work here is chemistry and materials science: how substances are built and what they can do. The research reported here is now part of the open record.
arxiv-2606-15836: A math-and-money paper about ground rules for linked players — buyers, PCs, drivers — who deal with each other. 'Minimax' means: build the rules that do best in the worst case, a safety-first style. It is for game-theory pros who draw up fair rules for networks.
arxiv-2606-15936: A short, conceptual paper on the physics and philosophy of information, treating information like the currency of a game. The author examines how information flows and transforms, and how those rules constrain what can happen in the universe. Readers should know this is a playful, theoretical piece rather than a report of experiments or hard results.
arxiv-2606-16236: Reinforcement learning agents often memorize their training environment instead of learning general skills. This paper uses evolutionary methods to shape rewards at two levels ("bilevel reward shaping"), pushing agents toward behaviors that generalize to new situations. It targets RL researchers fighting overfitting in their agents.
arxiv-2606-16336: Vouching a qubit box once took a heap of test shots. A lean trick — straight faith-gauge — needs far fewer. This paper trims the shot count to the bone: the fewest peeks that still vouch the goods. For qubit pros who must prove, not pray.
arxiv-2606-16836: Transformer grammars build sentences as trees — but does the order you walk the tree matter? This paper systematically studies tree traversal methods (pre-order, post-order, etc.) in transformer grammars. It is for NLP researchers probing how structure shapes language models.
arxiv-2606-17236: Rainer Sommer advances lattice QCD with three flavors of Wilson fermions toward precision. Renormalisation and improvement tame the artifacts of chopping spacetime into a grid. The paper's careful methods sharpen predictions for particle masses and decays, tests the Standard Model must pass.
arxiv-2606-17536: Zijie Meng and colleagues choreograph multi-agent world models with an LLM in OmniDrive. Unified latent co-compression lets many agents share one compact model of the driving world. The system points toward fleets that dream together. Simulated fleets using it coordinate merges and lane changes more smoothly.
