Through a small surgical opening, a Fogarty catheter, a balloon-tipped tube, removed the clot and rapidly restored flow. The patient had no limb ischaemia or new brain harm and did well. The authors urge immediate vascular checks when sheath reflux vanishes.
pmc-13272236:
Zhehua Zhang is lead author of a 2026 journal article mapping metabolic changes across stages of hepatitis B related acute-on-chronic liver failure. That is a sudden worsening of chronic liver disease. It carries high short-term death rates. The team used high-coverage chemical profiling of blood to trace how metabolism shifts from health through chronic hepatitis B to liver failure.

Samples came from 125 liver failure patients across three severity stages, 34 chronic hepatitis patients, and 32 healthy controls. The method detected 2,053 metabolites of one chemical family. Thirty-two changed persistently from the chronic hepatitis stage onward, peaking at 91 changed metabolites in stage one failure. Tryptophan pathway products split: one branch rose while the serotonin branch fell, and sulphur amino acid pathways switched on, suggesting compensation for oxidative stress.
pmc-13272536:
Hyungsuk Kim leads a 2026 web survey of how shoulder surgeons in South Korea treat impingement and torn rotator cuffs. Members of the Korean Arthroscopy Society answered questions on when to operate, how to repair tears, and how to handle related tendon problems. One hundred surgeons completed the survey.

Most said they rarely operate for impingement with no clear tear, and wait for lasting symptoms. During repair, most removed only a bone spur, and a suture-bridge repair was favored for full tears. Choices for partial tears varied more, and university surgeons used some added patches and treatments more often than others.
pmc-13272936:
Yuan Ren leads a 2026 narrative review of depression in medical students and how it is found and managed. Rates are high, tied to heavy study demands, identity strain, and thin support. The review gathers work on how common depression is, how it is spotted, and what digital and teaching tools may help.

Stigma, weak training, and uneven school rules hinder early detection, the authors find. Phone apps for self-screening, remote counseling, and prediction models offer scalable help, though privacy, fair access, and cultural fit remain concerns. They propose a framework linking prevalence, digital tools, teaching, and policy, and call for training that builds self-awareness, help-seeking, and peer support.
pmc-13273236:
Nicholas Balasus leads a 2026 study showing that ammonia emission plumes can be mapped with shortwave infrared imaging, a light-based method that uses reflected sunlight. Ammonia harms ecosystems and health and helps form fine particles. Current satellite tracking relies on thermal infrared, which needs temperature contrast and gives coarse images.

Using data from the Tanager-1 satellite, the team measured emissions from industrial point sources in Pakistan and Uzbekistan as a proof of concept. Because many existing and future imaging spectrometers work in shortwave infrared, the method could widen the ammonia observing system. It avoids thermal contrast limits and allows finer spatial detail than current thermal sensors.
pmc-13273636:
Gudeta and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on bed net ownership, use, and malaria in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia. The study was based at a local health center. It asked how many people own nets, how many sleep under them, and how that relates to malaria.

The team enrolled 403 participants and tested them for malaria. About 70 percent owned a bed net, at 70.2 percent. About two thirds, 66.5 percent, used a net on a regular basis. Malaria was found in 3.7 percent of participants. Most infections, 60 percent, were caused by Plasmodium falciparum. Infection was more common in rural residents. It was also more common in people who owned no net. The authors urge wider net access and steady use.
pmc-13274136:
Monika Kisielewska and co-authors wrote a 2026 review article on why melanoma, an aggressive skin cancer, so often outlasts modern drugs. Immune and targeted therapies changed care, yet lasting responses come in only a subset of patients. The review centers on MITF, a switch protein that sets the cancer cell's state.

Melanoma cells flip between fast-growing states and slow, invasive, drug-resistant states as MITF activity rises and falls. Signals driving the flips include inflammation, low oxygen, support cells, stiff tissue, and shifts in how cells burn fuel. The authors map how these cues connect. Targeting the switch itself, they argue, may help stop cancers from dodging therapy.
pmc-13274236:
Melkamu Dugassa Kassa and Jeanne Martin Grace present a 2026 systematic review on folding chronic disease care into primary healthcare in low-resource countries. Long-term diseases such as diabetes and heart disease kill heavily in poorer nations, yet front-line clinics are built mainly for infections and emergencies. The reviewers searched six databases plus grey literature for studies since 2016.

Twenty-three studies met their criteria. The main barriers were too few trained staff, weak buildings and equipment, patchy access to essential medicines, and split governance. Patients' low awareness and cultural hurdles added friction. What helped included shifting tasks to community health workers, strong policy backing, financial incentives, better information systems, and community engagement.
pmc-13276036:
Bassant Hamed and co-authors report a 2026 experiment on strengthening concrete beams with greener materials. Reinforced concrete carries much of modern building, but making steel bars uses huge energy. The team tested fabric-like geotextiles and steel wire mesh, plus tiny carbon tubes mixed into the concrete.

Seven small beams were bent until they failed, comparing plain and strengthened versions. Some had mesh or fabric buried inside; others wore it wrapped around the outside. Every strengthened beam carried more load than the plain one, with gains up to about forty-five percent. Beams also bent much farther before breaking and soaked up more energy. Buried wire mesh gave the highest load, while an outer fabric wrap gave the largest bend.
pmc-13277636:
Zhipeng Zhao leads a 2026 study that builds two combined DNA tests for bacterial lung diseases in cattle and sheep. Respiratory disease in livestock often involves several bacteria at once, and which germ is present guides treatment. Each test detects four targets at once, with one slot differing to match the main mycoplasma germ of cattle or of sheep.

After tuning, both tests showed good specificity, sensitivity, and repeatability, detecting very small amounts of target DNA. Early tests on clinical samples found the target bacteria as expected. The assays are a base for fuller validation, the authors say. Faster, combined testing could support better antibiotic choices and disease control on farms.
pmc-13278236:
Jenna Bernstein leads a 2026 cost-effectiveness study of computer-assisted navigation for hip replacement surgery in the United States. Navigation tools aim to place implants more accurately. The team built a decision model comparing fluoroscopic navigation, robotic help, and manual technique over one year, using published data and average patient age sixty-six.

The navigation approach saved about fifteen hundred ninety-five dollars per patient versus robotic surgery and about nine hundred forty-nine dollars versus manual surgery. Shorter hospital stays and fewer readmissions drove the savings. Health gains, measured in quality-adjusted life years, were tiny but positive. Results held across sensitivity tests, making navigation the model's preferred strategy on both cost and outcome.
pmc-13278336:
Kyu-Ho Yi leads a 2026 cadaver study of a little-known scalp muscle called the temporoparietalis. The thin, fan-shaped muscle lies over the side of the head and connects with layers surgeons use in reconstruction. The team dissected thirty embalmed cadavers, studying both sides of the head, for sixty sides in total, and graded the muscle as thick, indistinct, or absent.

The muscle was present on about sixty-two percent of sides. Only about seventeen percent were visibly thick, while about forty-five percent were faint and about thirty-eight percent absent. It is not a constant structure, the authors stress. Expecting this variation may help surgeons read dissection planes and plan operations around the temple region.
pmc-13278736:
Ryo Masumura leads a 2026 mouse study showing that cells called oligodendrocytes help organize early brain activity. These cells coat nerve fibers in the brain. Young brains show waves of activity in sync across cells, and that sync is thought to guide wiring. The team used gene tools in the cerebellum to remove the coating cells at set ages.

Loss in the first days of life, but not after weaning, broke the sync of Purkinje cell activity, both in pups and in adults. Lasting gaps followed in anxiety, social behavior, and movement. Restoring sync in adults with light-based tools rescued movement and social function, but not anxiety. Early support cells shape lifelong brain function through the activity patterns they enable.
pmc-13280436:
Maxime Jeanovitch Lignier and colleagues present a 2026 validation study of a core temperature algorithm in construction workers. Heat illness stalks construction work in summer, and core temperature reads can warn teams. The ECTemp algorithm estimates core temperature from heart rate inputs. Two inputs faced off: a photoplethysmography smartwatch, which reads pulse by light, and a chest strap monitor. A swallowed telemetric pill gave the reference temperature in a single work shift.

One hundred two workers took part, all with chest strap data and sixty with smartwatch data. Peak, mean and continuous series fed the algorithm from each device. Against the pill, the chest strap estimates showed a small mean bias, near a sixth of a degree low for continuous data. Rank correlations sat in the mid range. Agreement checks by Bland Altman and two correlation types weighed both inputs. Strap input looks firmer for field heat checks.
pmc-13280536:
Mingjia Li and colleagues report a 2026 cohort study of obesity, sex, comorbidities and survival in cancer patients on immune checkpoint inhibitors. Immune checkpoint inhibitors free the immune system to attack cancer, but obesity impact on their outcomes is poorly understood. The cohort involved six hundred eighty eight patients with metastatic cancer who got the inhibitors as first or second line therapy. Obesity was assessed using body mass index. Cox models and Kaplan Meier analysis examined survival associations.

Patients with higher BMI had longer overall survival, with a hazard ratio for death below one. Sex was examined alongside obesity, given its influence on body composition. Medical comorbidities were weighed in the models as joint predictors. The obesity paradox pattern, where higher weight links to better immunotherapy survival, appears in this cohort. Comorbidity burden may modify the link, so weight alone should not guide inhibitor care.
pmc-13280936:
Mohamed Hamdy Serour and colleagues shared a 2026 case report on a foot wound in a man with diabetes. The man was forty-seven, smoked, and had type two diabetes. A sore between his toes on the left foot would not heal. The sore deepened until a tendon, the cord that moves the toe, showed through. Standard wound care cleared an early infection but then stalled.

The team added a laser treatment that gently removes dead tissue with light. Week by week the wound shrank after that. Skin grew over the tendon, and the sore closed fully by eight weeks. The authors present the case as a step-by-step plan. They suggest laser care as a backup when standard care stalls, not as a first step.
pmc-13282336:
Silvana Piersanti and co-authors present a 2026 study of how smell and touch sensors and the brain develop in caddisflies, aquatic insects close to moths. The team examined young stages of one species with powerful microscopes. Larvae live in water, while adults fly, so their sensing needs differ sharply. The focus was the antennae, the insect feelers, and the brain regions that process their signals.

The larval antenna was a single segment bearing four large sensors, all of a touch type, and it did not change across larval stages. Adults of the same species instead carry many smell sensors. The larval brain lacked the smell-processing lobes entirely, and its other centres were simple. The pupal brain looked much like the adult's, with smell lobes and richer centres. The authors say the dramatic rebuild reflects the ecological jump from water to air, and informs how insect smell evolved.
pmc-13282436:
Zihang Xu and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on tiny packets from Schwann cells as a possible therapy for diabetic mouth wounds. Schwann cells support peripheral nerves, and their extracellular vesicles, packets of proteins and small RNAs, carry nerve repair programs. Diabetic wounds in the mouth heal poorly, with lasting inflammation, weak blood vessel growth, oxidative damage, and nerve-related repair defects. The review argues these packets match those problems unusually well.

The packets carry growth factors for nerves, regulatory RNAs, and antioxidant molecules. The authors describe how that cargo could calm inflammation, spur vessels, regrow nerves, and restore chemical balance. They compare this source with the better-studied stem cell packets, stressing its nerve-specific advantages. Production scale-up, targeted engineering, and delivery through biomaterials are reviewed. Remaining barriers include standardisation, potency testing, and long-term safety.
pmc-13282736:
Fabio Dennstädt and co-authors wrote a 2026 reply letter answering four questions raised about their earlier study of large language models in radiation oncology. The correspondents, Ilker Sengul and Demet Sengul, had pressed on how such evaluations can be trusted and repeated. Language models are being tested for clinical work in cancer treatment with radiation, where answers are open-ended and expert judgement matters.

The authors argue that evaluation must be continuous, because models change fast and clinical use demands constant monitoring and testing. They call for dedicated benchmark data sets and for practical checks, such as flagging clearly wrong advice or needlessly long answers. For complex, atypical cases, they say real-world open questions are fundamental, since exam-style questions cannot capture reasoning and ethics. The reply is candid that many challenges remain unsolved.
pmc-13282836:
Xue Fu and Juanjuan Li wrote a 2026 letter to the editor urging caution about a review that pooled trials of acupuncture plus robot therapy for limb problems after stroke. The original review had reported statistically significant gains on a standard arm and leg function scale. The letter writers accept the topic's importance but dispute how the results were framed.

Their first point is clinical meaning: pooled gains fell below the accepted threshold for a difference patients can feel, about six points, in every key comparison. Calling such gains clinically important overstates them. Second, the trials mixed upper and lower limb robots, device types, and widely varied acupuncture styles, making the combined treatment ill-defined. Third, most trials were small, single-centre, and positive, a pattern where unpublished negative results are likely, and the bias tests used are too weak to rule that out.
pmc-13283136:
Repeat colonoscopies often come too early in American practice, a pattern Kacey Idouchi's multicenter team documents for 2026. Guidelines from 2020 advise less frequent checks for low-risk patients. Early repeat scopes stay common, so the team tracked real practice over time.

Records covered 452 patients at many centers from 2020 to 2025. Early follow-up occurred in 58 percent of first repeat scopes in the cohort. Late follow-up occurred in 13 percent of cases in the study. Early scopes were most common when only low-risk growths were found. Patients with high-risk growths often waited too long instead. Guideline use still needs work in both directions.
pmc-13283236:
Small-incision plating versus open fixation for lower shin fractures ends in a statistical draw in Ahmed Mohamed Hassaan's 2026 pooling. Such breaks are hard to treat due to thin skin cover and poor blood flow. One method uses small cuts, while the other opens the site fully.

Nine studies with 530 patients in total met the review rules. Pooled results showed no clear gaps in foot function scores between methods. Healing time, surgery time, hospital stay, and return to work also matched closely. Major problem rates did not differ clearly in the pooled data. Small-cut surgery showed trends that favored it on some measures. More trials are needed to settle the choice.
pmc-13285536:
Screening thousands of plant oils by computer to find a safe mosquito killer is the plan in a 2026 study by Mohamed Nagy, Esraa Mansour, and Hanaa Elbrense. Mosquito-borne illness still burdens the world, and harsh chemical sprays need greener swaps. Their tiered sieve began with 5,183 oils and cut the field by harm scores.

Docking against nerve targets of a Culex mosquito left fifty-one top oils, with German chamomile showing up again and again. Egyptian chamomile oil went to lab tests next. It killed all larvae at top dose in one day, warped young forms, and upset nerve chemistry in ways that point to scrambled signaling. Field trials must still prove farm and home value.
pmc-13285636:
A single standard stem cell line can mint brain immune cells on demand, Brianne B. Rogers and co-authors show in a 2026 study. Human stem cell microglia models often wobble between lines, muddying gene network work. The KOLF2.1J line carries switches for six factors that flip it fast into microglia-like cells.

The lab-grown cells matched real brain microglia closely in gene and gene-control reads, both at rest and when inflamed. Maps found microglia-rich control zones and enhancer reshaping during growth and under two immune triggers. Active networks in the cells ran rich in gene variants tied to Alzheimer disease. The authors offer the line as a steady bench for brain illness work.
pmc-13285736:
Chen Wang led a 2026 randomized trial of oliceridine, a newer opioid, for pain control after stomach cancer surgery. Patients used a pump to give themselves the drug after laparoscopic removal of part of the stomach. The trial asked whether gut recovery would speed up compared with the standard drug sufentanil, without losing pain relief.

The trial enrolled 106 patients at one center, and 96 finished in the final count. Pain scores over 48 hours were much the same in both groups. Patients on oliceridine passed gas and stool sooner, ate sooner, and left hospital about a day earlier on average. They also reported far less nausea and vomiting than the sufentanil group. No breathing depression appeared in either group, which supports use in enhanced recovery plans.
pmc-13285836:
Brian N Lundstrom and Alexander Rotenberg look ahead for magnetic brain stimulation in epilepsy care in a 2026 forward-looking review. Pulses sent through the skull can stir the cortex without surgery or lasting harm, which sets the method apart from cutting or implant care. The authors ask what near-term studies could settle about its twin roles in testing and treatment.

Pulse responses already gauge how excitable the cortex is and whether a drug has hit its target in the brain. Repeated pulse trains might calm seizures that start in many spots or spread across both sides at once. Open questions cover which syndromes respond, which scalp targets work best, and how to pair pulses with drugs. The pair also float using these measures to tune other stimulation devices, a step that could sharpen care for resistant epilepsy.
pmc-13285936:
Fengting Ning and colleagues review strontium-loaded materials for bone repair in a 2026 survey of mechanisms and clinical progress. The trace element nudges bone to grow, slows bone loss, calms immune cells, feeds new vessels, and fights germs. Loading it into implants and scaffolds aims to place those effects right where a defect needs healing.

How much strontium a material holds and how fast it leaks out shape its power, and build method sets both traits. Paired with ions such as magnesium, zinc, or copper, strontium can steer growth, vessel formation, and infection control at once. Gaps block wider use for now: no shared best dose, thin long-term safety data, and few large-animal or patient studies. The authors lay out design rules meant to move these materials toward real bone care.
pmc-13287336:
Michael Narvey and Deima Alammary present in 2026 a newborn who developed severe bleeding into the lungs shortly after a difficult birth by emergency caesarean section. Blood appeared at the mouth and nose during resuscitation, and the baby needed breathing support from the first minutes of life.

No clear cause such as infection, clotting problems, or family history explained the bleeding. The authors argue that the label for this condition can only be given after other causes are excluded. They stress asking parents for autopsy permission when the diagnosis is suspected. Findings can guide staff review and may give grieving families clearer answers.
pmc-13287836:
Guoxian Zhu and co-authors studied rats in 2026 with an overactive thyroid to learn how one small gene regulator, miR-122-5p, affects liver injury tied to the condition. Animals were split into healthy, overactive, and overactive-plus-blocker groups, and liver cells in dishes were tested in parallel.

The regulator ran low in livers of overactive rats. Blocking it further made tissue injury worse and raised iron-linked cell death signals and inflammation. The regulator works by holding down a partner gene called CCDC6; dish tests showed injury grew through that partner. The authors name the pair a possible drug target for thyroid-linked liver harm.
pmc-13288536:
Jie Ma and a large team test two drug targets in sick mice in 2026. The mice had type 2 diabetes plus sepsis. That pairing worsens liver damage. One group got pioglitazone to switch on PPARG. One group got SC79 to switch on AKT1.

Both drugs raised survival in the mice. Blood and liver inflammation fell. Anti-inflammatory signals rose. Sugar and fat handling improved. Liver, lung, and gut harm partly eased. Each drug worked through its own path. Gut barrier and gut microbes partly healed. The paths were PPARG with AMPK, and PI3K with AKT1 and mTOR.
pmc-13289136:
Sohaima Samad and Hamna Samad report a 2026 project to speed prostate cancer checks in Karachi. The project ran at Lifeline Hospital. The hospital gets 60 to 70 such referrals a month. A first audit found long waits. Waits raise patient worry and delay care plans.

Three fixes were added in January 2025. A weekly one-stop clinic was added. Biopsy slots under local numbing grew. Urgent cases got admin priority. A second audit checked the results. Clinic-to-biopsy time fell by 40 percent. Biopsy-to-team time fell by over half. The share done in eight weeks rose to 58 percent.
pmc-13289636:
Sung Woo Moon and coauthors offer a 2026 claims study from South Korea on whether better hospital quality grades for COPD care link to fewer flare-ups. The national review service grades clinics and hospitals on lung disease management each cycle. The authors tracked grade moves between two cycles and compared flare rates in the later cycle across grade paths.

Claims covered 36,218 patients at 873 non-major institutions from May 2016 to April 2018. Groups split into improved, steady, and declined grade paths with very different patient counts. Improved sites already tested lung function more and prescribed long-acting inhalers more at baseline than declined sites. Flare incidence and severity in the outcome year were then compared with adjusted models.
pmc-13289936:
Alexander M. Pham and coauthors build a 2026 three-dimensional culture system to grow Merkel cell polyomavirus, a skin virus that can cause cancer. Study of this virus stalled for lack of culture methods supporting real infection, forcing reliance on imperfect models. Spheroids grown from primary human skin fibroblasts boosted viral genome copying and maintenance enough to harvest infectious particles from the medium.

Released virus rode inside tiny cell sacs called extracellular vesicles, and that route partly dodged antibody blocking, aiding immune evasion. Vesicle cargo showed fewer antiviral defense genes, priming uninfected cells for easier infection ahead. Gene reading in infected skin cells pointed to Wnt-driven remodeling like wound healing in skin. Natural skin infection gains a lab model.
pmc-13290636:
Recovering late after a brain bleed costs patients in memory and mood, Qiuyi Jiang and colleagues show in a cohort study from 2026. Most research on intracerebral hemorrhage stops at the event itself; this study follows how the rehabilitation path over the first year shapes thinking and feelings.

The cohort included 1,692 patients with small supratentorial bleeds treated between 2018 and 2020, and trajectory modeling split 1,563 of them into an early-rehabilitation group (75.5%) and a late group (24.5%). The late group carried more cognitive impairment and depression, and after adjustment their odds stayed higher for both, though not for anxiety. Jiang and colleagues urge early, sustained rehabilitation and personal plans for patients drifting onto the late path.
pmc-13290736:
Two vertebrae tell nearly the same bone story as four, Paul Köhli and colleagues report in a 2026 retrospective study of an MRI bone quality score. The vertebral bone quality score lets surgeons screen for weak bones from scans already taken. The team asked whether measuring only L1 and L2 works as well as the standard L1-to-L4 version.

Among 144 patients having lumbar surgery for degenerative spondylolisthesis, the short and long scores agreed almost perfectly, with an intraclass correlation of 0.988. Their accuracy for spotting osteoporosis and impaired bone quality was comparable, and the short version caught more true cases (94% sensitivity for osteoporosis) at the cost of more false alarms. Köhli and colleagues endorse the shortcut as a screening alternative while asking for validation and sharper thresholds.
pmc-13290836:
High blood pressure in childhood pushes a whole-body risk syndrome into higher gear, Jessica O'Keeffe and colleagues review in 2026. Their subject is the overlap between pediatric hypertension and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, the staged framework linking obesity, insulin resistance, kidney disease, and heart risk.

The review finds the syndrome common in children, seeded early: a mother's hypertensive pregnancy raises the child's risk, and food insecurity plus other social conditions drive the obesity that advances stages. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system emerges as a key mediator tying early exposures to later hypertension, and hypertension itself lifts a child's syndrome stage and heart risk. O'Keeffe and colleagues argue prevention must start with early-life nutrition and food access, not wait for clinic-stage disease.
pmc-13291036:
Major life changes that come with Friedreich ataxia are cataloged in a 2026 study led by Audrey Iskandar, comparing people whose disease began in childhood with those whose symptoms started as adults. Friedreich ataxia is a rare inherited nerve disease that often begins during the move into adulthood, reshaping school, work, and relationships as it advances.

Seventy-three patients in the PROFA study, 44 with childhood onset and 29 with adult onset, filled in a life events questionnaire covering disease, relationships, and work. Both groups reported a similar total count of events, with disease-related events most common. Greater disability went with more harmful events, mainly around relationships, and childhood-onset patients who could no longer walk looked most exposed, which argues for early psychosocial support.
pmc-13291136:
Baoyu Peng and colleagues review Xiaoqu starter for rice wine in a 2026 synthesis. Xiaoqu drives sweet glutinous rice wine in China. It is passed down through artisan use for generations. Pure mold cultures, used in Japan, work quite differently.

Molds, yeasts, and lactic bacteria form the core guilds. They share tasks across sugar release and flavor. Acid build-up and alcohol control also split among them. Plant inputs and workshop settings steer the mix. Succession follows that steering over time. The authors urge a systems view of the starter. Single species lists miss the real story, they argue.
pmc-13291236:
Cell power plants may link two core energy systems more closely than thought. Laura Pérez Pañeda leads a 2026 study of mouse heart tissue. ATP synthase makes the cell fuel ATP. The TCA cycle feeds that process with raw fuel.

The team used chemical linking plus mass reading tools. They found the head of ATP synthase touches many TCA enzymes. That contact web was unseen before this work. Sick hearts lacking a key RNA helper showed weaker synthase units. Contacts with TCA enzymes grew stronger in that state. A brake protein also bound the head more. Such shifts may help cells save energy under stress.
pmc-13291336:
A loose belt loop sets how fast botulinum toxin acts. Baohua Chen leads a 2026 study of this famed nerve poison. Two toxin types differ in onset speed. The cause of that gap was unknown.

Each toxin wraps a belt around its cutting part. A looser belt lets the cutter cross into nerve cells sooner. One fast type has a more flexible belt by nature. The team found a buckle point that locks the belt. Loosening that buckle sped the slow type up. An antibody locking the buckle blocked the toxin. Fast medical toxins and antidotes both gain a design clue.
pmc-13291636:
Cockroach genomes hide thousands of DNA gifts from their inner bacteria. Kyle M. Ewart leads a 2026 study of this gene flow. Cockroaches host Blattabacterium bacteria passed through eggs. That long bond gave DNA many chances to jump.

Fragments were matched across 23 cockroach and termite genomes. Eight genomes were newly sequenced for the study. Australian burrowing cockroaches held over three thousand inserts. That count dwarfs past records outside rotifers. Some inserts survived near thirty million years. Joined inserts stitched up to nine bacterial segments. Noncoding jumps may shape adaptation more than thought.
pmc-13292036: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2017 Oncology Research article that claimed CXCL5 promotes osteosarcoma cell migration and invasion through autocrine and paracrine routes. After publication, readers flagged problems in several figures, including a patch of similar cell data and western blot bands with odd shapes. The editors asked the authors for comment and the original figures, but the authors never replied. Losing confidence in the data, the editors-in-chief retracted the article, and no author responded to the retraction correspondence. The notice itself is all that is available here.
pmc-13292936:
Katie E. Copley and colleagues explain, in a 2026 study, why a shortened form of the protein TDP-43 clumps in nerve cells in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The short form lacks most of the stretch usually blamed for clumping, yet it is highly insoluble in patient tissue.

The short form ends in a unique 18-unit tail, and tests show that tail drives clumping through two tight zipper-like segments. Short RNA pieces could loosen the clumps, and breaking the zippers kept the protein soluble in pure form and in neurons. Those zippers also pushed the protein out of the nucleus. The work names a precise target in this disease protein.
pmc-13293436:
Mohammad Moniruzzaman and co-authors propose, in a 2026 paper, a privacy-preserving system called FEDI-CODE to predict dementia risk from patient data held at many sites. Health data sit scattered across hospitals, and moving them to one place raises privacy concerns.

The system trains shared models without pooling raw records, while also estimating how changeable risks like weight, drinking, and heart measures affect each person. On simulated multi-site data, the model reached accuracy the authors report above eighty percent and beat standard comparison models. It also held up on outside data. The authors pitch it for early screening with personal risk advice.
pmc-13294336:
Yunhan Zhao and coauthors mine United States adverse event reports for drugs that may trigger acute respiratory distress syndrome in a 2026 pharmacovigilance study. Case reports hinted at the danger, but broad real-world checks were missing. Reports were cleaned, deduplicated, and run through four signal methods plus regression models to flag independent links and time to onset.

Altogether 15,986 drug-related reports qualified, peaking in middle-aged and older adults with slightly more men. Immune suppressants, methotrexate, rituximab, tacrolimus, and amiodarone led report counts, and 22 drugs held significant links after adjustment. Median onset was 30 days, with about 75% of cases inside 150 days.
pmc-13294536:
Niamh Ryan and coauthors set out a 2026 protocol for a mixed methods review on why mothers choose human milk for infant feeding. Human milk carries tailored nutrition, helpful microbes, sugars that feed gut flora, and immune factors, yet feeding rates stay low in many countries. Knowing health perks may lift motivation, but scattered reasons research needs gathering first.

Five databases will be searched from the start of records, covering qualitative, quantitative, and mixed studies. Quality checks and extraction follow Joanna Briggs Institute tools, and findings will merge through a convergent integrated method. Clear themes on maternal motives can shape support that respects family realities.
pmc-13295036:
Bitania Teklu Yilma and colleagues build a tiny enzyme-like sensor from glycine and copper in a 2026 study. Simple, well-defined nanozymes are prized for sensing because their active sites are easier to understand. Here the smallest amino acid alone holds copper in two charge states at once.

The material oxidises epinephrine into a coloured product, letting concentration be read by light absorption at low levels. It worked three times faster than a bulkier cousin material and gave good recoveries in spiked urine samples. The same material also oxidised several phenolic pollutants, giving it a second possible role in cleaning contaminated water.
pmc-13295736:
Deborah F Nacer and colleagues compare seven ways to judge DNA repair weakness in breast cancer in a 2026 study. Triple-negative tumours often carry homologous recombination deficiency, which can guide drug choice. Tests based on DNA, RNA, function, or images had never been compared head-to-head in one fair group.

The group held 235 patients with early disease from southern Sweden, profiled by several data types. Most methods agreed substantially, with sequencing based tools and one scar method aligning closest. Remaining clashes traced to data handling and training that ignored known tumour variety. Survival checks used freedom from invasive disease after standard chemotherapy as the yardstick.
pmc-13296336:
Elena Coyago-Cruz and colleagues compare, in 2026, sweet and hot peppers across five ripeness stages, measuring minerals, vitamins and protective compounds in six varieties. They also test how well pepper extracts fight oxidation and microbes.

Variety mattered more than ripeness for nearly every measure. Potassium led the minerals, while single varieties peaked for vitamin C, heat compound and colour pigments at striking levels. Hot types showed the strongest antioxidant action, and extracts held back several bacteria and yeasts at low doses. The authors say breeders should pick variety first when chasing health compounds.
pmc-13296636:
Two RNA control systems in heart and vessel remodelling, m6A tags on RNA and tiny microRNAs, are reviewed in 2026 by Liujie Long and co-authors for their teamwork and friction. Together they add a fast, reversible layer of control beyond gene switching.

The review traces checkpoints where tags steer microRNA fate, feedback loops where microRNAs tune the tagging machinery, and cell-specific programmes in vessel lining, muscle, scar and heart cells. New measurement tools and treatment possibilities are weighed. The authors call for work proving cause, pinning down cell and stage, and testing clinical use.
pmc-13296736:
Martyna Drzycimska and colleagues review, in 2026, whether a blood marker ratio can predict bad outcomes when a fetus grows slowly late in pregnancy. The ratio compares two placenta-related proteins and might sharpen decisions beyond scans alone.

From a decade of literature across four databases, only six prospective studies covering about fourteen and a half thousand patients qualified. How well the approach spotted growth-restricted babies swung wildly between studies. The authors judge the evidence mixed and unsettled, saying routine clinical use for late growth problems is not yet supported by current evidence.
pmc-13298036:
Tiny alginate beads can shelter probiotic bacteria and meter their release, show Weichen Gong and colleagues in a 2026 study. They formed calcium alginate beads at several concentrations and loaded them with Lacticaseibacillus paracasei, a common probiotic species, to test growth, escape, and survival.

Beads made with 2.0% alginate were least permeable, around 40% versus roughly 60% for weaker gels, and held together even at pH 11 to 12. Bacteria multiplied mainly inside the beads; under 1% escaped within 12 hours and about 8% by 24 hours, while enclosed cells outlived those in liquid culture. The system even let an oxygen-sensitive Bifidobacterium strain grow in air.
pmc-13298236:
Light-based imaging turns the retina into a viewing port on the brain, and Alessandro Avitabile with colleagues survey the tools in a 2026 neuro-ophthalmology review. Photonic devices now let clinicians watch neurodegeneration unfold at the back of the eye without invasive testing.

Optical coherence tomography measures thinning of the nerve fiber and ganglion cell layers, giving biomarkers of axon loss in multiple sclerosis and optic nerve disease. A newer technique images dying retinal ganglion cells in real time, before structural loss becomes permanent, which matters most in glaucoma. Two-photon microscopy with adaptive optics reaches subcellular detail in living tissue. The authors weigh how these methods could advance earlier detection and monitoring.
pmc-13300736:
Papua New Guinea performed its first coronary artery bypass operations in 2025, and Ling Zhu and colleagues recount the launch in a 2026 report. A Singapore visiting team partnered with the national heart center in Port Moresby, using a twinning method where each local clinician paired with a trainer. Roles swapped across three cases until the local team operated alone.

The three patients received an average of 2.33 grafts each, with no deaths inside thirty days. One patient suffered a stroke on the fifth day yet recovered function and went home after a month. The authors call the pilot proof that mentored collaboration can seed surgical programs where none existed.
pmc-13300836:
Four months of vague right-sided belly pain led to an uncommon appendix diagnosis for a 45-year-old man, Marisela Silva García and colleagues recount in a 2026 case report. Scans showed a mucus-filled, swollen appendix about 22 millimeters wide, with wall thickening and calcification but no leak or spread.

Because the lump sat close to the cecum, surgeons removed the right colon segment rather than risk bursting the appendix during a smaller operation. Pathology confirmed a low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm, 10 centimeters long, with a clean base and no mucin outside the organ. Recovery was smooth, and the authors stress careful handling plus tailored follow-up for such lesions.
pmc-13301536:
Driving triglycerides down fast may not change the course of fat-driven pancreatitis, Meiling Yu and colleagues report in a 2026 retrospective study of 345 patients. The early goal meant reaching 5.65 mmol/L or below within seventy-two hours of admission, judged against severity grades and complications. Two hundred seventy-four patients hit the target and seventy-one did not.

Necrosis, hospital stay, and death matched between the goal and no-goal groups. Admission levels also misled: the very highest readings did not mark the sickest patients, and mid-range values carried lower odds of severe disease than the top band. A level near 56.5 mmol/L may flag progression risk, the authors suggest, pending firmer cut-off studies.
pmc-13303236:
Most "negative" fertility trials genuinely support the null, a Bayesian second look finds, Jiayi Gao and colleagues report in a 2026 reanalysis. Thirty-five assisted reproduction trials from four top journals between 2010 and 2025 had their primary outcomes recomputed as Bayes factors, weighing evidence for the null against the alternative directly. Sensitivity checks probed how fragile each verdict was.

Bayesian and classic readings agreed in 85.7 percent of trials. Nearly sixty-three percent of all trials supported the null hypothesis, while about twenty-three percent backed a real effect. In roughly one trial in nine, a non-significant p-value hid data too weak to conclude anything. The authors commend Bayes factors for telling "no effect" apart from "no answer."
pmc-13303336:
A toddler's runaway inflammation traced back to a hidden metabolic flaw, Frances Fuenmayor and colleagues recount in a 2026 case report. The eighteen-month-old boy met seven of eight criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis amid fever, falling blood counts, a swollen liver and spleen, and fading alertness. Two virus infections and confirmed anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis tangled the picture further.

Gene testing delivered the key result: a homozygous variant in the IVD gene proved isovaleric acidemia, a metabolic disorder. The authors argue the disorder fanned immune overreaction once infection struck, making the HLH a sign rather than the root disease. Like cases, they urge, deserve metabolic and gene workups.
pmc-13303436:
Luisa Pantoja, Hillary Sharid Manotas-Viloria, and Javier Vanegas describe a 2026 genomic study of gut bacteria from Tecia solanivora, a moth pest that damages potato crops in Central and South America. Little was known about what these microbes do for their host.

Seven bacterial strains were isolated and their genomes were examined for helpful and harmful traits. Genes pointed to roles in digestion, vitamin making, breaking down insecticides, and defense against enemies. Lab tests confirmed several of these roles. Two strains killed host larvae at notable rates, making them possible pest-control candidates, while two Rahnella strains badly damaged potato tubers and raise safety concerns.
pmc-13304236:
Jiewen Deng and co-authors simulate how an electric field changes heat flow inside a drying droplet in a 2026 modeling study. Field-assisted drying could cut the energy that evaporation steps consume across industry.

A pinned droplet between parallel plates was modeled as plate voltage rose. Stronger fields sped surface flow greatly in the early stage, though the boost faded as drying went on. High voltage split the inner swirl into two loops, while inner heat gaps stayed under one degree. Fields helped most in cooler air, cutting drying time by about one sixth there.
pmc-13304536:
Klaudia Sochacka, Agata Kotowska, and Sabina Lachowicz-Wiśniewska compare diet and well-being across life stages in Poland in a 2026 online survey. School youth, students, and older adults may share some patterns while differing in others.

A total of 360 people answered, split among teens in school, students in their twenties, and adults aged thirty or more. Adults carried the highest body mass, while school youth scored worst on unhealthy eating and ate processed foods most often. Only obesity knowledge differed clearly among knowledge and mood measures. Better diet quality tracked with better mental well-being after adjustments.
pmc-13305236:
Shasha Ma, Zhaobin Ye, Guang Shi, and Jianyong Zhang build porous polymers holding metal carbene units for splitting water in a 2026 study. Devices that make both hydrogen and oxygen with one catalyst could cut green hydrogen costs.

Polymers carrying palladium, silver, or copper were laid onto nickel foam. The palladium version led both half-reactions in alkaline water, needing modest extra voltage for each. A full cell using it on both sides ran at low voltage and stayed steady for over ninety hours of testing. Low precious metal use with lasting output marks the design as promising.
pmc-13305536:
Corey Scott, Nikoleta Stamataki, and John McLaughlin review human trials of stevia sweeteners as a sugar-cutting tool in a 2026 narrative synthesis. Stevia compounds taste sweet with almost no calories, but their metabolic and gut effects stay unsettled.

Most trials were short, from single doses to three months, and mixed stevia alone with blends alongside other sweeteners. Sugar control drew the most study, with heart, gut microbe, and weight outcomes covered less often. Across trials, stevia showed no firm effects on blood sugar or insulin measures. Longer, cleaner trials are needed before strong claims can stand.
pmc-13306236: Renfeng Zhang and co-authors issued a correction notice in 2026 for their study of depression, anxiety and sleep problems among older adults in rural China. Two workplace affiliations are fixed, one adding a neurology department and one changing a laboratory listing to vascular surgery. Zhang and Qian Yu are also now credited as equal first authors. The notice states that the original article itself has been updated to match.
pmc-13309236:
Kenneth Maiese reviews in 2026 how dementia and mood disorders share deep cell pathways as people age, with the risk of thought loss near doubling each five years past age 65. Alzheimer disease, multiple sclerosis, depression, and anxiety sit at the core, often tangled with diabetes and other metabolic states in older adults.

Care today mostly eases signs or slows pace, with harsh side effects at times, so the hunt turns to shared roots. Cell aging and worn telomeres, worn power plants, fat and sugar faults, harsh oxygen stress, and set cell death modes all cross both groups in his map. A rapamycin switch, gut hormone drugs, and forkhead switches join the list. One path may serve both mind and mood.
pmc-13309536:
Klaus Berger and colleagues assess Parkinson disease counts and outcomes in a large German cohort in a 2026 study. Reported cases and deaths from the disease have risen for three decades worldwide. Without brain exams for all, studies must sort true cases from self-reports and billing records with care.

Among about 205,000 adults, a drug-based sorting rule put prevalence well below the level in billing data, at 0.13 percent by the stricter rule in this cohort. Self-reported cases faced fourfold higher death risk and worse mood, movement, and smell. Rates from the strict rule matched older European studies of older groups. The authors warn that loose case rules inflate counts.
pmc-13310136:
Saurav Poudel and co-authors report a teenager with a late-found birth defect of the colon in a 2026 case article. Hirschsprung disease leaves a colon segment without the nerve cells that move stool along. It is usually caught before age five, so older patients are often misread as simply constipated.

The 17-year-old boy arrived with total blockage and a swollen belly after long constipation. Scans showed a widened colon with a narrowing point, and surgery plus tissue study confirmed the disease. A first operation removed only part of the affected bowel, and blockage returned a month later. Full colon removal with a stoma followed, and he recovered after intensive care. The authors stress complete removal and close follow-up.
pmc-13310836:
M Kiran and colleagues test a plant, germ, and biochar mix to clean pesticide laced soil in a 2026 study. Chlorpyrifos lingers in farm soil and harms health, so green cleanup methods are needed. The team hunted soil germs that eat the pesticide and paired the best one with castor plants and charred plant matter.

The winning germ, a Klebsiella strain named C78, broke down most pesticide in lab fluid within 72 hours and also helped plants grow. In pots, germs plus biochar cleared nearly all pesticide within 21 days, with no build up of toxic byproducts. Plants grew better under stress. Field tests should follow.
pmc-13310936:
Christian Gold and colleagues compare two pulsed field ablation systems for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 single center study. Electric pulse ablation isolates the lung veins that trigger faulty rhythm, and one system dominates past trials. A center skilled with that system tested how a newer rival performs in first time cases.

Care covered 150 patients in total, split evenly between the two systems. Success at isolating veins was near equal, and no major harm occurred in either group. The newer system took longer inside the left heart and released more heart injury markers, while the older system shifted blood break markers more. Skill with the new system grew with use.
pmc-13311136:
Jun-Ming Zhang led a 2026 trial of crutch aided walking for early hip bone death. Death of the femoral head ball causes pain, limping, and loss of hip function, and shielded weight bearing is often advised. Solid proof for a set crutch plan was lacking, so a randomized trial was run at one center.

Fifty six patients with 96 affected hips were split between daily crutch walking for three months and no aid care, with shared drug care. At 90 days the crutch group reported far lower pain and better hip scores and gait traits. Bone marker shifts also favored the crutch group, with no serious harms.
pmc-13311636:
Julia Rehn and co-authors describe the RESPONDER feasibility trial in a 2026 protocol from Skåne, Sweden. Trained community volunteers will be alerted by phone app to give nasal naloxone at suspected opioid overdoses before ambulances arrive.

Volunteers first take a course in life support, first aid, calm approach, and the legal and ethical side of the role, and carry a study naloxone routine. The trial's main questions are whether the scheme is workable and acceptable, and whether volunteers can spot and reverse overdoses in time. Results will show if the model deserves a larger test.
pmc-13311936:
Sonia Butalia and Kara Nerenberg comment in a 2026 article on a large population study linking unhealthy plant-based diets to higher heart risk in people with prediabetes or diabetes. Plant-based eating is not automatically healthy.

The discussed study by Zhuang and colleagues sorted diets by food quality, since refined grains, sugary drinks, and sweets can all be plant-based. The commentators stress that clinics should ask what a plant-based plan actually contains before endorsing it. They also call for population steps that cut unhealthy plant foods and widen fair access to healthy ones. Label alone, they warn, misleads patients.
pmc-13312136:
Vinod Vijayakurup and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for removing pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors from a transgenic mouse model and drawing out their protein cleanly. Getting intact protein from these tumors is key to studying how they grow, but pancreatic tissue easily adds background noise and stray tissue to samples.

The mice carry a highly active human thymidylate synthase gene on a Men1-deleted background, which makes tumors appear earlier and progress faster. The protocol gives steps for taking tumors from the same region at the tail of the pancreas, keeping euthanasia conditions the same, and extracting protein suited to immunoblotting. Careful work in that one region cuts contamination from nearby tissue. The authors say the method preserves protein quality while reducing the non-specific background common in pancreatic samples.
pmc-13312336:
Sheena Mariam Thomas and colleagues report a 2026 case-control study of gene variants and polycystic ovary syndrome in South Indian women. The syndrome has a strong inherited component, yet the roles of ERBB4, a gene tied to follicle development, and SHBG, which regulates androgens, were poorly charted in this population.

The hospital-based study genotyped 200 women with the syndrome and 200 matched healthy controls at four variant sites across the two genes. One ERBB4 variant raised risk in its AA form, and another conferred roughly threefold higher risk in carriers of one copy. A SHBG variant also linked to the syndrome, while the fourth site showed no variation to analyze. The authors read the results as locus-specific genetic contributions that help explain the syndrome's tangled inheritance.
pmc-13312836:
Thi Vinh Nguyen and co-authors assess, in a 2026 study, how responsively India's health system treats its most vulnerable older patients. Responsiveness, covering prompt attention, dignity, communication, confidentiality, provider choice, and amenities, is a stated health system goal. Nobody had measured it for Indians over 60 who live with functional limitations and economic insecurity.

Drawing on the national Longitudinal Ageing Study in India, the analysis covered 16,659 people for outpatient care and 2,358 for inpatient care. The median responsiveness score sat near 75 on a hundred-point scale. Older adults with functional limitations reported clearly poorer responsiveness in both settings, and the penalty was steepest in public facilities. Among limited patients, lower caste and poorer respondents fared worst of all. The authors name the pattern ableism inside the system and call for it to be tackled directly.
pmc-13313236:
Allison Staton, Melissa Abel, and William D. Figg review a targeted plan for advanced prostate cancer in a 2026 paper. Loss of the PTEN gene is common in such tumors and switches on the PI3K/AKT path, which drives cell growth and survival, leaving patients with poor outcomes and few aimed drugs.

The review centers on capivasertib, a pill that blocks AKT, and on the phase III CAPItello-281 trial, listed as NCT04493853. Adding capivasertib to abiraterone and hormone-blocking therapy lengthened the time before scans showed growth in men whose tumors lacked PTEN, and the mix won FDA approval. Side effects in that arm included high blood sugar, loose stools, and rash, as spelled in the report. The authors frame the trial as filling a real gap for this hard-to-treat group.
pmc-13314436:
Yesul Jeong, Sangjeong Ahn, and Sung Hak Lee review AI tools that read stomach cancer slides to predict biomarkers, in a 2026 journal article. Gastric cancer varies a lot at the molecular level, and the standard gene and protein tests are costly, slow, and hungry for tissue.

The review sums up work on AI that reads whole-slide images of standard stained tissue to infer molecular subtype, gene changes open to drugs, and immune traits of the tumor setting. Models have shown promise at spotting traits such as microsatellite instability and Epstein-Barr virus status, as the authors report. Blending image data with other data types is the next step they trace. Such tools could sort patients for precise care faster and with less tissue than lab tests alone.
pmc-13314736:
Ting Dong and co-workers survey female dentists across China on career state and mental health in a study from 2026. Women make up a large share of Chinese dentists and often carry heavy workloads and job strain.

A structured survey gathered 3504 valid replies, as counted in the report, covering background, workload, pay contentment, mood, stress, and stance toward the job. A share of 27.22 percent voiced pay discontent in the figures given, while a share of 55.5 percent felt pay did not match effort and 45.32 percent felt they earned less than male peers at the same rank, all kept as stated in the report. Models then sorted which factors tie to pay views, anxiety, low mood, and staying in the field. The census gives a base for easing strain on this workforce.
pmc-13316236:
Jingrong Chen and a large team identify in 2026 mitochondrial energy making as the early, required engine behind bone growth induced by calcium phosphate ceramics. Such ceramics promise bone repair, yet the metabolic rules behind their success were undefined, so the team compared an osteoinductive tricalcium phosphate with controls.

Oxidative phosphorylation switched on early and proved indispensable. It steers a macrophage to osteoclast relay for bone formation by supplying ATP and keeping reactive oxygen in balance. Blocking energy output or disturbing that balance, either by clearing or piling up reactive oxygen, broke the relay and stopped bone formation.
pmc-13316636:
Yanmei Yin and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, precision prebiotics: food fibers reshaped by design to feed gut microbes that make short-chain fatty acids, with the aim of protecting the brain. Those acids link gut health to nerve health, yet plain fibers act too broadly to dose well.

The review maps how microbe imbalances drive brain injury paths, weighs mixed evidence on the acids' double-edged effects, and lays out ways to cut, graft, or rebuild fiber structures for strain-level targeting. Safety checks, clashing rules across countries, and slow clinical uptake get frank treatment. A roadmap closes the piece, sketching machine-guided design and personal plans matched to each person's gut community.
pmc-13320336:
Mengting Liu and co-authors sort nerve cells in a mouse hearing hub by gene voice and place in a 2026 study. The hub sits in the midbrain and handles sound location and mixed sense replies, yet its cell roster was only partly known. Single core gene reads were paired with in place gene maps to name each type and show where it lives.

Fourteen nerve cell types stood out in adult mice, sorted into firing and calming camps. Firing types clustered by zone across the hub core and its outer shells, while calming types spread more evenly. One marked group, mostly firing in nature, split further into five subtypes with zone based quirks. The atlas aids work on how hearing circuits are wired.
pmc-13320536:
Ting Hu and colleagues review how chemical edits to proteins may shape mental illness in a 2026 article. Conditions covered include schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression, all of which impair thought, mood control, or behaviour and daily life. The edits in focus occur after a protein is built and can switch its action up or down.

Common edits such as phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and acetylation guide nerve cell growth, signal strength between cells, and memory forming steps. When those edit patterns go astray, brain networks may falter in ways tied to illness. The authors argue that mapping the full edit landscape could open fresh drug targets and a more joined up view of these disorders.
pmc-13323136:
Surui Yuan and co-authors set out a protocol in 2026 for a review of statins alongside targeted drugs in lung cancer. EGFR-blocking drugs help many patients whose non-small cell lung cancer carries an EGFR mutation, yet resistance limits long-term gains, and statins may shift cholesterol and EGFR signals in useful ways.

Following standard protocol guidance, the team will search eight databases plus society sites and trial registries for trials and observational studies of statin use in this setting. Two reviewers will screen and extract data, with bias judged by tools matched to study type. Efficacy is the main interest, with reported harms as a secondary safety outcome. No results are reported at this protocol stage.
pmc-13323236:
Wenpeng Tian and co-authors propose a step-by-step risk framework for henipa-related viruses, in a 2026 conceptual article. Spillover into people alone does not decide whether an outbreak follows, even though Nipah and Hendra viruses can cause severe disease after rare animal-to-human jumps.

Their gates run from first exposure through host entry, replication with immune evasion, and onward transmission. Langya and Mojiang viruses serve as newer comparison cases beside the two established threats. Each gate is tagged by strength of evidence, with gaps split between biological unknowns and practical limits in testing, infection control and response. The authors offer the scheme as a One Health comparison tool, not a validated predictor.
pmc-13323736:
Mengru Zhang, Hang Zhao and Yunfei Wang sort generative AI users by personality and experience to explain trust and dependence, in a 2026 latent profile survey of 502 users of text-based tools. Such tools now aid daily decisions, yet their errors and bias can invite blind reliance.

Three profiles emerged, and experience changed their standing. Well-adjusted high-experience users showed the highest dependence and self-efficacy with strong trust and critical thought. Outgoing-unstructured users trusted most overall, while emotionally sensitive users scored lowest across trust, dependence, self-efficacy and critical thinking, suggesting a cautious stance. The authors argue for personalised AI literacy that fits user type rather than one standard warning.
pmc-13324236:
Maria Camila Lopez-Duarte and co-authors track circulating extracellular vesicles through cow pregnancy, in a 2026 study of crossbred Angus cattle. Thirty pregnant cows gave blood at nine points from day 45 to day 270 of gestation after timed artificial insemination, and calf sex was recorded at birth.

Vesicles from five male-carrying and five female-carrying pregnancies were sized and counted by nanoparticle flow methods and electron microscopy, with surface proteins confirming vesicle identity. Most vesicles fell in the small class, sized 50 to 200 nanometres across in the reported range. Size did not shift with fetal sex or gestation day, and concentration followed no clear pattern. The authors judge vesicle traits conserved across bovine pregnancy.
pmc-13324336:
Li He leads a team building a two-stage MRI probe for early drug-induced kidney injury, reported in 2026. Their gadolinium probe, PAH-Gd, answers first to hydrogen peroxide and then to the enzyme myeloperoxidase, the pair marking oxidative stress and inflammation in sequence.

Peroxide contact converts the probe into a kidney-seeking form that gathers in kidneys and lifts the MRI signal moderately. The enzyme then oxidises it into dimers and protein adducts, pushing the signal higher. In cisplatin-treated animals the probe read stress at twelve hours and inflammation at twenty-four hours, flagging injury at least sixty hours before standard clinical assays and tracking how damage progressed over time.
pmc-13324436:
A case report by María Rodil Riera and Claudia Mañana Valdés, published in 2026, describes a man whose lung problem looked like pneumonia but was not. The 39-year-old patient had surgery three months earlier to fix scimitar syndrome, a rare heart and vein defect. He came in with chest pain, cough, mild shortness of breath, and coughing up blood.

A chest X-ray first suggested ordinary pneumonia, so doctors started antibiotics. A CT scan then showed a large clot in the right pulmonary vein reaching into the surgical repair, plus bleeding inside the lung air spaces. Treatment switched to heparin and then enoxaparin, and the man improved. The authors warn that vein clots after this repair can mimic infection and need different care.
pmc-13325236:
Qiu Zhong and colleagues feed onion powder to broiler chickens to test it as a natural growth aid in a 2026 animal study. Plant additives are gaining ground as farms cut back on routine antibiotics.

A total of 320 day-old chicks were raised for six weeks on plain feed or feed with onion powder at 3, 3.5, or 4 g per kg. Weight gain and feed intake rose with dose, and feed conversion improved, while deaths stayed flat across groups. Gut lining grew taller villi and shallower crypts. Blood cholesterol, triglycerides, and glucose fell, and antibody responses to Newcastle disease and infectious bronchitis vaccines rose. The top dose gave the strongest overall gains.
pmc-13325936:
Yichen Bao and colleagues review how sepsis wrecks gut balance and lay out a treatment roadmap in a 2026 article. Sepsis is a runaway body response to infection, and gut injury now looks like a driver of its course rather than a bystander.

Infection sparks oxidative stress and inflammation that loosen the gut barrier, letting bacteria slip into the body. Crosstalk along the gut-liver and gut-brain routes then fans body-wide inflammation. The review maps the signaling networks behind barrier failure and immune disorder. It also weighs candidate markers for early diagnosis and gut-guarding treatments, including ideas drawn from traditional Chinese medicine.
pmc-13326636:
Alan G Fraser argues in a 2026 essay that loose talk about artificial intelligence bends medical thinking. The blanket label covers unlike tools, and its human flavor invites readers to grant software a mind.

Large language models, he notes, are statistical text predictors, while learning algorithms find patterns and neural nets map inputs to outputs. None of them knows what it does or why. The real intelligence sits with the engineers who build each system and the skeptics who judge its output. First-person chat styling worsens the illusion. He proposes the word logimorphism for crediting software with word-based human traits, and urges exact terms in clinical work.
pmc-13327536:
Luv Kishore Srivastava and colleagues explain nuclear stiffening in a childhood aging disease in a 2026 study. Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome stems from progerin, a faulty form of lamin A that builds up at the nuclear edge. Whether stiffness came from sheer amount or from how progerin links together was unclear.

Cross-linking, not amount alone, drove stiffness, and the team built a factor joining protein level with the immobile share that predicted stiffness well, with a correlation of 0.84 across their tests. Stiff, wrinkled regions resisted swelling, and weakened sensing followed, shown by poor movement of the YAP signal into the nucleus. Loosening such links may be a route to restoring how these cells feel force.
pmc-13328036:
Xiaoyan Xue and a large team report magnetocardiography findings in suspected ANOCA in a 2026 case series. ANOCA means angina with no blocked coronary arteries, and sorting true low blood flow from other causes takes a long chain of tests. Three patients with chest pain and clear arteries on CT scans were sent for magnetic heart mapping.

The maps showed clear ischemic patterns even when standard ECG tracings showed nothing, the authors report. Such mapping reads the heart's tiny magnetic fields and may expose microvascular dysfunction, a common hidden cause in this group. Series work like this lays groundwork for testing whether the method can shorten the path to a firm diagnosis in chest pain clinics.
pmc-13328436:
Kensaku Mori and Hitoshi Sakano propose a breath-timed attention switch in the smell cortex in a 2026 article. While awake, sensory signals flow forward more strongly during inhalation, letting the brain name and judge an odor, and memory scenes tied to it surface. During exhalation, higher areas send back judgments that steer behavior and rewrite memories.

Both directions share the same piriform cortex pyramidal cells, so something must flip the traffic with each breath. Mori and Sakano point to basal forebrain input onto neurogliaform cells, whose layer-specific blanket inhibition could mute forward flow and open the return path. The scheme ties smelling, remembering, and feeling into one respiratory rhythm, offered as a testable framework.
pmc-13330536:
Geum-Jae Jeong and a large team develop natural nanoemulsions for safe surface disinfection in a 2026 study. Chemical disinfectants can fail when dose or contact time falls short, and weak use can push microbes toward tolerance. Nanoemulsions spread active oils finely, giving wide contact with bacterial surfaces.

The team built emulsions held stable by biosurfactants, aiming to join surface stability with germ killing in one system. Ultrasound mixing was used to break droplets down and keep the mix even, as framed in the study design. Such plant and microbe based systems may cut reliance on harsh chemicals in health and food settings. The work targets disinfection that stays effective under real use conditions.
pmc-13333736:
Juan Cai and co-authors pooled trials in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing two ways of giving furosemide in acute heart failure. The diuretic can run as a steady infusion or arrive as repeated injections, and past trials disagreed on which works better.

Six databases were searched for randomized trials through October 2025, and 22 trials qualified. The patients had acute heart failure or advanced class III to IV symptoms. Main outcomes were death from any cause and freedom from congestion, the fluid buildup the drug aims to clear. Pooling the trials updates earlier, conflicting syntheses with a larger evidence base. The comparison matters for everyday ward decisions about how to deliver the mainstay decongestive drug.
pmc-13335036:
Muy-Teck Teh and co-authors validated a brush-based molecular test for mouth cancer in a 2026 diagnostic case-control study. Most suspicious mouth lesions are benign, yet patients endure scalpel biopsies and anxious waits because early oral squamous cell carcinoma is hard to spot.

The test, qMIDSV3, measures messenger RNA from four genes, including INHBA and S100A16, in cells brushed from a lesion and from the opposite healthy side. The study gathered 1,090 brush samples from 545 patients, covering cancer, leukoplakia, and lichen planus cases. Building on an earlier microbiopsy assay, the brush version aims to separate cancer from low-risk lesions quickly and without cutting. A noninvasive triage tool of this kind could speed true cancers to treatment and spare benign cases the knife.
pmc-13336636:
Yuechao Chao and a large team present low-cost films in a 2026 study that pull moisture from indoor air and later release it as fresh water. Humid rooms in hot climates usually rely on power-hungry machines to dry the air. These films instead capture, store, and release water in one passive layer.

In tests the films drove relative humidity down to 21.6% from a starting 90.7% in one hour and kept working over time in the reported runs. Released water reached about 1.1 kg per square meter per day and fed an automatic plant watering setup. Global estimates suggest yearly energy and carbon savings per square meter, with costs repaid in 48 days in the modeled case.
pmc-13336836:
Zhi-hua Ye and colleagues screen the whole genome for genes that stop colorectal cancer spread in a 2026 study. Their living-animal screen used a hairpin RNA library plus sequencing to flag six candidate blockers. One gene, HOXD4, stood out with the strongest effect and was much lower in tumors than in nearby normal tissue.

Low HOXD4 matched more aggressive tumor traits. Removing it made cancer cells migrate, invade, and form spheres more readily, while adding it back reversed those behaviors. HOXD4 binds the promoter of FOXQ1, a driver of shape change and stemness, and switches it down. Patient tissue checks confirmed the inverse pattern. Restoring this brake could help intercept spread.
pmc-13337036:
Filippos Perdikos leads a large 2026 team making a soft magnetic-electric dressing for skin wounds. The dressing stacks a zinc oxide layer that makes voltage under strain over an iron-gallium layer that stretches in magnetic fields, all set in soft silicone rubber. Stiff older designs clamped the effect, so being soft and bendy came first.

Weak, slow magnetic fields switch the dressing on with no wires, making mild electric pulses at the wound. In lab dishes, two kinds of human skin cells stayed healthy under the pulses. One type layered better, the other made more collagen, and both moved faster than untreated cells. Such dressings could help chronic wounds that stall for months.
pmc-13337436:
Xiaoya Wang and co-authors recast acute lung injury as a failed conversation among innate immune cells in a 2026 review. The classic picture blames cytokine floods and barrier breakdown, yet it cannot explain why some lungs heal and others spiral into lasting damage. Macrophages and innate lymphoid cells, especially ILC2s, run tissue-centered circuits that decide the outcome.

Macrophages shift roles over time, from sentinels and amplifiers to cleaners and repair coordinators, guided by origin and local niche. ILCs translate epithelial alarms into protective responses and tune macrophage behavior. When this three-way network with epithelial cells breaks, inflammation persists and regeneration stalls. The review maps those circuits to find repair-restoring targets.
pmc-13337936:

pmc-13339436:

pmc-13340736:

pmc-13341436:

pmc-13341536:

pmc-13342436:

pmc-13344836:

pmc-13345836:
Mick O'Kelly, Serggio C. Lanata, and Jonathan K. Kleen present a perspective in 2026 on turning brainwaves into stained glass for people living with dementia. pmc-13346336:

pmc-13346836:

pmc-13348036:

pmc-13349836:

pmc-13350036:
Chen Zhang and fellow authors reviewed mast cells as a central hub in vitiligo in a 2026 article. Vitiligo, where skin loses its pigment, mixes inherited risk, chemical stress, autoimmunity, and nerve influences, and no single-cause model explains it fully.

pmc-13350236:

pmc-13350436:

pmc-13350536:

pmc-13351436:

pmc-13351636:
Paddy McCrossan, Michael D Shields, and James McElnay offer a 2026 editorial on paying children to keep up asthma medicine over the long term. pmc-13352336:
Rattan Singh and colleagues report airbag injuries to the eyes and face in two unrestrained children in 2026. Both children suffered eye and face injuries when the airbag deployed. The report sets out how deployment forces strike small front-seat passengers who sit too close and without restraints. pmc-13352636:
Quintashia D. Wilson and colleagues create silicon-bearing dyes that glow in the shortwave infrared in 2026. pmc-13356736:

pmc-13358536:

pmc-13358736:
Hajar Habibi and co-authors review how to give adults born with heart defects a stronger voice in their own care in a 2026 paper. Good care, the authors argue, must go beyond the medical side and build patient confidence and engagement.

pmc-13358836:

pmc-13359236:

pmc-13361636:

pmc-13361736:

A quick, portable scan that adds real warning power could help wards decide who needs close watch after delivery.
pmc-13361936:

pmc-13364236:

pmc-13364636:

pmc-13364736:

pmc-13365536:

pmc-13366536:

pmc-13367436:

pmc-13367536:

pmc-13371236:

pmc-13378136:

pmc-13391436:

pmc-13391736:

pmc-13392136:

pmc-13392636:

pmc-13393236:

pmc-13393336:

pmc-13394136:

pmc-13394336:

pmc-13395036:

pmc-13395436:
Mariana Tome and colleagues evaluate, in 2026, a digital helper for labour triage named Fit4Labour across three British hospitals. Sessions used set cases, ease scores, and group talks.

pmc-13395836:
David R. Clemmons and colleagues re-read, in 2026, trial data on a daily pill for acromegaly, a growth hormone excess illness. pmc-13396036:
Timothy Isaac Murphy and co-authors checked how faithfully near reading charts follow world standards, in a 2026 study drawn from charts used in community eye clinics. Near vision testing guides glasses and low-vision care, yet the print on many charts had never been verified.

Nineteen charts, from makers and device firms, were scanned at high resolution and their letter heights measured by three graders working alone. Contrast and line spacing were estimated too, and each chart was scored against the relevant ISO standard. Agreement among graders was checked with a standard statistic. pmc-13396236:

Earlier frameworks handled membrane pulses and impedance apart, or used cartoon cell shapes. By joining the two signal types, the authors aim for a label-free check that cell therapy makers could run before releasing a batch.
pmc-13396736:
Berihu Gebre and co-authors follow a two-year-old girl with a rare inherited disorder of energy use whose brain injury spread between scans, in a 2026 case report. pmc-13396936:
Tyler D. Coolman and co-authors write to the editor in 2026 about a stain called PRAME and the false alarms it can raise in sun-damaged skin. PRAME is a protein used to help diagnose melanoma. Gene tests for it now guide whether a pigmented spot gets biopsied, including a tape-based test used on the skin surface.

The authors characterize its staining in scaly sun spots called actinic keratoses and in surface squamous cell cancers. They warn that loose reading of the marker may push doctors to biopsy growths that are not melanoma at all.
pmc-13398136:

Their 2026 study presents ARGENT, a framework that scans a protein's DNA-contact surface and proposes arginine swaps likely to help. DNA-binding proteins are handy biotech scaffolds, but no general recipe existed for rewiring how they grip DNA.

Six single changes sped up cutting, and the best triple version ran about four times faster than the natural enzyme while still spotting mismatches. Plugged into a layered sensing cascade, the souped-up enzyme sharpened multiplex detection of viral RNA.
pmc-13398536:

Their 2026 study builds organoids from 35 tumours of pancreatic, small intestinal and gastric origin, taken from 17 patients. These slow cancers offer few drug targets, and the field lacked faithful lab models to screen therapies.
