Morita and co-authors introduce TENET, a deep learning system that sharpens two-photon microscope images, the workhorse tool for filming living tissue deep inside animals. TENET, described in 2026, learns without any paired sharp examples. It builds its own model of how the microscope blurs, using a trainable estimate of the blur pattern that needs only a rough starting guess. It then reverses the blur and labels structures in the same pass.

On synthetic images, fluorescent beads, and living brain tissue, TENET beat three established sharpening methods on both picture fidelity and how accurately it outlined cells. It could raise resolution by up to twelvefold along the blurred axis. Applied to time-lapse films of microglia, the brain's immune cells, swarming around metastatic tumours, it produced ready-made three-dimensional masks that revealed changing cell-tumour interactions automatically.
pmc-13499236:
Liu and co-authors attack turbulence modelling, the weak point of fluid simulation, by training one unified data-driven model instead of a shelf of special-purpose ones. Engineers usually average out turbulence's chaos with formulas tuned per flow type, and each fails outside its niche. Their 2026 framework bakes physical consistency into a frame-invariant model. It picks training cases by how similar their flow features are, and learns through multi-objective training that balances competing demands across flows.

Trained on nine canonical flows, from separated flow over a hill to free jets, the single model beat existing turbulence models across the test spectrum. It also held its advantage on realistic three-dimensional shapes: a gas turbine diffuser, one generic car, and one generic aircraft. When one application needs extra precision, the team additively fine-tunes a specialist on top without retraining everything.
pmc-13499636:
Samia Benlabed and colleagues report in 2026 a heart mass first taken for a giant blood clot that proved instead to be cancer growing inside the heart's vessels. Their patient had a metastatic solitary fibrous tumour, a rare growth of connective tissue. Scans showed a large, multi-lobed mass in the left upper heart chamber swinging through the mitral valve with each cycle. No irregular heartbeat rhythm or valve disease explained a clot, yet blockage or embolism risk was imminent.

Blood-thinning treatment began while a multidisciplinary team chose surgery, and the mass was removed. Lab examination showed a malignant growth of vessel-lining-like cells with severe abnormality and rapid division, and a positive marker test confirmed the fibrous tumour had spread there. The authors stress that ultrasound imaging and tissue proof play complementary roles when a mass could be either clot or cancer.
pmc-13499836:
Daniel P Marshall and colleagues review in 2026 why sacral neuromodulation, electrical stimulation of sacral nerves, helps some people with overactive bladder that resists other treatment while leaving others unhelped. Settings for the implanted device have barely changed since United States approval in 1997, and how the therapy works remains murky. Their analysis covered 45 clinical studies published from 1994 to 2023 and examined device design, anatomy, mechanisms, and programming choices.

Long-term symptom control rates showed no significant improvement across three decades despite better hardware, and in recent studies a large share of patients given a trial stimulation gained no benefit. Knowledge gaps span sacral nerve anatomy, which nerve fibres carry the effect, how body variation changes outcomes, and which patients will succeed long term. The authors propose realistic computer models of nerve and tissue plus systematic recording of settings and results.
pmc-13500836:
Yuan Jiang leads a four-author team with a 2026 survey of emergency nurses in Shanghai about AI-augmented triage systems, software that helps rank incoming patients by urgency. The cross-sectional survey covered 162 frontline triage nurses at nine pilot hospitals between June and August 2025. Every nurse had at least six months of triage experience and three months of hands-on use of the AI system. Responses were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling, a method for testing linked attitudes.

The model explained 57.2 percent of the variation in attitude and 41.0 percent of the variation in plans to use the system. Task-technology fit, perceived explainability, and psychological safety each related positively to nurses' stance, with coefficients between about 0.385 and 0.483 in size. That stance in turn related strongly to intention. Perceived risk slightly weakened the step from a favourable attitude to an intention to use the tool.
pmc-13505036:
Charles E Whitehead-Tillery leads a team comparing drug-resistant E. coli from people and dogs, in a 2026 genomic study. Some strains make enzymes that break down key antibiotics, and the genes ride on small DNA rings that jump between bacteria. Pets could share those rings with owners.

The team read 149 DNA rings from human and dog strains. Three quarters carried the resistance enzyme genes, with one variant ruling human samples and another leading in dogs. Ring families overlapped across hosts, and family trees mixed human and dog rings carrying like gene sets. A notorious human strain type was absent in dogs. The authors argue the shared elements support joint human-pet surveillance of resistance spread.
pmc-13505136:
Anna-Elisabeth Baumann and co-authors used a large Canadian cohort that followed children over time to trace how early language connects with later behaviour. They measured the words children could say at age two, then core and social language skills at age five. Behaviour problems at age eight were split into inward signs, such as anxiety, and outward signs, such as aggression.

Models that follow paths between measures showed indirect links running through both kinds of language skill at age five. Children with smaller early vocabularies tended to show more inward and outward symptoms later, with part of that pattern passing through their school-age language. The authors argue that social language, meaning language used with other people, deserves the same attention as basic vocabulary and grammar in this research.
pmc-13507136:
Wen Wang, Yi Zhang, and Risheng Gao study, in 2026 work, whether digital technology use links to cleaner home energy in rural China. Survey data come from the Hundred Villages and Thousand Households project in Jiangxi Province. Statistical matching compared adopters with similar non-adopters to limit bias from background differences.

Digital adoption linked to stronger clean energy use, and the link held after matching. Two paths stood out: more off-farm work, which raises the time cost of gathering wood fuels, and stronger social ties, which spread peer influence. The link was strongest for cooking energy and weakest for water heating. Information-focused use mattered more than entertainment use.
pmc-13507236:
Feng Zhang leads a 2026 survey team that measures what diabetes patients in Suzhou, China know and do about continuous glucose monitors, wearables that track sugar around the clock. A community health center enrolled 576 patients in late 2023, with average age near sixty-six. Questionnaires scored knowledge, attitudes, and daily practice separately.

Knowledge scored low, while attitudes and practice landed in the middle range. The three scores moved together, and modeling showed knowledge lifting practice both directly and through better attitudes. Older patients, those with less schooling, and those never taught about the devices lagged most. Targeted teaching could plausibly raise real-world monitor use in community care.
pmc-13508236:
Yael Yagur leads a nine-author team comparing molar pregnancies in younger and older women, in work published in 2026. A molar pregnancy is an abnormal growth in the womb that must be removed and watched. The team reviewed cases confirmed by tissue tests between 2014 and 2021. In all, 115 cases qualified, most of them partial moles and a smaller set complete moles. Women ranged from 16 to 55 years old.

Partial moles were far more common in women aged 40 and under. Complete moles were more common in women over 40, even after wider adjustments. The hormone marker fell fastest in the first month and cleared within three months in nine of ten cases. A later cancer-like complication arose in seven cases, with no age split. The authors conclude the outlook after treatment is good across ages, though complete moles deserve close care in older women.
pmc-13508336:
Conghui Guo and five co-authors study a calcium-channel helper protein that helps trigger egg release by drawing immune cells into the ovary, in 2026 work. Earlier cell-level work in goats flagged this protein, CACNA2D1, as a possible player in ovulation. The team blocked its signaling in a mouse ovulation model and measured immune cell entry and egg output. In dish tests, they raised and lowered the protein in ovarian support cells and watched calcium signals and the chemical calls those cells send out.

Blocking the protein in mice cut immune cell entry, above all macrophages, and lowered egg release. In support cells, lowering the protein drained calcium signals and muted three immune call chemicals. Restoring calcium brought those calls back. The cells also lost their power to draw immune cells across a filter. The work ties a calcium pathway to the immune surge that healthy ovulation needs.
pmc-13509736:
Sun and colleagues present a 2026 review of optical sensing arrays paired with machine learning for disease diagnosis. These arrays use sets of light-based sensors, colored, glowing, or laser-scattering, whose combined pattern forms a fingerprint of a sample.  The review covers the three sensor families and the learning methods behind them.

Reported uses reach high accuracy in detecting cancers and infections from blood and other samples, at low cost and speed. The authors weigh strengths by family: color tests are cheapest, fluorescence is sensitive, and Raman scattering gives the richest fingerprints. Open problems include handling varied real-world samples and proving accuracy outside the lab. Cheap sensors plus smart software could bring lab-grade screening to thin clinics.
pmc-13510836:
Antoine and co-authors wrote a 2026 state of the art review on plasticizers, chemicals that soften plastics, and female reproductive health. Classic phthalates disrupt hormones and have been tied to problems with egg growth, implantation, and pregnancy. Newer substitutes are sold as safer, and the review checks that claim against lab evidence.

Antoine links phthalate exposure to miscarriage, preeclampsia, and preterm birth through effects on hormone output and on the placenta. The common substitutes, including DINCH, TOTM, DEHA, and ATBC, also disturb hormone pathways in newer studies. Both groups act on nuclear receptors that control ovary function and pregnancy upkeep, above all in the placenta and fetal membranes. The authors urge cutting exposure for women of childbearing age while evidence grows.
pmc-13511536:
Ayfer Aydın, Merve Ertunç Soycan, Özlem Şensoy, Hülya Dalkılıç Bingöl, and Rejin Kebudi interview nurses in children's cancer units about the borders of empathy, in a 2026 qualitative study. Seventeen nurses with at least two years in pediatric blood and cancer units spoke in individual video interviews until no new themes appeared. Empathy sits at the heart of care for children with cancer, yet closeness carries emotional costs.

Three themes organized the accounts: grasping what empathy means, living its path over a career, and paying its price. Nurses called empathy a core skill that grows with experience and separates good care from routine care. Holding a line between deep engagement and professional distance proved hard, and heavy involvement fed compassion fatigue and exhaustion. The authors call for structured training and stronger workplace support so nurses can stay empathic without burning out.
pmc-13514736:
Osonoi and co-authors published a 2026 post hoc analysis of imeglimin, a diabetes drug aimed at mitochondria, and how blood flows in type 2 diabetes. Stiff red blood cells that cannot bend well contribute to small vessel damage in this disease. The parent INFINITY study had already found the drug lengthens red cell lifespan.

Twenty-five patients finished six months on the drug followed by three months off it for this analysis. Osonoi timed how fast whole blood passed through a microchannel device mimicking tiny vessels. Passage time improved significantly by months four to six, then slipped back after the drug stopped. Red cell lifespan rose by ten to twenty percent and stayed longer after stopping, while blood counts dipped during treatment and recovered.
pmc-13514936:
Ioannis Ilias and eleven colleagues map a hormone network in critical illness in a 2026 prospective pilot study. They measured ten components of the growth hormone system plus the stress protein GDF-15 in forty-three intensive care patients. Each marker had been proposed separately as a survival signal, yet nobody had charted how they relate in the same patients. Blood drawn at admission anchored the analysis, with follow-up through day fifteen and checks against standard severity scores.

Four markers clustered tightly together: GDF-15 rose and fell with two binding proteins and the growth hormone's carrier protein, forming a group set apart from classic hormone-resistance signals. Those links barely budged after adjusting for illness severity, age, inflammation, and other factors, though one pairing weakened once inflammation entered the model. GDF-15 alone discriminated survivors moderately, while the standard severity scores did better.
pmc-13515136:
Huiting Zhu, Douyan Cao, and Jigang Zhao test electrodialysis for a chemical separation problem in a 2026 process study. Making taurine, an ingredient in infant formula and energy drinks, leaves a mother liquor mixed with sodium sulfate salt. The team instead drove the salt out with electric fields across membranes, tuning voltage, flow, and starting strength, with computer modelling of ion movement.

At their best settings the process reached taurine purity near ninety-nine point eight percent and recovered nearly ninety-nine percent of it. One insight stood out: the final low-salt stage eats most of the cost. Stopping once the salt fell to a set low level cut energy use by a sixth. Within their lab-scale, two-component test system, the method beat the standard route on recovery and estimated cost.
pmc-13515836:
Chenguang Zhang and five colleagues show how laser pulses can stand in for cosmic rays when testing power transistors for space, in a 2026 study. Silicon carbide MOSFETs can burn out in a single radiation strike, yet heavy-ion beam tests are slow and costly. The team used femtosecond laser pulses absorbed in pairs inside a commercial 1200 volt device. They built a corrected formula that maps laser energy onto the ion scale, fixing the classic square law where it breaks at high intensity.

Three failure signs appeared as energy climbed: two kinds of leakage and full burnout. The burnout threshold settled near five hundred volts once the ion-equivalent dose passed a set level, well below the device rating. Their safe-area map marks voltages below two hundred as safe and those above six hundred as high risk. Laser results matched published ion data closely.
pmc-13516036:
Imola-Rebeka Turac and colleagues review how quality-by-design thinking and live process checks could make 3D-printed medicines safe to produce on demand. Printed doses can be tailored to each patient at the care site, but ready quality checks are missing.

Light-based tools, near-infrared and Raman scans, can check printed tablets without destroying them, the review finds. So far these tools mostly check finished products, not the printing process live as a full quality loop needs. Most scan models also work for just one recipe, printer, and drug, with little proof they transfer elsewhere. Turac notes regulators are drafting point-of-care rules, but standard quality demands remain the main barrier to routine use.
pmc-13517236:
Ashfaq and colleagues reviewed in 2026 ways to improve the microbes living in dairy cows to lift health and milk output. Farmers must produce more milk while cutting disease, antibiotic use, and environmental harm. The review compares probiotics, meaning helpful live microbes fed to cows, transfers of gut microbes, data-guided farm management, and gene-based methods. It judges how close each approach is to routine farm use.

Probiotics are already delivering gains: better milk production, healthier animals, less disease, and lower antibiotic need. Microbe transfers and gene-based tools show promise but need more research before wide, safe use. The authors argue future progress depends on matching the approach to each animal rather than one solution for every herd. The review gives farmers and researchers a readiness map of the options now emerging.
pmc-13518836:
Lin and colleagues build paper-ready risk calculators for the two microvascular complications that stalk type 2 diabetes: eye damage and kidney damage. Using records from 6,043 patients, their 2026 study started from 38 candidate variables. A selection algorithm called LASSO kept only the informative ones, eight for eye disease and fifteen for kidney disease, before the final models were fitted. Each model was drawn as a nomogram, a chart where clinicians add up points to read off a patient's risk.

The two models leaned on different variable sets, the kidney model's list running longer. Accuracy was moderate rather than spectacular, with discrimination scores in the low seventies on validation in the reported analysis, and calibration looked satisfactory. The authors pitch the charts for busy clinics that need a fast, transparent way to flag high-risk patients for screening.
pmc-13518936:
Jicheng Yu and four colleagues design a 2026 sensor array for measuring current in electric vehicle charging cables without touching them. Accurate cable current readings govern charging station safety and performance, since insulation faults can cause shocks or fires. Their array uses tunnel magnetoresistance sensors, which sense magnetic fields from the cable's current.

Bench tests showed the array beat a single sensor, with best accuracy at a 3 centimeter distance from the cable. The setup then tracked real-time charging current across ten different vehicle brands and models. Yu and co-authors present the array as a precise, stable, non-contact monitor suited to the fast-growing charging networks that new energy vehicles depend on.
pmc-13520336:
Mona Michaud and colleagues review in 2026 wearable sensors for walking checks in Parkinson disease during daily life. Home checks may show day-to-day swings that a single office walk can miss. Sensor scores are called digital mobility outcomes in this field.

Searches of three databases for 2013 to 2023 found 63 studies. All used body-worn motion sensors at home or in the wild. Stride speed stood out as the most settled and useful score. Stride length, timing and pace also look strong for care and research. Study designs varied a lot, and group sizes were often small. Shared methods would help future work compare cleanly.
pmc-13521536:
Maheshwari and colleagues examined in 2026 whether adding silver nanoparticles improves two root canal sealers, using microscope imaging and X-ray element analysis. They treated 52 extracted single-rooted teeth, split into four groups covering a resin sealer and a bioceramic sealer, each with and without the silver particles.

All sealers entered the tiny dentin tubules, reaching deeper in the crown and middle parts of the root than near the tip. The nanoparticle versions penetrated further and fit the canal walls better than the plain sealers. Element analysis confirmed silver was spread evenly through the modified materials. The authors conclude the particles improve sealing behavior, a property that helps keep treated canals free of bacteria.
pmc-13522436:
Xiaoxue Guan, Qiang Zhao, Yong Deng, and Zuneng Lu search for an inflammation-linked marker for Parkinson disease in a 2026 analysis that combines several data types. Single-cell and bulk gene data were joined with network analysis to find genes tied to inflammation. Cell experiments and blood specimens from patients were then used to check one leading candidate.

Inflammation rose as disease advanced and tracked shifts in cell makeup, with microglia, the immune cells of the brain, playing a central part. The candidate gene, TBXAS1, affected nerve cell growth and death in laboratory tests, possibly by shaping inflammatory signals released by microglia. The authors propose it as a possible marker and target for later work on prediction and treatment.
pmc-13522536:
Alison T Cribb, Simon A F Darroch, and William Gearty ask whether animals that reshape their surroundings raised ocean diversity across deep time in a 2026 fossil study. Such ecosystem engineers include reef builders and burrowing animals that stir the seafloor. Fossil communities with and without engineers were compared at each stage of the Phanerozoic, the long span of visible animal life.

Communities containing engineers held significantly higher diversity during most of that span, including a role in sustaining diversity through mass extinctions. Reef builders of the last quarter-billion years proved more sensitive to climate stress than burrowers. Both groups had their strongest effects at moderate temperatures. The results credit habitat-shaping animals with a central part in the long history of marine diversity.
pmc-13522736:
Jian He leads a multicenter 2026 study asking whether the timing of immunotherapy matters in unresectable liver cancer treated with combined therapy. Three hundred fifty patients at six academic centers received local artery-based treatment plus the drug lenvatinib and a PD-1 inhibitor, a type of immune checkpoint drug. Patients were grouped by whether the immune drug started before or after the local treatment.

Starting the immune drug first was linked to longer overall survival in the full group, driven mainly by patients receiving arterial infusion chemotherapy rather than artery-blocking treatment. The benefit held after statistical matching and landmark checks, and response rates were higher with early immune treatment. Progression-free survival also improved in the infusion group. The authors suggest sequencing deserves attention when planning triple therapy.
pmc-13522936:
Stefano Lasaponara leads a team linking temperament traits to sleep quality in a 2026 cross-sectional study of three hundred ninety-four healthy adults. Temperament was measured with a questionnaire grounded in a model that ties personality traits to brain chemical systems also involved in sleep and body rhythms. Participants also completed validated measures of sleep quality, insomnia, daytime sleepiness, and arousal before sleep, plus anxiety and depression scales.

Neuroticism and impulsivity tracked poorer sleep, worse insomnia, and stronger mental arousal before sleep, with much of the effect passing through anxiety and depression. Faster social tempo linked to better sleep and less daytime sleepiness. Other traits, including empathy and physical endurance, also played a part. The authors argue that temperament profiling could guide personalized sleep interventions.
pmc-13523336:
Kaikai Zhao and colleagues review CD45 as both an immune regulator and a delivery target in a 2026 article. CD45 is an enzyme found on nearly all white blood cells, where it sets signaling thresholds that control cell activation. Its disruption is implicated in immune diseases and blood cancers. The review gathers mechanisms across immune cell types and the strategies built around them.

Approaches covered include changing CD45 levels, altering its shape, and redistributing it on the cell membrane. Because CD45 is specific to white cells and widely expressed, it also serves as an address for drug delivery, including antibody-drug conjugates and living cell carriers loaded through CD45 binding. The authors aim to connect basic immunology with practical therapeutic design.
pmc-13523436:
Zhenyu Zhai and colleagues present a 2026 case report about a patient with giant aneurysms of a diagonal branch of a coronary artery, together with blocked coronary disease. Coronary aneurysms are focal widenings at least one and a half times the width of nearby normal vessel. Imaging alone left the size, origin, and relations of the aneurysm uncertain, so the team built printed heart models before operating.

Computed tomography data were turned into multicolor, multiplanar three-dimensional models that showed the vessels and nearby tissue in physical form. Surgeons then carried out bypass grafting followed by removal of the aneurysm. The authors argue that model-guided planning helps a team judge dimensions and vessel relationships more confidently before a difficult operation, and they frame the case as guidance for similar rare presentations.
pmc-13526036:
Tala H. Fakhouri and others argue, in a 2026 perspective, that real-world evidence remains underused in drug approvals despite a decade of investment and supportive legislation. Evidence from records, claims, and registries can complement trials, notably for rare diseases. Three operational barriers, the authors say, keep otherwise usable data from regulators.

First, submission standards were built around a trial data format ill-suited to varied real-world sources. Second, expectations about when patient-level data sets must go in, and how inspectors may access source records, stay unclear. Third, uncertainty surrounds applying human-subject rules written for interventional research to non-interventional studies. Their recommendations target each barrier, warning that ambiguity wastes sponsor resources, sidelines good data, and can delay patient access to effective therapies.
pmc-13526536:
Bauerle traces the rise and fall of phrenology, the claim that skull bumps reveal mind and character. Franz Joseph Gall and Johann Gaspar Spurzheim launched the idea in the early eighteen hundreds. It drew wide fame in Europe and America despite weak proof from the start.

Bauerle shows the idea was used to back racist and sexist claims of its day. Yet some shut-out groups used its readings for self-checks and hopes of rising in life. One core idea, that set brain areas serve set tasks, later proved partly right. That seed fed real brain science, even as bump reading fell as fraud. The tale warns how a false scheme can still spur true finds.
pmc-13526736:
Marion Berdal and colleagues adapt, in a 2026 radiochemistry study, the production of a gallium-68 labeled imaging tracer for clinical use. The tracer targets fibroblast activation protein, a tumor marker, using a single-domain antibody, a tiny antibody fragment with favorable body handling for PET scanning. A preclinical recipe existed, yet robust clinical manufacturing did not.

Both a manual kit method and automated synthesis on two platforms were developed. Labeling ran at fifty degrees for ten minutes, converted over ninety percent of material, and needed no purification, with radiochemical purity near ninety-nine percent by one method. Stress testing across activity levels and buffer conditions showed stability, two generator systems performed alike, and the product stayed usable for at least three hours. The authors claim broader clinical access will follow.
pmc-13528036:
Berhanu Fikadie Endehabtu and eight colleagues chart implementation research in Ethiopia's health system in a 2026 scoping review. Such research tests how proven ideas get used in real clinics. The search found 10,853 records. Ninety-six studies passed full review.

Most studies targeted service delivery, above all maternal, newborn, child, and reproductive care. Health information systems drew sixteen studies. Leadership and financing drew only five. Mixed methods were the most common design. Reported outcomes included fidelity, feasibility, acceptability, and cost-effectiveness. Many studies named barriers and supports that shape success on the ground. The authors say the field is growing but lopsided. They urge more work on governance and money, which decide whether good programs survive.
pmc-13528136:
Zhou Fang and seven colleagues fuse tiny vesicles from two kingdoms of life to carry cancer drugs in a 2026 study. One partner was vesicles shed by mouse breast tumor cells. The other came from kiwifruit. The hybrid homes to tumors like the tumor vesicles do. It was loaded with the drug doxorubicin plus a gene silencer against Bcl-2.

The fruit part woke up dendritic cells, the immune system's teachers. That boosted antigen display and killer T cell entry into tumors. The drug and silencer together killed tumor cells more strongly. In mice with breast tumors, the combo beat plain approaches clearly. The authors claim a first: cross-species fusion boosting aim and immunity at once. They offer the platform as a template for safer chemo-immune mixes.
pmc-13530136:
Deepak Chandra Joshi and co-authors present a 2026 system that detects grip and elbow bending at the same time for prosthetic control. Muscle signals alone often blur when movements overlap, so the team added pressure and motion sensing. Data flowed from arm electrodes, a balance board with pressure sensors, and a nine-axis motion unit.

A neural network with memory and attention read the combined streams in short windows. Scores for correct detection stayed high at both window and whole-file levels. Motion and pressure signals carried the most weight, while muscle signals filled gaps, supporting steadier control of assistive arms.
pmc-13530236:
Quentin Hallez, Diana Reyes Pavón, and Valentin Flaudias study in 2026 how food pictures warp time judgment in teenage girls. Fifty-five students aged 14 to 19 from a French high school judged how long high-calorie and low-calorie food images stayed on screen. Questionnaires then measured media pressure, body appreciation, and eating attitudes.

Rich food images made durations feel longer than lean food images did. Stronger felt media pressure magnified that stretch, while stronger body appreciation tended to shrink it. The authors read the pattern as social pressure reshaping a basic mental process through feelings about food, and they call for longer studies.
pmc-13530536:
Abdalla and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 174, a study linking youth sport specialization to performance on a deep squat test they graded with a new two-part classification. Early single-sport focus is suspected of raising overuse injury risk, but clinics lack a quick whole-body screen like a cholesterol panel.

At Detroit school sports physicals, 136 athletes from kindergarten through twelfth grade were sorted into 63 single-sport and 73 multi-sport athletes. They were graded on squat depth and on rising strength, with 4C the perfect mark. Multi-sport athletes hit that top grade far more often, about fifty-five percent against thirty-three percent for single-sport athletes in this screening sample. The chance of a top grade also rose steadily with each additional sport played. The authors propose the squat grade as a preseason risk indicator.
pmc-13531536:
Dowrick and co-authors examine a hidden casualty of digital-first primary care in this 2026 analysis: patients living with domestic abuse. A face-to-face visit can be a rare safe space away from a controlling partner's surveillance, where a trusted clinician might spot trouble. Phone and online consultations, taken from home under that same surveillance, change the equation entirely.

The authors describe how survivors test the waters with safer complaints like headaches or tiredness while judging whether a clinician can be trusted, a negotiation that monitored remote contact can foreclose. Digital triage forms and shared devices can also expose help-seeking to the abuser. Their recommendations push practices to preserve in-person routes. Practices should also build safe contact protocols. Staff should be trained to create private moments within remote care. That way, modernization does not quietly lock out the patients who most need a refuge.
pmc-13531736:
Nubwa Medugu leads a 2026 genome study of drug-resistant E. coli in Nigeria, where key antibiotics often fail. Whole-genome reading of 107 clinical isolates mapped the mutations and mobile genes behind resistance, and sorted strain families. Lab testing measured how each isolate handled two key drugs.

Resistance to ciprofloxacin reached 86 percent. A fixed trio of chromosome mutations predicted that resistance perfectly when present, while plasmid-carried genes alone did not. A high-risk strain family dominated and always carried the full trio. Six urine isolates resisted without any known mechanism, signaling unknown routes.
pmc-13531936:
Supakorn Chaiyakarn leads a 2026 randomized trial on using neck-of-womb length to guide care for threatened early labor. Many women with warning contractions never deliver soon, yet receive steroids and contraction drugs anyway. Fifty women with cervix lengths in a middle range were split between watchful waiting and standard treatment.

The watchful group received drugs only if the cervix shrank notably or fell below a floor value. Inappropriate treatment dropped by about 92 percent against the treated group. Mothers in the watchful arm also saw fewer racing heart, pressure, and potassium side effects, plus shorter stays.
pmc-13534436:
Mohammad Khosravi and colleagues simulate in 2026 a way to keep MRI magnetic fields even when a patient moves. Uneven fields blur images and widen spectral lines, and standard shim coils have limited power to fix them. Their system pairs standard shims with a 31-channel local coil array.

Adding the local coils improved field evenness in tests, yet motion quickly eroded the gain. A deep learning tool predicted field changes in real time and restored evenness during large moves. Performance matched methods that need extra scans, while adding no scan time to main sequences.
pmc-13534636:
Gina Picchiarelli and colleagues show in 2026 that FUS, a protein mutated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, directly supports muscle formation. Muscle weakness in the disease is often blamed only on nerve loss, yet muscle defects may start inside muscle cells. Mouse and fly models with a knock-in change showed cell-level harm.

Muscle fibres showed broken internal structure and faulty energy parts even without nerve input. FUS helps switch on muscle genes by joining two gene-control factors, forming droplets that gather them at gene start sites. Lowering one partner worsened weakness in mutant mice.
pmc-13536536:
Mostafa Sajedi Nia, Mehdi Khaleghi Tazji, and Ali Abbasi study in 2026 how two deadlift loading orders affect spine and pelvis coordination. Lifters often raise loads step by step or start heavy and drop down, with unlike demands on the trunk. Twelve trained male powerlifters lifted under both orders while motion capture tracked segment links.

In-phase patterns dominated key couplings under both orders. Rising loads shifted control toward distal segments and cut proximal input, most at the heaviest step. Variability did not differ clearly, so the authors flag rising loads as riskier for coordination breakdown.
pmc-13536636:
Meltem Ozduyan Kilic, Ergun Kaplan, and Fatos Korkmaz adapt in 2026 the Shinners scale on views of artificial intelligence for Turkish nursing students. Sound tools to gauge student views of AI were scarce outside English settings. Translation and expert review shaped the Turkish form, tested on 412 students in Ankara.

The adapted scale kept eight items in two factors, one on AI impact on the nursing role and one on readiness for AI. Scores were consistent over time and across repeat testing rounds. The authors advise wider checks before use beyond similar student groups.
pmc-13536836:
Marie Chantal Ingabire surveys what nurses know about mental health at rural community health centers in western Rwanda in a 2026 study. Primary clinics now carry much mental health care, yet nurse knowledge is poorly known. Seventy-four nurses from thirteen centers judged case stories, listed risk factors, and named helpful people and steps. Answers were related to schooling and work variables.

Recognition was strongest for trauma stress disorder and depression, each spotted by about six in ten nurses, and weakest for generalized anxiety. Most nurses named true risk factors such as loss of a loved one, yet many also endorsed false causes such as evil possession or weak character. Counselors were most often named as helpful. Schooling and in-service training showed no link to knowledge, prompting a call for stronger training.
pmc-13538536:
Wenbao Shi and colleagues probe how prior damage alters sandstone behavior under fast pulling loads in a 2026 rock mechanics study. Deep mines subject surrounding rock to repeated loading plus sudden impacts, and failure tends to be tensile. Sandstone samples were pre-damaged by cyclic loading, then split dynamically in a pressure bar rig, while X-ray scanning mapped inner crack growth at each damage level.

Cyclic loading merged inner cracks and raised starting damage. Strongly damaged samples kept barely half the pulling strength of intact rock. Cracks still ran mainly in tension, yet shear strain and sideways shifts grew markedly. Pre-existing cracks acted as energy soaking zones, so more energy went into damage while less passed through. The authors frame the findings for mine stability checks and disaster warning.
pmc-13540836:
Anagha Wankhade, Ashlynn Clark, and David W Britt study two helpful bacteria in 2026. Both bacteria share the roots of wheat plants. One lives inside the seed and root. The other coats the root surface from the soil. Such microbes are sold as crop aids, yet they may fight each other.

In sterile sand, the seed-born Bacillus settled on roots first. The Pseudomonas partner then moved in and took over the root surface. On plates, it suppressed its partner at mild temperatures. That happened in lean food, not in rich food or heat. A small, heat-proof compound in its spent medium did the work. The authors link scarce food to sharper rivalry.
pmc-13540936:
Jun-Hao Su and four colleagues improve, in a 2026 engineering study, a bacterial production route to xylitol, the sugar substitute used in foods and medicines for people who must limit sugar. The bottleneck was a sluggish enzyme converting an intermediate, D-arabitol, into the final product.

Systematic mutation of the enzyme in Gluconobacter oxydans bacteria produced a variant carrying three changes that more than doubled catalytic activity. Structural analysis credited faster charge transfer and a steadier enzyme frame. With the helper cofactor system tuned and oxygen delivery improved, resting cells turned most of a forty-gram feed into xylitol within thirty hours. The authors claim a meaningful step toward industrial output.
pmc-13543436:
Usamah Sayed and colleagues published a 2026 review of single-cell RNA sequencing in ovarian cancer, a disease whose deadliness stems from deep variation between and within tumours. The technology reads gene activity cell by cell, exposing rare populations and the conversations between cancer, immune, stromal, and vessel cells in the tumour neighbourhood. The review surveys recent applications and their push toward personalised treatment.

Single-cell studies have surfaced prognostic markers, immune signatures, and candidate drug targets that bulk analysis, which averages millions of cells, would smear away. Combining the method with spatial mapping, other molecular layers, and artificial intelligence sharpens patient grouping further. Obstacles remain: some cell types are undercounted, results vary between laboratories, and costs are high. Even so, the authors see single-cell profiling steadily moving ovarian cancer care toward treatments chosen for the individual tumour's cellular makeup.
pmc-13543536:
Lwando Mjacu, Vikela Liso Sithole, and Palesa Makhetha-Kosi published a 2026 study of how financial inclusion, formal and informal, relates to health in South Africa. Access to banking shapes whether people can pay for care, yet informal arrangements such as stokvel savings clubs and mashonisa lenders dominate many communities. The team combined all five waves of a national income study into panel data and modelled self-rated health with a random-effects ordered probit approach suited to repeated answers.

Formal inclusion behaved as hoped: people with savings or credit access were more likely to report better health. Informal inclusion pointed the other way, with heavier reliance on informal finance shifting people toward worse reported health. The contrast drives the policy advice: pull informal savings and credit inside the formal digital economy and dismantle the barriers that keep the formal system from serving everyone well.
pmc-13543636:
Feng Gao's team published a 2026 study of what makes an Ahmed glaucoma valve become exposed through the eye's surface. The valve is a drainage implant for hard-to-treat glaucoma, and exposure is a failure that can end its usefulness. Records covered 2,905 eyes receiving a first implant at a Shanghai eye hospital across ten years. The team compared eyes that suffered exposure with those that did not, hunting for surgical and patient predictors.

Exposure occurred in seventy-five eyes, an incidence of 2.6 percent. One factor stood out in every analysis: having undergone capsulectomy shunt revision, a follow-up operation that cuts away scar tissue around the device. That operation carried roughly four times the odds of later exposure. Because the design is retrospective, the authors urge caution, but they advise careful planning and close watching after revision surgery, when the implant's cover may be thinnest.
pmc-13546536:
Benjamin Ascherman and Daniel King reviewed in 2026 how circulating tumor DNA, fragments of cancer DNA found in blood, might guide pancreatic cancer care. Pancreatic cancer is usually tracked with scans and a blood marker that misses many changes, and neither keeps pace with the disease. The authors examine the blood test across five settings along the treatment path, pairing published evidence with real cases from practice.

Possible uses include judging whether pre-surgery treatment worked, catching recurrence early during follow-up, and telling true progression apart from changes that only look like growth. Evidence remains thin and largely observational for this cancer. The review closes with trial designs meant to test the test properly before it enters routine care.
pmc-13547336:
Abdul Rehman, Ilona Heldal, and Jerry Chun-Wei Lin presented in 2026 a visualization tool, VisiTrail, that turns eye-tracking recordings into timelines teachers and psychologists can read. Ordinary gaze statistics hide how attention unfolds during a task, so the tool plots gaze against actions and performance over time. The test data came from a serious game in which players hunt target mushrooms among look-alikes across three difficulty levels.

Individual views show one learner's path through every level, while group views compare cohorts from projects in Romania and Portugal. Gaze steadiness looked similar across groups, and Romanian players answered faster at the median. Yet with only seven players per group and glitches in some sessions, the authors treat that gap as a lead for study, not a finding.
pmc-13548536:
Rumeysa İnci and Nurhayat Başkaya test a simple blood index as a warning tool for serious upper gut bleeding, in a 2026 retrospective study from an Istanbul hospital. Doctors already use several scoring systems for this emergency, yet each has limits. The pair analyzed 812 adults whose bleeding came from causes other than enlarged veins, calculating an index that combines platelet, neutrophil, and lymphocyte counts.

Within twenty-eight days, about one patient in fifteen had died, and roughly one in nine bled again within three days. Patients who died had markedly higher index values. For predicting death, the index matched the established scores, while for predicting early rebleeding it clearly beat all four of them. Because the index comes from a routine blood count, the authors suggest adding it to existing tools at the emergency department door.
pmc-13548636:
Tomoya Nozaki and a large team test stem cells harvested from the amnion, the membrane collected after birth, against a severe kidney inflammation in rats, in a 2026 study. Bone marrow stem cells help in this disease model, yet harvesting them is invasive. Amnion cells come without that burden. Rats with anti-GBM nephritis, an immune attack on the kidney filter, received human amnion cells, marrow cells, or a dummy infusion.

Amnion cells protected the kidneys as well as or better than marrow cells. Live imaging showed neutrophils, the first-responder white cells, lingering less inside the kidney's filters after amnion treatment, and those cells carried less of the adhesion molecule CD44. Blocking CD44 with an antibody copied much of the benefit, including reduced neutrophil entry. The authors propose amnion cells as a practical cell source that works partly by loosening this molecular grip.
pmc-13550336:
Qiqi Deng and colleagues sample an estuary every hour for a full day to watch its microbial communities ride the tide, in a 2026 study of the Pearl River Estuary. Tides swing salinity up and down, and how the active microbes respond was poorly known. By sequencing RNA, which reflects living activity, with long-read technology, the team captured both bacterial and single-celled eukaryotic communities at fine taxonomic detail across one tidal cycle.

Saltiness ruled the changes: diversity fell as salinity rose. Community networks, maps of which species rise and fall together, bent in a curved pattern with salinity, and their stability tracked how connected and how positive the links were. Networks spanning both domains were more intricate yet more fragile than single-domain ones. The authors say tidal rhythm must enter any model of estuary ecology.
pmc-13550436:
Lik Xian Lim and colleagues test whether a year in oak barrels can soften the ashtray taint that wildfire smoke leaves in wine, in a 2026 enology study. California's 2020 fires cost the industry billions, and smoke phenols absorbed by grapes produce medicinal, ashy flavors. The team diluted smoked and clean Cabernet Sauvignon from Napa and Lodi to graded taint levels. Some lots finished in stainless steel, others in new oak. The phenols were measured chemically, while trained judges and experts scored the wines.

Barrel-aged wines showed less ashy aftertaste and fewer smoke attributes than their steel counterparts at the same taint level. Heavily tainted wines still earned significantly lower quality ratings. Curiously, lightly tainted wines edged slightly, though not significantly, above completely clean ones in expert esteem. The authors offer barrel aging as a partial rescue tool for smoke-exposed vintages.
pmc-13550636:
Mohammed Naif Alatawi published a 2026 study proposing a secure way to spot attacks across networks of industrial devices. Factories connect many small sensors and machines, and central detection raises privacy risks while inviting tampering. His framework, SAFNet-IoT, lets devices train together without sharing raw data, and uses blockchain records to check that model updates are genuine.

A combined autoencoder and memory network adjusts its own settings as conditions change, hunting for anomalies in device traffic. Experiments reported detection accuracy of 94.7 percent, beating two comparison approaches, while cutting communication overhead by about a third. The blockchain layer caught most malicious updates, and the author points to contract costs and larger real-time tests as next steps.
pmc-13551736:
A 2026 study by Jindong Sheng and eleven colleagues examined a protein called SFRP2 that helps ovarian cancer grow by rewiring its energy use. The team mined public tumor data sets, checked a human tissue array, and then lowered or raised SFRP2 in two ovarian cancer cell lines. Assays measured growth, movement, death, and sugar burning, while mouse tumors tested the mechanism in living tissue.

Tumors carried excess SFRP2, and high levels tracked with advanced disease and poorer survival in the reported data. SFRP2 partnered with a transcription factor to switch on a gene called PTK2B, which fired a growth pathway and raised glycolysis, the sugar-burning route. Blocking glycolysis or PTK2B reversed the cancer-promoting effects in cells and mice, marking the chain as a drug target.
pmc-13551836:
Morvarid Meamar, leading five colleagues, published a 2026 rat study testing Ginkgo biloba extract against post-traumatic stress symptoms. Male rats underwent a single prolonged stress protocol, a standard trauma model, then received the plant extract at a low or high dose for fourteen days. Behavior tests covered anxiety, fear extinction, and memory, while hippocampus tissue was checked for oxidative damage, a growth factor, and dendrite shape.

Stress produced behavioral deficits, oxidative stress, lower growth factor levels, and shrunken dendrites in a memory-related hippocampal region. The higher extract dose eased anxiety, sped fear extinction, improved memory, and restored molecular and structural measures in the reported results. The authors stress that rat findings need clinical testing before any human claim.
pmc-13554136:
Xiaoli Huang leads a nine-author team building a glowing probe that tracks an enzyme tied to bowel cancer in a 2026 study. The enzyme, beta-galactosidase, rises in this cancer and can flag it early. Their probe locks onto the enzyme with high precision, giving a strong glow over a wide range. It resists interference from other substances and harms living cells little.

The probe followed enzyme shifts live inside cells over time. In nude mice it lit up the enzyme at work inside the body. Samples from patients and healthy people were told apart by their glow patterns. The team sees a path toward early diagnosis and judging how well treatment works, pending wider clinical checks.
pmc-13554236:
Ingridh Medeiros Simões leads a ten-author team growing seedlings of a threatened Brazilian hardwood in soils from different sources in a 2026 study. The tree, Melanoxylum brauna, is prized for dense, lasting wood and now classed as vulnerable. Nursery survival is poor, so the team tried seeds from two places across varied soil mixes. Soil dug near grown mother trees stood out among all the mixes.

Seedlings in pure mother-tree soil survived at near-total rates and grew the strongest shoots and roots. Their leaves also used light more efficiently, whatever the seed source. That soil brimmed with helper fungi spores, missing from shop substrates where every seedling died within sixty days. Richer stores of sugars, proteins, and fats filled the thriving seedlings, hinting that native soil microbes drive the gain.
pmc-13556036:
Tong Wu proposed in 2026 a new way to group cells from single-cell RNA sequencing data, a task made hard by sparse, noisy measurements across thousands of genes. Clustering decides which cells count as the same type, so unstable groupings distort everything built on top of them. Wu's framework, called SSGL, learns from the data itself without needing labelled examples.

The method hides random genes twice to make two altered views of each cell, then trains a momentum encoder to keep those views in agreement. A refined cell-to-cell graph, filtered by early label guesses, keeps neighbourhood structure intact during learning. Tested on eight public datasets from different tissues and platforms, the approach beat rival methods on both standard agreement scores. Ablation tests confirmed that each part of the design contributed to the gain.
pmc-13558336:
Iris Willaert and five colleagues asked in 2026 whether distorting a virtual body's stride can quietly change how a person actually walks. In virtual reality, people often adjust their real arm movements to match an avatar whose motion has been offset. Whether the same pull works on walking was unknown. Thirty healthy adults walked on a treadmill wearing a headset that showed an embodied avatar mirroring them, while software lengthened one of the avatar's steps in real time.

Participants did not meaningfully change their own gait symmetry to match the avatar, whether the longer step was placed on their dominant or non-dominant side. Healthy walkers, the authors conclude, resist visual feedback of this kind far more than arm users do. The negative result matters for rehabilitation design: avatar tricks that retrain reaching may not transfer to gait, and walking therapies need other levers.
pmc-13558736:
Qitian Fu and six colleagues built in 2026 a two-track prediction model for grading crow's feet, the wrinkles fanning from the eye's outer corner. Clinicians grade them by eye, and single instruments capture only one dimension of ageing skin. The team recruited 350 healthy Chinese women, photographed and scanned their skin with surface and two-photon microscopy, and had experts assign clinical grades before modelling.

Severity rose with age in a curved rather than steady pattern, and microscopy suggested that barrier breakdown marks one grade while deeper matrix disorder marks the worst. A plain ridge regression translated surface measures into scores with a solid overall fit, while a tuned support vector model read the early grades better by catching subtle texture shifts. Explanation analysis backed the complex model's choices as physiologically sensible. Stage-specific modelling, the authors argue, beats one formula for all ages.
pmc-13562336:
Caroline A. Stiver and five colleagues examine how emotional eating changes after sleeve gastrectomy, a weight-loss operation that removes much of the stomach. Their 2026 study, set at a university hospital in the United States, followed 122 patients. Eating driven by feelings was scored with a standard questionnaire before surgery and one year later. Ninety-five patients completed both rounds of surveys.

Scores fell across the group, yet the change sat almost entirely with women, whose scores dropped clearly. Men started lower and showed no real change after a year. Patients who ate more for emotional reasons before surgery tended to lose more excess weight. The authors suggest that better control of feeling-driven eating may be one path through which the operation helps.
pmc-13562636:
Xiangji Ye and six colleagues rework the maths behind stone columns driven into coral sand, a ground material whose grains crush under load. Standard bearing formulas assume soil swells or holds its volume, but coral sand shrinks as particles break, wasting energy that older models ignore. The 2026 paper proposes a three-step field method for measuring porosity in place, then builds a coupled model. Breakage energy loss is converted into extra confining pressure, and the sand's friction angle evolves as its density changes.

An airport runway project on coral sand ground supplied the test. The model's predicted sideways limit stress, 166.3 kilopascals, landed inside the field-measured range of 158.0 to 175.0 kilopascals from nine plate load tests. Prediction error across the full data span ran from minus 5.3 to plus 5.0 percent, far tighter than standard methods. The authors offer the model as a reliable design basis for building on coral sand.
pmc-13562736:
Lide Su and seven colleagues find that deleting a stress-response gene frees embryonic stem cells to become heart muscle. Heart attacks destroy muscle cells that adults cannot replace, so growing replacements from stem cells is a prime goal. The gene in question, Atf3, was suspected of braking that conversion. The 2026 team knocked it out of mouse embryonic stem cells with gene editing, then grew the cells in clusters for six days and on dishes to trigger development.

Knockout clusters began beating earlier, from day 8, and beat more often than normal ones. Their marker genes lit up in the right order: body-layer markers mid-course, heart-progenitor markers next, and finally the heart muscle protein cardiac troponin T. Genome-wide expression checks agreed. Restoring the gene reversed every gain, which pins the effect on Atf3 itself. The authors nominate the gene as a target for heart repair.
pmc-13563736:
Joseph Opeolu Ashaolu and four colleagues revisit what drives diarrhoea in Nigerian children under five, and show how missing data handling can bend the answer. Their 2026 analysis drew on the 2018 national demographic and health survey, covering 33,924 children. Diarrhoea in the survey window affected 12.0 percent. The team modelled social, geographic, nutrition, and water-and-sanitation factors twice: once by filling gaps with a chained imputation method, and once by dropping incomplete records.

Living in the North-East more than doubled the odds, the strongest single risk at an adjusted ratio of 2.61. Wealth and mother's schooling protected. Poor nutrition and poor water conditions multiplied each other, pushing prevalence to 15.4 percent where both ran high, while eating eggs protected. The drop-incomplete approach hid education's benefit and invented risks for vitamin A and fruit. Control, the authors argue, needs nutrition, water, and poverty tackled, and analysts must handle gaps with care.
pmc-13563836:
T. B. Garcia and two colleagues test a blood marker borrowed from a rare immune disorder as a warning in children arriving with septic shock. Spotting which child will deteriorate during emergency evaluation is hard. The marker, soluble CD25, is a diagnostic pillar of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, an immune condition that overlaps sepsis and worsens it. Their 2026 study compared levels across children with that disorder, children with septic shock, and children with infection but no sepsis.

The disorder group towered over the rest, at a median of 25,800 picograms per millilitre against about 5,200 for septic shock. Shock and plain infection groups overlapped on average, yet a slice of shock patients reached disorder-level values. That slice fared badly: every one needed intensive care, half needed circulation drugs, and stays stretched to sixteen days. Bloodstream infections carried the highest levels. The authors call for larger studies to confirm the marker.
pmc-13563936:
Xuewei Wang and colleagues review, in a 2026 single-center study, 232 hospitalized patients with Salmonella infection treated between 2014 and early 2026. Patients were grouped by strain type and by the source of any immune suppression. They were also grouped by whether infection stayed in the gut or spread to blood and other sites.

About one in ten patients had a serious outcome within thirty days, and about one in five had trouble clearing the infection. Immune-suppressed patients more often had bloodstream or widespread infection, yet suppression alone did not predict the thirty-day outcome once other factors were weighed. A simple severity score and drug resistance carried clearer prognostic weight, which helps clinicians triage such patients.
pmc-13569636:
Danny A. Elias and co-authors review, in a 2026 study, whether children with very severe sleep apnea need heart testing before surgery to remove tonsils and adenoids. Records covered 144 children aged two to eighteen with the highest severity scores who had the operation between 2018 and 2024.

About a quarter received a heart workup, and only three of those children had abnormal findings. All three were obese teenagers with the most extreme breathing scores, and none needed extra treatment or breathing support before surgery. Workup results did not change the hospital course. The authors suggest reserving heart testing for that narrow high-risk profile, cutting cost and delay for most families.
pmc-13570336:
Hamzah M. Al-Qadiri leads a 2026 methods study on how heating changes measured antibiotic resistance in multidrug-resistant Salmonella and Campylobacter found in raw chicken meat. Bacteria were heated at two temperatures, then tested both by growing them against antibiotic discs and by genetic tests for resistance genes.

The hotter treatment reduced visible resistance across several drug classes, while the milder heat changed little. Genetic tests, though, kept finding resistance genes in every condition, even where no living cells remained. The split warns food safety labs that gene detection alone can overstate living risk after cooking, and it supplies a paired testing framework for heat studies.
pmc-13570836:
Sonia Luque and nine colleagues wrote this 2026 commentary on how to value new antibiotics, using two Spanish studies of aztreonam-avibactam, a drug aimed at drug-resistant infections. Standard appraisal counts benefits to the treated patient. But antibiotics also slow the spread of resistance and cut transmission, gains that standard methods miss. The authors compare the two Spanish analyses, which used similar data yet reached different value estimates.

One study used a standard model comparing costs and quality-adjusted life years for patients against a payment threshold. The other used a dynamic spread model inside the STEDI value framework. It added wider effects: less spread of resistant bacteria, more treatment options kept alive, and safer surgery thanks to preventive drugs. Both models agreed on many inputs and outcomes, so the gap came from modelling choices. The authors argue that fuller valuation is needed to justify investment in new antibiotics.
pmc-13572336:
Adnan Gündoğdu and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 retrospective study, artificial intelligence reading of three-dimensional mammography to guide breast cancer surgery after chemotherapy given before the operation. Images from 151 patients were scored by a commercial program, with a score of seventy splitting low from high, and seventy patients also had before-treatment scores for comparison.

About forty-one percent had no cancer left at surgery. Low scores after chemotherapy matched higher complete-response rates, while high scores tracked with leftover calcium deposits and in-situ disease. Overall accuracy was modest and varied by tumor subtype, working best in triple-negative cancers. Score drops after treatment did not separate responders. The tool may support, not replace, surgical judgment in selected subtypes.
pmc-13572436:
Radhey Shyam Tyagi, with two colleagues, lays out a 2026 plan for Delhi to close a large water gap and clean its rivers. The city faces a shortfall near 2,000 million litres a day as growth and climate shifts strain supply. Much of its water comes from other states or from the ground.

The plan uses official data, site visits, talks, and scenario models to map a phased path to self-reliance by 2045. Filtered supply now stands at 4,540 million litres a day against demand of 6,540. By 2045, demand could reach 10,880 to 14,797, based on the norm used. Reuse of wastewater, cuts to leaks, rain capture, and ground recharge could lift supply to near 14,928. Random runs gave a 90 percent band from a 1,200 shortfall to a 2,500 surplus.
pmc-13573336:
Wenwen Wei, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 survey study of how childhood abuse links to suicidal thoughts in Chinese college students. Abuse in childhood is a strong risk factor for later suicidal thinking, yet the inner paths from one to the other are not fully mapped. The team tested two paths: hope traits and psychological distress.

A total of 1,908 students filled in set scales for abuse history, hope, distress symptoms, and suicidal thinking. Abuse went with higher suicidal thinking in a direct link. It also acted through hope and through distress, each on its own and as a chain from hope into distress. All those indirect paths held even with the direct link counted. The authors say boosting hope and easing distress may blunt one route from early harm to later risk.
pmc-13573436:
Guangxia Zhang, with nine colleagues, reports a 2026 study of whether a mother's glucose test values predict low blood sugar in her newborn. The mothers all had gestational diabetes held in check by diet alone. A mid-pregnancy glucose test is a tempting early flag, yet past results disagreed.

Records covered 2,051 single births at a mother and child centre in Liaocheng, China, from 2019 to 2023. Low newborn blood sugar hit 12 percent of babies. Neither straight nor curved models tied the test values, at fasting or after the drink, to newborn sugar or to low sugar events. Later birth week by week lowered the risk, while caesarean birth raised it. The authors say care after diagnosis and birth factors matter more than the first test score.
pmc-13574536:
Huaiqing Zhi, with 12 colleagues, presents a model that spots muscle wasting in stomach cancer patients from scans and clinical data. Muscle wasting, called sarcopenia, is common in this cancer and tracks with worse survival. Standard diagnosis takes grip tests, gait timing, and body measures, which is too slow for large-scale screening.

The study drew 1,067 patients from two centres. Scan texture features came from CT images at the third lower-back vertebra, and two deep learning shapes read the images as well. A transformer model that fused clinical facts, texture, and deep features topped the set. Its sorting scores for wasting reached the high range across training, check, and outside sets. A rival fusion model also did well. The authors aim the tool at screening and risk sorting in clinics.
pmc-13574836:
Sebastian Wegmann, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 anatomy study linking a shoulder angle to the size of the tendon anchors on the bone. The critical shoulder angle, read from an X-ray, already predicts cuff tears and joint wear. Why it does so was unclear, and tendon footprint size was a suspect.

The team measured the angle on X-rays of 28 shoulders from 14 preserved cadavers, then dissected and sized the anchor patches of all four cuff muscles. Every muscle showed the same pattern: a wider angle went with a smaller anchor patch, with moderate strength. The link was firmest for two of the four muscles. A wide angle may thus load a smaller patch of tendon, raising strain per area. The authors offer the link as groundwork for risk models in shoulder care.
pmc-13576136:
Ting Lei and six colleagues identify a gene switch that turns on flavonol production in Chinese raspberry in a 2026 study. This raspberry is valued as food and traditional medicine, and flavonoids are among its key active compounds. How their production is controlled was poorly known.

The switch, named RcMYB21, sits in the cell nucleus and activates other genes through its tail end. Tests showed it binds the control regions of flavonoid pathway genes and switches on RcFLS, the enzyme gene for flavonol building. Extra copies in raspberry leaves raised that gene's activity, while tobacco plants carrying the switch made more flavonols and fewer red pigments. Plants with the switch also handled salt stress better, growing stronger side roots. The authors credit one regulator with two jobs.
pmc-13576336:
Jibon Kumar Sarker and four colleagues pool studies of malaria in Bangladesh in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Malaria still circulates in the country, driven mainly by two parasite species. Fourteen studies published between 2005 and 2025 met the quality rules after screening more than ten thousand records.

The pooled prevalence came to 16 percent, with very wide variation between studies. Among infections, Plasmodium falciparum dominated at 80 percent, with Plasmodium vivax at 14 percent and mixed infections at 7 percent in the subgroup shares reported. Prevalence ran higher in males, at 20 percent against 12 percent in females. Checks suggested the pooled figures were stable, though most studies used microscopy or rapid tests that miss low-level and mixed infections. The authors call for species-specific and gender-aware control work.
pmc-13578436:
Jierui Zhao and co-authors test a walnut compound called juglone on bone cancer cells, in a 2026 lab study. Juglone was known to slow cancer cell growth and movement, yet whether it could trigger a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis was open. In that death route the cell swells and bursts, spilling signals that can rouse immune attack.

Dish tests on osteosarcoma cells showed juglone did trigger the burst route. The path ran through a stress signal chain that switched on an executioner protein, which then poked holes in the cell skin. The same chain also drove the quieter death route called apoptosis in parallel. The authors present juglone as a candidate worth deeper study for a cancer that badly needs new options.
pmc-13579836:
Amanda Li and a large team of co-authors build a single cell atlas of the late pregnancy placenta in pigtail macaques, in a 2026 study. The monkey placenta mirrors the human one closely, which makes this species a key stand in for studying pregnancy trouble. Three tissues at the mother and fetus border were pulled apart into single cells and read gene by gene: the placental disc, the membranes, and the mother's lining layer.

Cell types and their shares matched the human placenta strikingly well, across support cells, surface cells, and immune families. Tracing each cell's likely origin, mother or fetus, added depth, as did maps of how cells signal to each other. Rare cell groups surfaced thanks to the deep read across three tissues. The authors offer the atlas as a shared base for testing what goes wrong in pregnancy.
pmc-13580336:
Koichiro Yuji and Wakako Yuji argue that a new gene therapy for Dravet syndrome should face its hardest test: living with drugs it once forbade, in a 2026 commentary. The therapy lifts output of a sodium channel that calming brain cells need, and early trials cut seizures. Sodium channel blockers are banned in this disease because they weaken those same calming cells and worsen seizures.

If the therapy truly restores the channel, the ban's reason should melt away. Trial plans still exclude patients on those drugs, leaving the question open by design. The authors point to emergency care, where one blocker is already allowed for runaway seizures, as a natural record to mine. Incidental exposures in follow up studies could show whether the old harm still strikes.
pmc-13586736:
Lisa Fedina, Xinlu Li, and Todd I. Herrenkohl map household firearm access among young adults in the United States in this 2026 study. Emerging adults, aged 18 to 29, face the country's highest rates of firearm injury, yet most past work studied teens or lumped all adults together. Using a nationally representative sample, the team asked who in this age band can reach a gun at home and how that access shifts across groups.

Just under a quarter of the young adults reported a firearm in the household. Access ran higher among White and multiracial respondents, men, married people, and those in the Midwest and South. The patterns also crossed in finer ways when age, identity, and region were combined. The authors say prevention work should be tailored to those subgroups rather than aimed at young adults as one block.
pmc-13587136:
Fengze Li, Jiaying Yu, Minglei Sun, and Xiang Li design a leaner computer system for reading facial expressions. Reading faces can give psychiatry an objective handle on the flattened or slowed expression that many mental illnesses bring. Existing two-stream networks are accurate but heavy, which blocks their use on small clinic devices for long-term watching. Their system, KGLA-Net, runs a landmark stream beside an image stream across three stages.

Facial landmark features are cleaned up first, then used to steer the gathering of image features inside small local windows at several scales. That steering cuts the work from a heavy global match to a lighter local one. Tests showed expression reading that held its own against bigger systems at a fraction of the computing cost. The authors offer the design as a base for future tools in computational psychiatry.
pmc-13589136:
Xiaorong He and nine colleagues feed geese a modified starch to protect their guts and kidneys. Goose gout, driven by uric acid buildup, kills many farmed birds, and fiber-like feeds seem to guard against it. Their 2026 trial assigned 240 young Yangzhou geese to three diets: plain feed, feed with hydroxypropyl starch, or feed spiked with sodium urate to provoke the disease. Blood, kidney, and gut were checked after three weeks.

The starch group showed a downward drift in blood uric acid and kept cleaner kidney and gut tissue. There were no shed lining cells or invading inflammation, though the shifts fell short of statistical proof. Its gut held more of a microbe called Rothia, and gut contents leaned toward amino acid building pathways with cysteine as a key product. The urate group instead leaned toward bile acid pathways. The authors read a protective trend worth larger trials.
pmc-13589936:
Ruiyi Tang heads a 2026 trial of Xiangshao granules, a Chinese herbal mix, for anxiety in women near or past menopause. The trial ran at 18 sites in China and enrolled 360 women aged 40 to 65. Half took a full dose and half took a very low dose that acted as a placebo, each for eight weeks. Staff tracked anxiety with a standard self rating scale, plus mood, body signs, and stomach signs.

Anxiety scores fell more in the full dose group, and more women there met the mark for clear gain. Side effects were much the same in both groups. Tang and the team also ran gene and chemical tests on blood, which pointed to a brain path tied to dopamine. Other scores improved in both groups with no clear gap.
pmc-13591736:
Yu-Sha Zhang leads a 2026 case report warning that a heart attack's ECG pattern can point to the wrong artery. A 46 year old heavy smoker arrived with five hours of chest pain. His tracing showed the classic lift in the lower leads, which usually means the right or side artery is blocked. Heart enzyme levels at first sat in the normal range, deepening the puzzle.

Vessel imaging instead found the front artery fully blocked near its start. That artery wrapped around the heart's tip and fed the lower wall, which explains the false signal. After flow was restored, the lower lift faded and front changes appeared. Zhang and the team urge reading tracings as a moving story, not a single frame.
pmc-13591836:
Takasuke Asakawa, writing alone in 2026, asks whether uric acid in blood truly tracks metabolic risk in slim working women, or merely rides along with weight. Uric acid has been linked to insulin trouble and poor blood fats. His group held 630 women with body mass index under 25, drawn from routine work health checks. A ratio of triglycerides to HDL cholesterol stood in as a rough risk marker.

That ratio rose across higher uric acid bands at first glance. Once age, blood pressure, habits, and body size were factored in, the uric acid link faded away. Body size and weight gained since early adulthood carried the stronger ties. Asakawa calls uric acid a shadow of deeper metabolic state in this group.
pmc-13592536:
Bennett and colleagues argued that brain-wasting diseases should be understood as a breakdown of talk between the nervous and immune systems, in a 2026 essay. Studies now show immune cells stationed at the brain's borders and entering the tissue, acting as guards that shape nerve-cell strength and repair.

Bennett groups the field into lenses: outside-in signals, in which adaptive immune responses from the rest of the body engage the brain. Inside-out circuits are those in which the brain's cells direct communication. And gene-regulatory programs lock immune states in. Faulty immunity is cast as a cause alongside nerve-cell fragility, not a side effect. The authors point to the Alzheimer's antibodies as evidence that tuning this dialogue can change a disease. They call for treatments that restore immune balance or reset the epigenetic switches, chemical marks that hold cell states and guide behavior.
pmc-13592636:
Chunmeng Wang and four colleagues build a network that fuses several exposures of one scene into a single wide range image. Older fusion methods tend to lose fine detail, global structure, or true color. Their design runs three branches in parallel: one reads local features with attention, one reads global links with a transformer, and one restores natural color. Merging blocks blend the first two branches' weight maps before guided filtering lifts them to full size.

Against nine rival methods on three datasets, the network topped most detail and human perception scores and placed second on a structural similarity measure. Gains over a leading transformer method reached about twenty percent on one visual quality score. Wang and the team present the three branch split as the fix for detail and color losses.
pmc-13592736:
Chloe A. McGhee-Deakin and three colleagues rethink how brain size differences are measured in RASopathies, a family of genetic disorders hitting a growth signaling pathway. Youth with these conditions show odd total brain and deep brain volumes, but standard fixes assume each region scales in simple proportion. Their allometric approach instead models curved scaling norms. Scans covered 132 affected youth, mostly Noonan syndrome, plus 80 matched controls.

Deviations clustered by gene: thalamus in one condition, several striatal regions in the commonest Noonan gene group, and ventral striatum in another. Simple linear fixes tended to inflate regional gaps, while a few effects survived every method. Girls showed somewhat larger deviations in early checks. McGhee-Deakin and the team urge curved scaling as the default lens for such scans.
pmc-13593636:
Maria Cláudia Soares Cruz Coelho and a team of co-authors tested whether Pornunça hay can replace Tifton 85 hay as the roughage in feedlot lamb diets. Thirty-six young Santa Inês male lambs spent 71 days in confinement while the share of Pornunça in the roughage rose across four groups, from none to complete replacement.

Lambs on the Pornunça diets ate more dry matter and organic matter, though they digested protein and fiber less well. Final weight, daily gain, and feed conversion stayed the same across groups, while hot and cold carcass weights and yields rose as Pornunça increased. Meat color, tenderness, water holding, and basic composition did not change. On that basis the authors recommend swapping Tifton 85 hay fully for Pornunça hay for feedlot lambs.
pmc-13598136:
Hiroki Tanaka and co-authors used cryo-electron microscopy to watch how the HIV drug lenacapavir sabotages the virus's shell during the late stage of replication, when new viruses assemble and mature. The drug's early-stage actions were already charted; its late work was not, and the team imaged capsid lattices formed inside virus-like particles with the drug present.

Lenacapavir wedged between the shell's hexagonal units, warping the lattice's curvature so the proper cone shape could never close.
