Cores built under the drug leaked their reverse transcriptase enzyme while keeping integrase and the viral RNA, leaving the particle unable to copy itself properly. Viruses produced this way showed sharply reduced infectivity and poor integration. The authors say the distorted geometry explains the drug's second punch and points inhibitor designers toward the seams between hexamers.
pmc-13603236:
Chao Wang and colleagues engineer a single molecule that carries two gastric cancer drugs and releases them inside tumors. Combination chemotherapy often fails on timing: two free drugs circulate differently and poison healthy tissue. Their prodrug joins combretastatin A-4, a tubulin blocker, to gefitinib, an EGFR blocker, through a disulfide link that snaps open inside cancer cells. The design aims to synchronize delivery and concentrate both attacks on the tumor.

Against SGC-7901 gastric cancer cells, the conjugate killed potently while sparing normal cells, scoring a safety index of 98. It jammed microtubule assembly, froze cells at the G2/M checkpoint, dampened ERK signaling, and pushed cells into apoptosis. In mice, it circulated longer, exposed the body to less free combretastatin, shrank tumors better than the free-drug pair, and caused markedly less toxicity. The authors offer the conjugate as a general platform for combination therapy.
pmc-13612336:
Xu Chen leads an eight-author team proposing that inflammation over time should steer recovery after knee replacement. Total knee arthroplasty reliably fixes the joint, yet a stubborn minority keep hurting under identical enhanced-recovery protocols. Their framework sorts each patient along three axes: inflammatory tone before surgery, the size of the inflammatory surge surgery triggers, and how fast that surge resolves.

Cheap blood indices anchor the scheme. The systemic immune-inflammation index feeds the first axis, and the modified frailty index captures pre-existing deficit. Interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, swelling, and temperature studies supply supporting signals. Trials show the acute response can be shifted with drugs. The model pairs each phenotype with matched treatments, from compression and electrical stimulation to extended supervised rehab. Five testable predictions and a staged validation plan complete the blueprint. The authors insist the phenotype must still prove it beats existing indices.
pmc-13614936:
Hussein and colleagues published a 2026 study on what happens when a cancer signal link is cut. A growth pathway ending in ERK often runs wild in many cancers. The team cut a side link between ERK and an inflammation adapter, MyD88. Past work showed the cut triggers a kind of cell death that alerts immunity.

The cut rerouted signals through two makeshift hubs inside the cells. One hub drove stress alarms ending in a self-kill program. The other built an assembly that pumped out inflammation-calling chemicals. Together, they paired cell suicide with a call for immune help. That pairing makes the death immunogenic, meaning it recruits immune attack. The hubs form without any outside immune signal switching them on.
pmc-13617236:
Jack H. Donne and five colleagues report a 2026 international survey of children who toe walk, asking parents about sensory processing and pain. Families of children aged three to fourteen, across many diagnoses, completed validated questionnaires on sensory profiles and activity limits between July 2024 and March 2025. One hundred seventy-six parents reported on one hundred eighty-seven children.

Sensory processing challenges were common and near-universal among children with autism in the group. Almost half of the children were reported to have pain, most often in the feet and ankles, lower legs, and hips or thighs, and most parents and clinicians blamed toe walking itself. Children with pain faced significantly greater limits in sports, running, and social participation. The authors recommend routine checks for sensory issues and pain so treatment can target participation and quality of life, not just gait.
pmc-13618336:
Fábris Kossoski, writing alone, challenges a standard belief in the complex absorbing potential method, a technique for studying molecular resonances, states that decay by ejecting an electron. Tuning the method's strength yields several possible solutions, and common practice keeps one as the true resonance and discards the rest as fake. Kossoski argues that this tidy habit hides a real problem.

He shows that several solutions can be acceptable approximations of the same resonance at once. That ambiguity, he shows, injects more uncertainty into energies than basis set limits or the electronic structure method itself. Proposed fixes, including larger basis sets, subtracting the potential's energy part, and adding a real perturbative potential, all fail to remove it. He concludes the method keeps its proven merits for anionic resonances, but the multiplicity stands as a critical unsolved problem.
pmc-13619036:
Romain Barus and six colleagues offer a 2026 proof of concept for machine learning in drug-safety surveillance, a field dominated by manual review. From the French national pharmacovigilance database they pulled every report involving warfarin, the blood thinner notorious for gastrointestinal bleeding. They trained an extreme gradient boosting model to sort reports into gut-bleeding versus other adverse reactions. An explanation method then exposed which features drove its calls.

After cleaning, one thousand forty-five reports remained. On a test set the model reached moderate discrimination, catching eighty percent of true bleeding reports with overall accuracy just under seventy percent. The explanation analysis ranked age, baseline gastrointestinal bleeding risk, antiplatelet use, and a history of kidney dysfunction as the top features, a list pharmacologists checked afterward. The authors present the pairing of model plus explanation as a template for triaging safety reports and surfacing risk factors.
pmc-13620136:
Raul Y Sanchez-David and eight colleagues found a way to make self-amplifying RNA work harder inside cells without muting its immune spark. Such RNA copies itself after delivery, so it can produce a target protein for longer at lower doses, which suits vaccines. The catch is that cells sense its double-stranded forms and shut production down. Adding a small protein from Nodamura virus, called B2, changed that balance.

In stem cells, B2 limited the chopped viral RNA fragments that mark an active antiviral defense. In ordinary body cells, it stopped a sensor protein from halting protein production. The viral protein gathers the double-stranded RNA at the cell's edge, hiding it from defenders, yet the interferon alarm still sounds, preserving the built-in immune stimulation. The authors propose building B2 into future self-amplifying vaccines and therapies.
pmc-13621336:
Wataru Yoshioka and eight colleagues compared two shapes of plastic stent for draining bile ducts blocked by cancer low in the duct. One design ends in double half-pigtail curls, the other runs straight. Their single-center review covered procedures done from late 2022 into 2026, focusing on each patient's first stent placement: twenty with the curled design and fifty-two with the straight one.

Time until the stent blocked or slipped again came out nearly identical between designs, at just under four months, and blockage rates matched too. One difference stood out: no curled stent migrated, while seven straight stents slipped out of place. Overall side effect rates also looked similar. The authors conclude the curled design buys no extra open time, so its real promise, if any, lies in holding position rather than resisting clogging.
pmc-13622336:
James H Acuff and co-authors ask how serious blood infection with Streptococcus mitis group bacteria really is. These bacteria normally live in the mouth and throat and were long dismissed as harmless, except when they infect heart valves. Better lab tools now identify them more often, which raises the question of when a positive blood culture signals true disease.

The team reviewed records for 253 adults treated at three hospitals in the Texas Medical Center between 2017 and 2025. The most common setting was low white blood cell counts, a state that weakens infection defences, followed by pneumonia and heart valve infection. Only about a quarter of cases were judged contamination, meaning stray bacteria from sampling rather than disease. Cases called real infection usually grew bacteria in several blood bottles, while contamination usually meant one bottle. The authors conclude that most such infections deserve prompt treatment.
pmc-13623136:
Shauna A Rasmussen leads a rat study of classic galactosemia, an inherited disorder where the body cannot process the sugar galactose because an enzyme called GALT is missing. Harmful sugar by-products build up before birth, yet babies do well at first, which puzzles doctors. The team used rats lacking GALT to test whether the mother's genes change the picture.

Breeding crosses produced affected pups carried either by affected mothers or by carrier mothers, who keep some enzyme activity. By-products in the fluid around pups stayed high in affected litters but rose in steps as the enzyme supply fell. They were lowest with a carrier mother, highest when mother and all siblings lacked the enzyme. Growth delay appeared only in that worst-supplied group. A carrier mother protected growth despite moderate by-product levels. The authors suggest human babies carried by carrier mothers may gain protection before birth.
pmc-13623536:
Elisa Zoe Battistelli leads the authors of a protocol for a pilot study testing whether intensive care survivors can report their quality of life by phone surveys over time. Quality of life after critical illness matters to patients, yet trials measure it clumsily, often once and by interview. The pilot sits inside a platform trial of intensive care treatments.

The plan enrols one hundred trial participants who will answer a standard survey, delivered by text message, every month from six to twelve months after entering the trial. The team will track how many join, how many keep answering, how fast answers come, and how much reminders matter. Survey results will be compared against a telephone assessment at six months, both for the group and person by person. Plotting the monthly scores as curves should reveal recovery shapes. Special analyses will check whether deaths among dropouts bend the picture.
pmc-13623636:
Qinghua Zhao leads a team that published a 2026 report of X-ray detectors made by rubbing a lead-free crystal film onto ordinary office paper. The crystal, a caesium bismuth bromide perovskite, avoids the toxic lead found in many high-performing detector materials. The challenge was a cheap, scalable way to lay it down on a flexible base.

The dry abrasion method needs no solvents or heat, and it works at room temperature on biodegradable paper. The finished detectors sensed X-rays strongly, and narrowing the gap between electrodes pushed sensitivity to among the highest values reported for thin-film devices. Imaging tests resolved fine detail, and the paper devices still worked steadily after more than a month in open air. The authors present the platform as a green route to cheap, bendable detectors for medical and security scanning.
pmc-13624036:
Quinn Johnson and colleagues run decompression experiments to learn how bubbles are born on crystals inside rhyolitic magma, the thick, silica-rich melt behind many explosive eruptions. Bubbles drive eruptions, and crystals give bubbles an easier birthplace than the melt alone. The team mixed hydrated melt with crystals of two minerals at two size ranges and dropped the pressure.

Bubbles appeared on both crystal types at pressure undershoots far smaller than bubbles in pure melt would need. Tiny crystals hosted about one bubble each, while bigger crystals hosted more, in line with their larger surface area. Raising the pressure drop also packed nucleation sites closer together, which the authors explain as a race between bubble birth and water diffusion in the melt. They built an updated equation that folds crystal surface area into bubble counts, plus a spreadsheet so other researchers can run their own eruption conditions.
pmc-13624236:
Carl P C Chen and Areerat Suputtitada published a 2026 ultrasound study testing whether rolling a patient onto their side widens the safety gap for a common nerve block near the collarbone. In the supraclavicular block, the needle targets nerve bundles that sit close to the membrane around the lung, and puncture there is a feared complication. The gap between that membrane, the pleura, and the nerve bundle is the margin measured.

Ninety adults, including pain patients, neck patients, and healthy volunteers, were scanned at the end of a breath out in three positions: half-reclined, tilted partway, and fully on the side. The safety gap grew at each step and more than doubled in the full side position in every group. Heavier patients showed wider gaps in the side position, age made no difference. The authors propose position as a free adjustment that could make targeting safer.
pmc-13627236:
Nobuaki Yoshikura leads a large Japanese team describing a rare autoimmune attack on balance. Antibodies against a brain receptor called mGluR1 can inflame the cerebellum, the coordination center, causing ataxia, and nearly all published cases came from Western countries. Their laboratory found twelve positive patients among 699 screened between 2018 and 2025, and the team set their charts beside forty overseas cases.

Three quarters of the Japanese patients had one-sided limb clumsiness, a pattern rarely noted abroad, though uneven record-keeping may explain part of the gap. Spinal fluid inflammation ran milder in Japan, and two patients fell ill within a month of COVID-19. Every patient received immune therapy, mostly steroids, yet only a third of those followed long-term regained independence, a sobering recovery rate for a treatable disease.
pmc-13628136:
Jiang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how artificial intelligence is reshaping antibody drug development by judging developability, not just binding strength. A lab antibody that grips its target tightly can still fail as a medicine if it clumps, thickens, dissolves poorly, or provokes immune reactions. Testing all that in the lab is slow, so teams now train models to predict these traits early.

The review surveys the data sources behind such models and the main predictor types for traits from clumping to shelf stability. It then covers methods that balance rival goals at once, including Pareto and Bayesian optimization, active learning, and models that generate new candidates to order. Special sections treat two-armed antibodies and nanobodies. The authors argue these tools serve best as guides that rank experiments, not as stand-ins for testing.
pmc-13628736:
Su-Yuan He and three colleagues asked whether a combined blood index can flag which atrial fibrillation patients will relapse after catheter ablation. Their 2026 retrospective study followed 591 patients for one year after radiofrequency ablation, an operation that scars small areas of heart tissue to restore normal rhythm.

The index blends inflammation and metabolic markers from C-reactive protein, triglycerides, and glucose readings. Ninety-two patients suffered a late recurrence, and higher index values tracked that risk closely, staying predictive after statistical adjustment for other factors. Extra analyses suggested the index adds information beyond standard predictors. The authors propose it as an inexpensive aid for spotting patients who need closer follow-up after ablation.
pmc-13629336:
Chotprom and colleagues develop smart packaging that both preserves chicken meat and visibly reports its freshness, in 2026 food science research. Their film combines gelatin and alginate, natural gelling materials, with lemongrass essential oil as an antimicrobial. A second element uses anthocyanins, the pigments in butterfly pea flowers, as a color indicator. The film changes color as meat spoils, giving a real-time freshness signal without opening the pack or running laboratory tests.

The active film extended the refrigerated shelf life of broiler breast meat by 3 days in the storage trials reported. Its color shifts correlated strongly with two standard spoilage measures, total volatile basic nitrogen and rising pH, as the meat aged. Lemongrass oil gave the film strong antimicrobial activity against the microbes tested. Chotprom argues such proactive packaging could cut food loss across the poultry supply chain by flagging spoilage at a glance.
pmc-13631036:
Chaiane Goulart Soares and seven colleagues review the pulp of Butia palms. The genus holds about two dozen subtropical species native to southern South America. Their aromatic fruits are eaten locally but barely studied. The review gathers proof on makeup, health effects, storage, and food uses.

Across species the pulp supplies fibre, minerals, and vitamin C. It also gives carotenoids and phenolic compounds, with mostly unsaturated fats. Values swing with species, ripeness, and growing conditions. Lab and animal studies suggest protective, calming, and blood sugar benefits. None are confirmed in people yet. The pulp has been trialled in drinks, dairy products, and frozen desserts. The authors flag how much remains unknown. It runs from spoilage behaviour to nutrient uptake.
pmc-13631236:
William J Flerlage and twelve colleagues characterise a previously unrecognised population of neurons inside the mouse lateral habenula, a small brain hub for stress and disappointment, published in 2026. These cells make corticotropin-releasing factor, the classic stress signal, and the team mapped them with high-resolution imaging, gene probes, and viral tracing.

Most of the neurons were of the excitatory type, with a front subpopulation also carrying inhibitory markers. Switching them on did not change reward seeking or anxiety behaviour, but it pushed threatened mice toward passive freezing, stretching escape times in males and shelter stays in females. The sexes also differed in cell numbers, excitability, and wiring. The authors frame the circuit as a sex-specific dial on defensive strategy.
pmc-13633336:
Andrea Spinelli and four colleagues studied root canal sealer that squeezes past the tooth root tip. The material, a premixed bioceramic sealer called NeoSealer Flo, sets by absorbing moisture. Dentists worry about how extra material behaves outside the root. The team filled thirty-two extracted human teeth with enlarged tips and sorted them into four conditions. The setups varied by canal moisture and by sponge support around the tip, mimicking tissue.

Standard X-rays were taken right after filling and again at one and four weeks. The bright area inside the canal stayed nearly unchanged in every group. The bright patch beyond the tip behaved differently by condition. It grew most in dry canals with sponge support and barely moved in moist ones. The authors note that X-ray change alone cannot prove swelling, dissolving, or merging with tissue. Keeping sealer inside the root remains the goal.
pmc-13635036:
Näslund and colleagues ran a 2026 proof of concept study on a gentler way to track blood oxygen in the body. Mixed venous oxygen saturation shows whether oxygen delivery matches what tissues use, but measuring it needs a catheter in the lung artery. The team tested light based sensing on the breastbone of pigs instead.

In fifteen anaesthetised pigs, Näslund lowered oxygen with low oxygen gas mixes and removed blood in two stages. Light readings from the sternum were calibrated against catheter samples from the lung artery. The two measures moved together in each animal, with agreement on change direction reaching eighty-seven percent across the tests. Only severe blood loss broke the pattern, so the authors back more technical work on the approach.
pmc-13636036:
Andy Bridger and seven colleagues describe a software pipeline that turns neutron measurements into maps of crystal orientation inside solid materials. Texture, the statistical alignment of tiny crystals, steers strength, stiffness, and conductivity in metals, ceramics, and rocks. Neutron beams can read texture deep inside whole engineering parts without cutting them open. The team's workflow lives inside the Mantid analysis framework and handles planning, calibration, and data processing in one place.

The pipeline converts time-of-flight diffraction data into corrected pole figures, the standard charts of crystal alignment. Its outputs plug directly into popular texture software for deeper analysis. A test on an aluminum alloy dataset already analyzed by an older tool gave matching figures and texture components. The new workflow adds flexible detector grouping and lets users study how shorter measurement times affect quality. The authors aim to streamline texture work across neutron facilities.
pmc-13642036:
Marie-Odile Baudement and thirty colleagues present a study of how gene control changed after the salmon family copied its whole genome. Salmon did this more lately than most backboned animals. So they give a clearer view of how copied genes and their switches drift apart.

The team built 771 data sets from embryos and adult tissues of two fish, Atlantic salmon and rainbow trout. Change followed rules set by tissue type and by stage of growth. The tightest control sat at one key embryo stage. Kept switch pairs and jumping DNA both shaped which gene copies stayed on. The open data also serve fish farming and wild stock care.
pmc-13642236:
Roman Delucenay-Clarke and fourteen colleagues present a 2026 research letter on noninvasive spinal stimulation for weak breathing in obesity hypoventilation syndrome. In this disorder, obesity combines with blunted central breathing drive, and no curative treatment exists.

The team had earlier shown that gentle direct current applied over the upper neck spine raised diaphragm excitability and breath size in healthy people. Here they test the same trans-spinal approach in mice modeling the syndrome's central breathing failure. The letter frames stimulation-induced plasticity as a possible route to restore ventilation without drugs or machines, pending what the animal results show.
pmc-13643436:
Ahmed A Hassan and two colleagues report a 2026 case from a child with Shone's complex, a set of left-heart defects. The case used a third heart valve placed inside two earlier ones. Severe mitral valve disease in small children is hard to treat. Few valve options fit, and children outgrow them.

The boy was six years old. He got his first Melody valve as a baby. A second valve went inside it at age two. The valve failed again four years later. Widening it with a balloon made the leak worse. So the team placed a third valve through the leg, guided by a wire rail through the chest. The pressure result was good.
pmc-13645936:
Rodriguez and co-authors dissect an iron enzyme in this 2026 biochemistry study. The enzyme helps make ergothioneine, a protective antioxidant that bacteria and fungi produce and humans must eat. The enzyme EgtB welds a sulfur bond between two building blocks using oxygen, and the team used spectroscopy and rapid kinetics to watch its active site reorganize as ingredients arrive.

Working with the enzyme from a heat-loving bacterium, they showed iron loading and then step-by-step substrate binding each reshape the metal's setting and stabilize the protein. Activity peaked at neutral pH 7.0 in their stopped-flow readings, and reaction speed scaled with oxygen levels, evidence of tightly coupled oxygen handling. Mass spectrometry confirmed the oxygen-dependent sulfoxide product. A practical warning emerged too: the common laboratory habit of leaving a purification tag attached plainly weakened the enzyme's activity and stability.
pmc-13648836:
Oleg V. Kim and five colleagues find when platelet parent cells first learn to squeeze blood clots. Platelets are the cell shards that seal wounds. Their parents, called megakaryocytes, grow in the marrow and shed them into the blood. The team raised these parents from human stem cells in steps.

Plain stem cells could not squeeze at all. Blood starter cells already pulled on clot strands when roused, though weakly. The pull came from the subset pledged to the platelet line, and wiping that subset out erased the pull. Grown parents pulled far harder and faster. One surface switch, flipped on by the pledge, drove the act. The team calls squeeze power an early badge of the line.
pmc-13649436:
Kun Wang and six colleagues gathered case data on 279 people with a rare hormone condition that blunts the making of a potent male hormone before birth. The cause lies in changes to one gene, and the outward signs vary a great deal. Reports came from 36 lands, most of them in Asia.

The team found 78 distinct gene changes, with one change the most common of all. Children who got the same faulty copy from both parents had more severe signs than those with two distinct faults. Some gene changes tied to higher or lower odds of specific signs, such as a cleft in the urine tube. The authors show that gene type alone does not set the outcome.
pmc-13651536:
Alicia M Kirk and ten colleagues unravel how a bacterial enzyme performs one of chemistry's rarer tricks: attaching a nitro group to an aromatic ring. The enzyme, a cytochrome P450 from the pathway that builds the antibiotic rufomycin, nitrates a tyrosine inside a five-piece peptide, and the details matter because the product feeds the fight against tuberculosis.

Test peptides, simulations, quantum-level modeling, and a fresh crystal structure of a sister enzyme converged on one actor: a histidine sitting inside the peptide substrate itself. Its presence is required for clean nitration. The protonation state of a key iron-oxygen intermediate appears to decide whether the reaction yields the wanted nitrated tyrosine or wasteful nitrate instead. Sequence differences between enzyme cousins and the peptide's own shape jointly tune the outcome. The authors say the mechanism explains the family's behavior and could guide engineered nitration chemistry.
pmc-1934936:
Winter, Vinegar, Nahal, and co-authors present a browser that turns large biology datasets into pictures researchers can explore. Microarrays and other high-throughput tools produce vast tables of gene activity. For scientists who are not computing specialists, such output can overwhelm rather than inform.

Their Electronic Fluorescent Pictograph browser shows data as visual displays that can be browsed and probed. Pictures help users spot patterns and form new hypotheses without deep coding skill. Tools that open big data to bench scientists widen who can take part in genome-era research.  Colour-coded displays let users compare tissues and conditions side by side.
pmc-2689936:
Howie, Donnelly, and Marchini present a flexible and accurate method for genotype imputation in large association studies. Imputation fills in unmeasured DNA variants by matching a person's measured variants to fully typed reference panels. Most studies then relied on the HapMap reference set.

Newer panels, typed densely on several platforms, were becoming available as the authors wrote. Their method was built to use such richer references well. Accurate filling-in lets studies compare results across different genotyping chips and boosts power to find variants linked to disease, without retesting every participant.
pmc-2835736:
Price, Dehal, and Arkin present FastTree 2, a tool for inferring family trees from very large sequence alignments. Their first FastTree could handle alignments with hundreds of thousands of sequences. Speed came with some loss of accuracy, which the new version aims to recover.

Improvements sharpen the tree search without sacrificing the ability to scale. Earlier versions relied heavily on simple neighbour swaps to refine trees. Better accuracy at the same scale matters for tracking fast-spreading microbes and for studies that compare thousands of species at once.  Microbial ecologists use it to track thousands of species in one alignment.
pmc-3276136:
Catchen, Amores, Hohenlohe, and co-authors present Stacks, software for building and genotyping genetic loci from short-read sequences. New sequencing gave chances to genotype individuals quickly and cheaply. Progress was hindered, though, by a lack of software to call tens of thousands of genotypes across hundreds of individuals automatically.

Stacks builds loci from scratch, without needing a reference genome, and scores each individual's variants. That opened population genetics for species never sequenced before. Ecologists and breeders use it to map traits, track parentage, and measure diversity in wild populations.  Fisheries and crop wild-relative studies both picked up the system quickly afterwards.
pmc-4330336:
Croucher, Page, Connor, and their colleagues presented Gubbins in 2015 for bacterial genome analysis. New sequencing tools made whole genome alignments common for evolution studies and outbreak work. Such data often contain stretches gained by horizontal transfer, where bacteria swap DNA directly.

Gubbins finds those recombinant stretches quickly and accounts for them when building family trees. Without that step, swapped DNA can distort the tree and hide the true pattern of spread. The tool handles large samples fast enough for routine outbreak use. Public health teams use it to trace how bacterial strains emerge and move between people.
pmc-5333436:
FitzGerald and Hurst reviewed implicit bias in healthcare professionals in 2017. Implicit biases are associations outside conscious awareness. They can tilt judgment against a person for traits that should not matter, such as race or gender.

The review weighs the studies on whether doctors and nurses show such bias toward patients. If doctors and nurses carry the same biases as the general public, care may differ by patient group without anyone intending it. The authors weigh study quality and what the findings mean for training and practice. Their synthesis informs efforts to make diagnosis and treatment more equal.
pmc-5993836:
Benjamin Saunders, Julius Sim, Tom Kingstone, and colleagues examined the idea of saturation in qualitative research in 2017. Saturation is widely taken to mean that new data would add nothing new. Funders and reviewers often demand it as a quality sign.

The authors show the term hides several different ideas that are often mixed up. They sort these into types and ask when each one fits a study design. Vague use lets weak sampling pass as rigorous. Clearer language would help researchers defend sample sizes honestly. The paper is now a common citation when methods sections mention saturation.
pmc-6249736:
Konstantinos Vasileiou, Julie Barnett, Susan Thorpe, and coauthors studied sample size in interview research in 2018. How many interviews are enough is a debated and practical question. Many tools promise to justify a number, but their logic often stays vague.

Reviewing past studies, the authors find that saturation is the most common defense, yet it is often claimed with little proof. Typical interview studies cluster in a modest range of sizes. The paper urges researchers to explain their reasoning in concrete terms. Reviewers and funders can use it to spot empty claims about sample adequacy.
pmc-6315036:
Maksim Kunitski, Nicolas Eicke, Pia Huber, and coauthors reported a quantum interference experiment in 2019. The double-slit experiment is the classic display of wave-particle duality. Interference appears when no record shows which path a particle took.

Working with the neon dimer under strong laser fields, the team watched photoelectrons interfere like waves from two slits. The molecule's two atoms act as the pair of slits. Careful measurement kept the which-way record hidden, so fringes survived. The result gives a clean atomic-scale test of a foundational quantum idea. The authors discuss what such interference means for telling which slit a particle passed through.
pmc-6450036:
Oscar Franzén, Li-Ming Gan, and Johan Björkegren built PanglaoDB for single-cell data browsing in 2019. Hundreds of single-cell RNA studies have been published across human and mouse tissues. Most sit in archives as raw files that few can easily open.

PanglaoDB processes those studies into a uniform form and serves them on the web. Users can search a gene and see which cell types use it, tissue by tissue. Curated marker lists help name clusters in new data. The resource turns scattered public data into a quick reference for cell-type questions.
pmc-6834636:
J Spencer Johnson, Daniel Spakowicz, Bo-Young Hong, and coauthors evaluated 16S gene sequencing for fine microbe identification in 2019. The 16S gene has anchored bacterial analysis for decades. Reading the full gene only recently became practical at scale.

Through computer simulations and real sequencing tests, the team judged how well species and strains can be told apart. Full-length reads do far better than the short fragments long in use. Some close relatives still blur together. The results guide labs choosing between cheap short surveys and richer full-gene studies. Mock communities with known members gave the team ground truth for judging each approach.
pmc-6919336:
Regina Guthold, Gretchen Stevens, Leanne Riley, and coauthors pooled data on teen physical activity in 2020. Activity brings many health gains for young people. The World Health Organization set a target to cut inactivity among teens by a set share within a decade.

Pooling hundreds of school-based surveys, the team finds most adolescents worldwide do not move enough. Girls are less active than boys in nearly every country. Trends barely improved over the study years. The authors call for urgent action in schools and city design, since adult habits often start in these years.
pmc-6954236:
Gommaar D'Hulst and colleagues reported how the oxygen sensor PHD1 controls muscle growth signaling in 2020. The mTORC1 pathway is a key regulator of muscle mass. How oxygen and nutrients tune it was not fully understood.

In mice lacking PHD1 in muscle, growth signaling faltered and muscle mass fell. The effect ran through stabilization of an enzyme that charges transfer RNA with leucine, not through the classic oxygen route. Leucine is itself a growth trigger, so the link closes a neat loop. The work reveals an unexpected way oxygen sensing shapes muscle.
pmc-7243036:
Annemarie Docherty and a large team of co-authors reported in 2020 on more than twenty thousand patients admitted to hospitals in the United Kingdom with COVID-19. Their prospective cohort study used a shared clinical protocol from an international respiratory infections consortium and the World Health Organization. The patients were enrolled during the fast growing first wave of the outbreak.

The authors describe who these patients were, what symptoms they arrived with, what other health problems they carried, and how their hospital stays unfolded. Because every site recorded the same details in the same way, the study gives one of the earliest clear pictures of severe COVID-19 in Britain. It helped doctors and planners judge what hospital care the pandemic would demand.
practical-phrenology-1836:
Silas Jones published his Practical Phrenology in Boston in 1836, from the house of Russell, Shattuck. Williams, sold by the principal booksellers in the United States, and entered for copyright in Massachusetts in 1835. The title page, worn in transmission, still shows its essentials plainly. Phrenology, the reading of character from the shape of the skull, was then sweeping America as a practical science of self-knowledge, and Jones wrote for the market it created.

Practical was the selling word: not the theory of Gall and Spurzheim in the abstract, but a manual for examining heads and drawing conclusions about talents, tempers, and callings. Books like Jones's taught parlor phrenology to thousands and filled the lecture halls where itinerant professors mapped bumps for a fee. Modern readers meet in it a complete, confident system that science later discarded entire, preserved at the height of its American vogue.
pushkin-captains-daughter-1836:
Alexander Pushkin published The Captain's Daughter in 1836, his perfect historical tale of Pugachev's rebellion in Russia. The tale tests young Pyotr Grinyov's honor in the Cossack rising of 1773 to 1775. Pushkin researched the rebellion in archives and on the ground, then distilled it into limpid prose fiction.

Grinyov, sent to a remote fort, is saved in a blizzard by a guide he rewards with a coat. That guide is Pugachev, who later spares the fort's survivors for the young officer's sake in war. Grinyov's love for Marya, the captain's daughter, drives rescues, trials, and a plea to the empress herself. Pugachev is drawn with respect, a rebel of charm, cruelty, and a strange rough honor in arms. The tale's economy and fairness set the pattern for the Russian historical novel.
qu-est-ce-que-la-phrenologie-ou-essai-su: Qu'est-ce que la phrénologie is a French work on phrenology. Its opening pages survive here only as a garbled library scan. Stamps of the Yale Medical Library are legible. A digitization notice is legible too. The title itself begins the book. The rest of the title page is broken type. It cannot be read with confidence. No author, place, or date is claimed for it.
remarks-on-the-erroneous-impressions-and:
H. G. Wright of Edinburgh published this twopenny pamphlet in 1836 against the hostility then felt toward science, and toward phrenology above all. His title names its target: false impressions and a spirit of hostility, chiefly among the religious public. John Anderson of Edinburgh and Longman of London sold the piece.

Wright opens by granting that phrenologists cannot answer every passing objection flung at their science. Yet when weightier arguments appear, he says, the world should be shown how little ground they have. The present moment, with feeling running high against the spread of scientific knowledge, seemed to him the right time to reply.
richardson-dictionary-1836:
Charles Richardson published his New Dictionary of the English Language in 1836, built on a bold new method. Where Johnson had defined words in his own phrases, Richardson built every entry out of quotations from real writers. The historical method, showing a word's life through its uses, here reached English lexicography a generation before the Oxford English Dictionary was planned.

Each word is followed by dated quotations that trace its meanings from early use toward Richardson's own day. The reader sees the definition emerge from evidence rather than from one man's authority. The book was the nineteenth century's great rival to Johnson, and its two heavy volumes sat in every serious library. Our words are explained here by the writers who used them best. Richardson's faith in quotation became the method of all later historical dictionaries.
selections-from-the-phrenological-journa:
Forty pieces from the first five volumes of a journal of phrenology, the study of mind through the skull's shape, make up this 1836 gathering. George Combe, James Simpson, and Dr. Andrew Combe wrote most of the pieces. The title page names them as the chief hands behind the work.

Phrenology drew wide crowds in its day, promising a science of character read from bumps on the head. Papers here argue that case in earnest terms for new readers. The book preserves an early, confident stage of a field that later science set aside, yet one that shaped talk on schools, prisons, and self-knowledge.
senior-outline-science-political-economy:
Senior published his Outline of the Science of Political Economy in 1836, the fullest system of his teaching. The book began as an encyclopaedia article and grew into the clearest classical treatise after Ricardo. Senior aimed to state what the science is, what it assumes, and what it may conclude.

He builds the whole doctrine from four plain premises about wealth and human desire, reasoning by strict logic. Value, wages, rent, and profit are drawn out in order, each term defined before it is used. Senior also separates the science from the art of policy, a distinction later economists prized. The Outline became the handbook of the deductive school and a model of economic reasoning for a generation. Mill's great treatise followed its plan more closely than Mill ever quite admitted.
soviet-constitution-1936:
The Soviet Union adopted a new constitution in 1936, with Joseph Stalin as its presiding name. Soviet spokesmen praised it as the most democratic constitution in the world. It arrived at the very height of the Great Terror, when show trials and arrests were sweeping the country. The gap between text and terror was the point its critics seized on.

On paper the charter guarantees work, rest, education, free speech, and the vote for every citizen, priests included. It describes a federation of republics with an elected Supreme Soviet at its head. In practice, the Communist Party's grip, mentioned in a single article, overrode every promise. Foreign admirers quoted the rights; Soviet citizens learned not to test them. The constitution of the purges' apogee remains the classic case of rights proclaimed by a state that honored none of them.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5036:
Calvin Coolidge gives six yearly addresses, from December 6, 1923, to December 4, 1928, parted by three stars. The first opens with a death. Since the close of the last Congress, the nation has lost President Harding, whose kindness, humanity, greatness, and character the world knew. He has left his mark on the past, Coolidge says, and made justice more sure and peace more fast.

The flood of honor paid as Harding was borne across the continent to rest at home showed the place he held in the people's hearts. Those who worked with him, Coolidge says, could not take up their office again without a pause to bind themselves anew to the country's service in his memory. Under a head for foreign affairs, he adds that peace reigns in all parts, to be kept by granting full justice to others and asking it of them.
statistics-of-phrenology-being-a-sketch-: The opening of this record holds no page of the book itself. What survives at the front is the standard wrapper Google Books placed on its public-domain scans. The notice explains that the volume was copied from a library shelf copy whose copyright had expired. The record is Statistics of Phrenology, dated 1836 in the record's title. Beyond the wrapper, nothing of the book's text is visible in this record, so its contents cannot be described from it.
texas-declaration-independence-1836:
The Texas Declaration of Independence was made by the delegates of the people of Texas in general convention at the town of Washington on March 2, 1836. It states the case for breaking from Mexico in a long chain of charges.

The delegates charge that Mexico's rule no longer guards life, liberty, or property, the ends for which rule exists. They say the federal republic of their sworn charter has been crushed into a central armed despotism ruled for army and priesthood. Petitions were spurned and the men who bore them thrown in cells. Readers get the founding paper of the Republic of Texas, cast in the style of the American declaration of 1776.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum:
Volume 3 in this second listing of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer covers chapters XVIII to XXIII, printed at Dublin in 1839. The contents promise detachment duty in an assize town, a day in Dublin, a night at Howth, a journey, and Calais. Chapter XVIII opens with Fitzgerald hiding in his room.

Fitzgerald fears to venture out, lest he be recognised and prosecuted for abduction, so no explanation of that morning's events will be needed from Harry. Harry keeps his own secret too. An order to march on detachment duty, which would usually make him miserable, arrives almost as a relief. Anyone who knows army life, he remarks, knows how unpleasant such a chance can be. The volume's numbering clashes with another record also called Volume 3, a defect worth noting. Within its own pages, Lever continues the episodic garrison tale toward Dublin and the Channel crossing.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Vol. 1, No. 36 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated July 15, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a premium list of books. A subscriber who secures one new subscription may choose any one of them. They are printed on extra laid paper, bound in red buckram with gilt top. The list names Andersen's Fairy Tales and Haggard's Allan Quatermain. It names Adam Bede and Black Beauty.
the-harmony-of-phrenology-with-scripture: The Harmony of Phrenology with Scripture, 1836. The biblical harmony. This book preserves that work. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
the-two-gentlemen-of-verona-pg2236: In this edition of Shakespeare's early comedy, Launce and his dog Crab steal the show from the two gentlemen's romantic tangle. Valentine, Proteus, and the ladies of Milan play out love's follies while the clown and his cur get the biggest laughs. Youthful, sunny, and full of charm.
tholosan-ut-magorum-et-maleficiorum-erro:
Claude Tholosan lays down the law on witches in his Latin tract of near 1436. Tholosan was a judge in the Dauphine, in the hills of France. His tract's name means on the false claims of mages and witches. It is one of the first to make a bold claim. Witches, it says, fly to a sabbath rite and make pacts with the Devil.

He writes from trials at his own bench. The claims here fed the great hunts that came next. The text, in Latin, is a root source of the hunts. Its cold tone chills.
timon-of-athens-pg1536: The great hater of mankind takes center stage in this edition of Shakespeare's bleakest play. Ruined by false friends, Timon flees Athens to curse the whole race from a cave, digging up gold only to find more reasons for scorn. Strange, savage, and oddly modern in its disgust.
tob-0036:
James McAndrew of the United States Air Force wrote the 1997 report that closed the service's Roswell file. Fifty years after debris was found in New Mexico in 1947, the report gives the official answer to the most famous flying saucer story of all.

The wreckage, it says, came from Project Mogul, a secret balloon train built to listen for Soviet atomic tests. The alien bodies of later tales are matched to crash-test dummies dropped in tests years afterward. Witness memory, stretched across decades, did the rest. Doubters were not persuaded, but the report stands as the government's fullest public account, document by document.
tob-10036:
William Ralph Inge delivered the lectures in Christian Mysticism as the Bampton Lectures at Oxford. Inge was an English theologian interested in what mystics claim to know directly about God. His study moves from the early church through the Middle Ages.

Along the way he examines leading mystics, defines terms that are often used loosely, and weighs where mystical claims hold up under criticism. V1 evidence calls the survey demanding but rewarding, and one that shaped a century of scholarship. Readers who want history and judgment together, rather than devotion alone, will find Inge a careful and sometimes stern guide.
tob-10236:
W. E. Soothill's English version of the Lotus Sutra follows the old Chinese text linked with Kumarajiva. Called the Lotus of the Wonderful Law, it is the most loved scripture of East Asian Buddhism. Its teaching comes through tales and scenes more than through dry argument.

A house on fire, a lost son who does not know his rich father, and a false city made for tired men all point one way. All beings, the sutra says, hold the seed of Buddhahood and can wake at last. That hope of a saved world for all made the book the heart of schools from Tiantai to Nichiren.
tob-10836:
King James VI of Scotland, later James I of England, wrote Daemonologie in 1597 after personally interrogating accused witches in the North Berwick trials. Cast as a dialogue, the treatise sets out to prove that witchcraft and demonology are real. James argues from Scripture, law, and reported cases.

Kinds of spirits, the devil's pacts, and how witches may be detected and punished all receive the king's attention. The book served as part legal manual, part theology, and helped fuel witch prosecutions on both sides of the Scottish border. Readers meet a learned monarch's mind on demons in his own words, chilling precisely because he was intelligent.
tob-13136:
Seven Hermetic laws for the practical occultist stand at the center of The Kybalion, credited to the anonymous Three Initiates. Mind rules matter, rhythms rise and fall, and every cause has its effect. The laws are presented as one connected system, not a miscellany of sayings, and as principles meant to be applied.

A century of New Thought readers has treated the slim volume as a working manual for mastering one's own mental world. Passages explain polarity, gender, and vibration as patterns running through nature and thought alike. Readers can finish it quickly, but its admirers tend to reread and annotate it for years.
tob-13336:
Lectures by Swami Vivekananda, the monk who carried Vedanta to the West, stand behind How to Be a Yogi. He taught that yoga is a practical discipline, not a set of beliefs. The book speaks to beginners who want instruction they can use.

It sets out the main yogas side by side: work done without selfish aim, devotion to God, control of the mind, and knowledge of the self. Each path suits a different temper, and all aim at the same freedom. As a teacher's handbook from the man who brought these ideas to America, it keeps the plain, direct manner of his talks.
tob-13736:
Annie Besant and C. W. Leadbeater claimed clairvoyant sight of thoughts themselves, and Thought-Forms publishes what they said they saw. Feelings, in their account, build colored forms in subtle matter around the thinker. Anger appears as scarlet spikes, devotion as rising blue forms, and music as elaborate structures.

Dozens of illustrations accompany the explanations, making the book as much picture gallery as text. Leadbeater and Besant presented their observations as research, with methods and cautions. Whether readers judge the work science or fantasy, its images shaped a century of New Age art and the very idea that emotions have visible auras and colors.
tob-4136:
Waite argued in The Secret Tradition in Freemasonry, volume one of 1911, that a hidden initiatory tradition runs behind the public life of the lodges. Rituals, grades, and symbols become, on his reading, the outer dress of an inner path toward divine union.

He pursues the claim through archives and rites with dogged learning. Other Masonic scholars hotly disputed his case, and the quarrel made the book famous. Waite writes as both insider and mystic, which is the source of its charm and its trouble. Verified from the 1919 edition, volume one made him Masonry's most debated scholar of his generation.
tob-4236:
John Burnet mapped the birth of Western philosophy in Early Greek Philosophy, here in its revised second edition of 1908. Thales, who said all is water, opens the line that runs through Heraclitus, Parmenides, and Empedocles to the Atomists. Burnet prints the surviving fragments in Greek and English.

His strong claim, that the Greeks invented scientific thought by asking how the world works without myth, shaped teaching for decades. Later scholars argue with Burnet often, which proves his place. Verified public-domain text supports the entry. For a standard, learned road into the Presocratics, Burnet's book still leads.
un-ga-res-3236:
Palestinian rights took a landmark turn in Resolution 3236, adopted by the General Assembly in 1974. The Assembly had heard the Palestine Liberation Organization, named in the text as the voice of the Palestinian people. It voices deep concern that no just fix to the Palestine problem had yet been found, and that the open sore still put world peace at risk.

The text states again the fixed rights of the Palestinian people in Palestine. Those rights are spelled out: self-rule free of outside meddling, and a national state of their own. The vote, passed 89 to 8, is still cited as the moment the UN put Palestinian statehood at the heart of its terms.
un-ga-res-36: Who gets in, and by what rules? Resolution 36 of the General Assembly, from November 1946, asks the Security Council to name a team to meet with an Assembly team on that question. The two teams were to draft entry rules both bodies could accept. The Assembly later named Australia, Cuba, India, Norway, and the Soviet Union to its side; the Council sent China, Brazil, and Poland.
un-ga-res-49-236:
Guatemala's new UN mission took the field under Resolution 49/236, passed in the fall of 1994. The Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala had been set up that September, for a first term of six months. It would check that the state and the rebel URNG kept the pledges of their rights deal. A December vote had asked the Secretary-General to keep backing the peace with his own staff as well.

The start and full spread of the mission across the land are welcomed. The help and joint work of both the state and the URNG are praised. A status deal between Guatemala and the Secretary-General, which set the mission's rights on the ground, had just been signed.
un-ga-res-a-69-36:
Central Asia's ban on nuclear arms is welcomed in Resolution A/69/36, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Five states of the region had signed a treaty that made their lands a zone free of nuclear weapons. The pact took force on 21 March 2009. The Assembly calls it a real step for the world ban on the spread of such arms, and a guard against atomic goods falling into the hands of terror groups.

The text also welcomes the signing, on 6 May 2014, of the treaty's protocol by the nuclear-armed states. They are called on to ratify it fast. Note is taken of talks among the five states. They met in Ashgabat in 2009 and in Almaty in 2014. Joint work to clean lands hurt by past atomic tests and mines is also noted.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 3236 (XXIX), adopted at the twenty-ninth session in 1974, is titled Question of Palestine. The Assembly heard the Palestine Liberation Organization as the voice of the Palestinian people. It voiced deep concern that no just settlement had been reached, while the problem still put world peace at risk.

The text restates the firm rights of the Palestinian people in Palestine. Above all, it restates self-rule free of outside meddling, and national freedom and sovereignty. It also restates the right of Palestinians driven from their homes and land to return. It calls on all states to back their fight to regain their rights. It asks the Secretary-General to deal with the Palestine Liberation Organization on the matter.

General Assembly Resolution 36, adopted on 19 November 1946 at the forty-ninth plenary meeting, is a brief procedural step on admissions. The Assembly asked the Security Council to name a committee to meet with an Assembly committee on procedure, so the two bodies could draft shared rules for admitting new members. A note in the text records the members later named to each side's committee.

General Assembly Resolution 49/236, adopted on 31 March 1995, renewed the human rights verification mission in Guatemala for six more months. The Assembly welcomed the mission's opening and full deployment. It welcomed its status agreement passed by Guatemala's Congress. It welcomed its director's report on the first three months of work.

Both the Government of Guatemala and the Unidad Revolucionaria Nacional Guatemalteca were called on to follow the mission's advice. They were called on to keep their promises under the Comprehensive Agreement on Human Rights. The Assembly also voiced concern that the peace talks had slowed in the second half of 1994, missing agreed target dates. It urged fresh drive toward a full peace package.

Resolution 69/36 of the General Assembly welcomes the Treaty on a Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone in Central Asia, in force since 21 March 2009. It welcomes the signing of its protocol by the nuclear-weapon states on 6 May 2014, calling for early ratification. The Assembly treats the treaty as a step for non-proliferation and regional security. It treats it as a step for keeping nuclear materials from terrorists. It notes the Central Asian states' consultative meetings. It notes their action plan on nuclear security and on dealing with radioactive contamination from uranium mining.
un-sc-res-1036:
Georgia and Abkhazia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1036, adopted on 12 January 1996. Georgia had held presidential elections in November 1995. The cease-fire broadly held, yet talks on a full settlement dragged on. Conditions in the Gali region had grown worse, with killings and rights abuses reported.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 12 July 1996. It condemns ethnic killings and demands that the Abkhaz side keep people under its control safe. Both sides must work with the observers and let them inspect heavy weapons stores. Refugees keep their right to return, and the Abkhaz side must stop blocking that return.
un-sc-res-1336:
A team that watched for sanctions-busting in Angola's civil war received more time on 23 January 2001. The team had been set up in 2000 to track how the UNITA rebel movement got around sanctions. Those sanctions, on arms and on diamonds, dated back to Resolution 864 of 1993. The team's final report was before the Council. Resolution 1336 was adopted unanimously.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council took note of the monitors' final report. It extended the team's mandate for three more months. The Secretary-General was told to reappoint up to five of the experts. The team had to send the sanctions committee a written follow-up by 19 April 2001. All states were called on to cooperate fully with the monitors. The work mattered because diamonds and arms kept UNITA's war alive, long after the Council had banned both trades.
un-sc-res-1436: One entry in the Council's numbered series is Resolution 1436, catalogued for 2002 by this library. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1536:
Afghanistan's assistance mission was renewed for the election year on 26 March 2004. The Loya Jirga had adopted a constitution on 4 January 2004. The Berlin conference was about to open, on 31 March, to renew the world's long-term pledge. Elections under the Bonn Agreement were the next great test.

The Council extended UNAMA for twelve more months from the day of adoption. It welcomed the Secretary-General's report of 23 March and the advice it carried. Security and donor support were named vital if the coming national elections were to be credible. Afghan authorities were urged to shape a vote open to all parts of the population. UNAMA and Kabul had to speed voter registration together. The Council welcomed the disarmament program's progress since October 2003. It also backed the national drug control strategy and pressed Kabul to apply it with force.
un-sc-res-1636:
Formal Council action on the killing of Rafiq Hariri arrived as Resolution 1636, adopted on 31 October 2005. A bomb in Beirut on 14 February 2005 killed the former Lebanese prime minister and twenty-two others. An international investigation pointed to joint Lebanese and Syrian official involvement. The inquiry was not finished, and some Syrian officials had misled investigators.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council orders travel bans and asset freezes on people the investigators name as suspects. A new committee will run the list of names. Syria must hand over suspects for questioning and cooperate fully and without conditions. The investigation's mandate runs to 15 December 2005, with reports due to the Council by then.
un-sc-res-1736: Resolution 1736, from 2006, is preserved here as a Security Council decision in official-record wording. English Wikisource is the transcription source. The entry gives the complete act: the preamble's account of the situation, then the numbered decisions. In the Council's world, those decisions are the unit of action, and each one is filed like this.
un-sc-res-1836:
UNMIL was extended with endorsed cuts on 29 September 2008. The Secretary-General's report of 15 August 2008 set out his advice. Liberia's government was improving governance and security and fighting corruption. Its first poverty reduction strategy, for 2008 to 2011, had been adopted. Police rebuilding and army restructuring moved forward. United Nations police advisers were still needed beside the national force.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate until 30 September 2009. It restated its plan to let the Secretary-General shift troops between UNMIL and the Côte d'Ivoire mission as needed. His advice for a reduction in the mission's military strength was endorsed. A change to the police element, with immediate effect, was endorsed as well. He would track progress against the mission's benchmarks and report. The Council planned to review his findings by 31 March 2009. Liberia's own forces would take a further step toward holding the country alone.
un-sc-res-1936:
Iraq's assistance mission was renewed on 5 August 2010. Security had improved through joint political and security work, the Council welcomed. Yet challenges to safety remained, and the gains had to be held by dialogue and national unity. All communities had to share in the political process. A fair answer on resources and on the disputed internal boundaries was still owed.

The Council extended UNAMI's mandate for twelve months. The special representative and the mission would keep advising and helping Iraq's people and government. Their work covered elections, dialogue, human rights, and the return of refugees. The safety of United Nations staff was named essential to the mission's work. Member states' contributions of staff, funds, and logistics were welcomed. The Secretary-General had to report to the Council every four months on the mission's progress. The Council meant to review the mandate again within twelve months.
un-sc-res-236:
Resolution 236 addressed the Israel-Syria ceasefire when the Council adopted it unanimously on 11 June 1967. The Six-Day War had just ended. A ceasefire was in force but reports of breaches kept coming. The Secretary-General had briefed the Council across four meetings.

The Council condemns each and every breach of the ceasefire. It says the halt bars any forward move by troops after the truce took hold. Any troops that pushed forward after 1630 GMT on 10 June must pull back to the ceasefire lines. Both sides must give the UN truce observers full freedom to work. The Secretary-General must keep probing and report back soon.
un-sc-res-36:
Indonesia's ceasefire of August 1947 had not fully taken hold by autumn. A consular commission reported that neither side had tried to agree on how to apply it. On 1 November 1947 the Security Council told the parties to consult at once. They could talk directly or through the Committee of Good Offices. Until they agreed, all hostile acts and incitement had to stop. The committee would help them reach a workable arrangement.

The consular commission and its military staff had to aid the committee. The Council also explained its August resolution. Force could not be used to extend control over land not held when the ceasefire began. That reading closed a loophole both sides had tested.
un-sc-res-736:
Security Council Resolution 736, adopted on January 29, 1992, recommended Kyrgyzstan for membership in the United Nations. Some older notes attach this number to Slovenia, but Slovenia's turn came later that spring under a different text. Kyrgyzstan, a mountain land in central Asia, had declared independence from the failing Soviet Union the previous August and sought quick entry to the world body.

The Assembly seated Kyrgyzstan on March 2, alongside several other former Soviet republics. The council's wording is the standard form for admissions. Read in sequence, these brief votes of early 1992 record the map of Eurasia being remade in peace, republic by republic, after the Soviet collapse.
un-sc-res-936: Filed in the official record under number 936, this Council resolution is catalogued with a 1994 date. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Georgia's frozen Abkhazia conflict is the subject of Resolution 1036, adopted on 12 January 1996. The 1994 Moscow ceasefire broadly held, watched by UNOMIG and the CIS peacekeeping force. Talks on a political settlement, including Abkhazia's status, were deadlocked. The Abkhaz authorities kept blocking refugee returns, and killings in the Gali region were reported. Georgia had held elections in November 1995.

The Council extends the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, to 12 July 1996. It calls on the parties, above all the Abkhaz side, to make substantive progress without delay and cooperate with the Secretary-General's efforts, assisted by Russia as facilitator and the OSCE. It demands the Abkhaz side speed up voluntary returns, starting with the Gali region, and guarantee the safety of those already back. It backs a concrete human rights programme for Abkhazia and asks for a report in three months.

Resolution 1336 is a UN Security Council extension of sanctions monitoring on Angola, adopted unanimously on 23 January 2001 under Chapter VII. Angola's long civil war was fueled by UNITA's defiance of sanctions, and a monitoring mechanism of experts had just delivered its final report on how the sanctions were being broken.

The resolution takes note of that report, promises it full consideration, and extends the monitors' mandate for three months, asking for an addendum by 19 April 2001. The Secretary-General is to reappoint up to five experts, and all states are called on to cooperate. The expert panels' naming-and-shaming reports were the Council's tool for squeezing UNITA's diamond and arms networks.

Togo, a narrow West African state, gained independence from France in April 1960. Its government quickly applied to join the United Nations. Resolution 136, adopted unanimously on 31 May 1960, took up that request. The Council had the application papers before it, filed as document S/4318.

The members recommended the Togolese Republic for membership. Final approval belonged to the General Assembly. It admitted Togo later that year, in the famous wave of new members. Seventeen states joined in 1960 alone. Most were newly free African nations. Their arrival changed the UN's balance. Debates tilted toward decolonization and development from then on.

Peaceful elections in May 2002, held with the mission's support, frame this Sierra Leone text of 24 September 2002. UNAMSIL's mandate is extended, and at the same time its drawdown begins. The Special Court for Sierra Leone had also just opened, though war in neighbouring Liberia still threatened the region.

The mandate is renewed for six months from 30 September 2002. The mission is directed to complete the first phases of the Secretary-General's plan, including cutting 4,500 troops within eight months, as Sierra Leone's own forces take on more responsibility. Extending state authority, controlling the diamond fields, and reintegrating former fighters remain central goals.

Resolution 1536, adopted on 26 March 2004, extends help to Afghanistan as it moves toward its first elections. A new constitution had been adopted that January, and a voter sign-up effort was under way. The Bonn Agreement set the path from interim rule to elected government. A Berlin conference on long-term support was about to open.

The Council extends the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, for twelve more months. It stresses that safety and donor support are vital for a believable vote and urges Afghans, including women and refugees, to take part in full. It welcomes headway in disarming armed factions since October 2003. It also presses action on the drug trade and asks UNAMA to keep backing human rights work and a fair court system.

The Hariri assassination investigation hardens into sanctions in Resolution 1636, adopted on 31 October 2005. The international investigation commission had reported converging evidence that Lebanese and Syrian officials were involved in the 14 February 2005 Beirut bombing that killed former Prime Minister Rafiq Hariri and 22 others. It found Syrian officials had misled investigators, while Lebanon asked that the commission's mandate be extended.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council sets up a committee to designate individuals suspected of involvement; those designated face a travel ban and asset freeze and must be made available for interview. It decides Syria must detain the Syrian officials and individuals the commission suspects and give the commission full, unconditional cooperation, including the right to choose where and how interviews happen. It insists Syria not interfere in Lebanon's affairs. The commission, extended to 15 December 2005, must report by then, sooner if Syria's cooperation falls short.

Troops move between the Burundi and Congo operations under this text of 22 December 2006. Fifty military observers serving under the Burundi operation's strength in Congo had watched the electoral process and were due to leave by the end of December. Fighting by militias and foreign armed groups in eastern Congo still threatened civilians.

The Secretary-General is authorized, from 1 January 2007 until the Congo mission's current mandate expires, to redeploy troops between the two missions as needed. The arrangement lets the United Nations shift scarce peacekeepers across the two neighbouring operations without new authorizations each time. Congolese citizens are praised again for their commitment to the democratic process shown in the 2006 elections.

Resolution 1836, adopted on 29 September 2008, extends the UN Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, while shrinking it. Liberia's government was fighting corruption, taking firmer control of its natural wealth, and working from its first national poverty plan. Police and army rebuilding had moved ahead, and ex-fighters were being settled back into civilian life, though courts and state authority still needed work.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends UNMIL until 30 September 2009. It approves cutting 1,460 more troops between October 2008 and March 2009 and merging four sectors into two. At the same time it adds 240 police staff for expert advice and rapid response. It asks for progress reports tied to clear benchmarks, plus long-range plans for a phased pullout that does not put Liberia's safety at risk.

Iraq's politics after the March 2010 parliamentary election frame Resolution 1936, adopted on 5 August 2010. The results had been certified, and the Council called on Iraq's leaders to form a broad government quickly. Safety had improved, though terrorism and sectarian violence remained. The UN Assistance Mission for Iraq, UNAMI, advised on elections, rights, and talks among Iraq's communities.

The Council extends UNAMI until 31 July 2011, keeping the mandate set in Resolution 1883. It asks Iraq's government and member states to keep giving UNAMI the safety cover and supply support it needs. It stresses aid for refugees and displaced people and the need for their safe, willing return. It notes Iraq's steps toward regaining the standing it held before Resolution 661 and urges it to close the Oil-for-Food programme with speed. Reports are due every four months.

The Six-Day War had just ended when Resolution 236 passed unanimously on 11 June 1967. Fighting between Israel and Syria had flared again after the ceasefire call. The Secretary-General briefed members across four straight meetings. His reports described troops moving and guns still firing on the Syrian front.

The Council condemned every violation of the ceasefire. It banned any forward military movement after the truce. Troops that had advanced past their lines after 4:30 p.m. Greenwich time on 10 June had to pull back. UN truce observers were promised full cooperation. They needed freedom of movement and working communications to watch the lines.

On 18 July 1973 the Council adopted Resolution 336, recommending the Commonwealth of the Bahamas for United Nations membership. The application, filed as document S/10966, had just been examined. The Bahamas had become independent from Britain eight days earlier, ending more than three centuries of colonial rule over the Atlantic archipelago.

The decision itself is one sentence long: the General Assembly is asked to admit the Bahamas. That formality was required, since no country joins the UN without the Council first recommending it. The resolution stands as the paper trail of a new Caribbean state stepping into the international system in the summer of 1973, alongside other former colonies doing the same.

A truce in Indonesia was failing in the fall of 1947. Consuls on the ground sent a report on 14 October. It said the August ceasefire call had not worked in full. Neither side had tried to meet the other halfway. Resolution 36 passed on 1 November 1947. Seven members voted yes. Poland voted no. Three held back.

Both sides were told to talk at once. They could meet face to face or use the UN good offices team. All acts against the truce had to stop. Lives and goods had to be kept safe. One key point was spelled out. Seizing land not held on 4 August broke the truce. If troops had to pull back, a pact on that had to come fast.

Two Central Asian bids moved side by side in January 1992, and this is one. On the twenty-ninth, the Council adopted Resolution 736 without a vote. The Republic of Kyrgyzstan had claimed freedom the August before. It made that freedom final as the Soviet Union dissolved in December. The new state was suddenly on its own.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Kyrgyzstan. Admission followed in early March 1992. Uzbekistan's bid was handled the same day, in a twin meeting. The paired steps form a small paper trail. They mark Central Asia's arrival on the world map as a set of sovereign states.

The top legal post at the Yugoslavia war crimes court was filled on 8 July 1994. Resolution 936 appoints the prosecutor of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. The man named in the text is Richard J. Goldstone. The Secretary-General had put his name forward. Under the court's statute, the Council appoints the prosecutor from that nomination. The appointment put a chief prosecutor in place to bring charges for grave crimes committed in the former Yugoslavia since 1991.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
The eighth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/5736, covers the force in its later years, in 1963 and 1964. UNEF had stood on the Egypt-Israel frontier since the Suez Crisis of 1956. By now its patrols were routine, and its presence was part of the region's uneasy calm.

The report reviews troop strength, costs, incidents along the line, and talks with the host state. It notes how a force sent for a crisis had become a long-term fixture. Within three years the force would be withdrawn at Egypt's demand, days before a new war.
worm-runir-danica-1636:
Ole Worm, a Danish scholar and doctor, gave the runes their first full learned study in this Latin book of 1636. The text here is from the 1651 second edition. Worm gathered rune stones and carved sticks from across the north lands. He was a keen hoarder of old things, and his rooms held a famed store of them.

He set out each rune sign, its name, and its sound, and matched them with old verse. He also drew the stones so readers far away could see the cuts for themselves. The book marks the birth of rune study as a true field of learning.
